3.q: Bronwen Hale, the commercial director, is explaining to Larkspur Rail's leadership team why Fair Fares will use agile ways of working. Release 1 is planned to go live in month four so that real usage data from passengers can shape Releases 2 and 3, and nobody yet knows how passengers will react to one-tap claims. Which explanation BEST describes the benefit of working this way on Fair Fares?
o: Adopting Scrum in all three teams will make delivery faster and raise the quality of the app, because the framework sets the pace of the work.
Agreeing the full feature list for all three releases at the start lets the board hold all three teams to a predictable, fixed scope for the ten months.
Short feedback loops from real passenger use let the teams adapt the later releases to what passengers need, cutting work on features of little value.
Releasing early means the board can extend the December end date if passengers ask for more features after Release 1 goes live.
3.w: Agile helps where work is complex and uncertain: rather than hunting for a perfect plan, teams stay adaptable, and feedback loops with continual improvement reduce waste and lead to better solutions (book 2.4, responsiveness and innovation). An early MVP release used by real passengers provides exactly that feedback for Releases 2 and 3.

n.0: This is the classic misconception the book warns against: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from the mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: Fixing every feature up front is the linear approach whose weakness is a lack of adaptability; with this much uncertainty agile favours staying able to pivot (book 2.2, 2.4).
n.3: The board has fixed the end date and budget, and PRINCE2 Agile keeps zero tolerance on time and cost; early feedback reshapes what is delivered, not when (Table 3.1).

3.q: In sprint 3 of stage 2, the Coinbridge Payments developers stop joining the daily stand-ups they share with the app team. Instead they post short written updates when they have time, and two integration problems come to light a week late. Owen Thackeray, the app team's Scrum master, asks how to respond. Which action would restore the agile mindset characteristic that is lacking?
o: Agree with both teams that everyone joins the joint stand-ups, and keep blockers and integration work visible on a shared board.
Let the Coinbridge developers keep posting written updates, and ask Rhys Pengelly to summarize them for the app team every Friday.
Ask Gemma Lowther to remind her developers that the fixed-price contract requires them to deliver the integration on time.
Hold a separate weekly integration meeting for the two team leads, so that the developers can concentrate on building.
3.w: The missing characteristic is transparency and rich communication: information should flow openly, through regular meetings and visible work status, so that obstacles are shared early and without fear (book 2.6.2). Bringing both teams back into the shared stand-up and making blockers visible restores it.

n.1: A weekly summary passed on by the project manager keeps information slow and filtered; it does not restore open, timely and rich communication between the teams (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Contract pressure does nothing to rebuild the open sharing of progress and obstacles that the teams have lost; the gap is in mindset, not in the contract (book 2.6.2).
n.3: This narrows the flow of information to two people and makes it less frequent, which is the opposite of transparency and rich communication across the teams (book 2.6.2).

3.q: During initiation, the Fair Fares project board sets zero tolerance on time and cost for every level of plan but allows the Should have and Could have stories in each release to be flexed. Rhys Pengelly, the project manager, may reprioritize those stories with the product owners without asking the board, and must escalate if the Must haves for a release are forecast to be missed. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board authorizes the work release by release and reviews each one at a stage boundary.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the board has stated who may reprioritize the stories in each team.
Focus on products, because the Must have, Should have and Could have stories describe the products to be delivered.
Manage by exception, because tolerances let the board delegate day-to-day decisions and hear of a forecast breach.
3.w: Manage by exception sets tolerances for the performance aspects and delegates authority within them, with escalation when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. In agile it allows tolerance on what is delivered while restricting time and cost, which empowers teams within control (book 5.2.1.5, Table 5.1).

n.0: Stage-by-stage authorization is not what is described; the board is setting tolerances and the escalation point for flexing scope (book 5.2.1.4, 5.2.1.5).
n.1: Roles are mentioned, but the mechanism is delegated authority within set tolerances with escalation on a forecast breach, which is manage by exception (book 5.2.1.5).
n.2: Prioritized stories make flexing possible, but the decision being made is about tolerances and delegation, not about defining products (book 5.2.1.6, Table 5.1).

3.q: At the project canvas workshop, Bronwen Hale says Fair Fares must at least reach the contract level of 80% of eligible app journeys receiving compensation automatically, to avoid the penalties from January. Any level above 80% would be welcome but is not required. Which performance aspect is she describing, and how should PRINCE2 Agile treat it?
o: Scope, fixed for the Must have stories that produce the 80% level and flexed for the Should and Could haves.
Benefits, fixed at the minimum viable level of 80% and flexed for any improvement above it.
Quality, fixed for the acceptance criteria of the matching model and flexed for the look of the screens.
Sustainability, fixed for the minimum contract criteria and flexed above those criteria.
3.w: A measurable improvement with a minimum the business must reach and room for more is the benefits aspect. PRINCE2 Agile fixes benefits at minimum viability and flexes them above it (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

n.0: Scope is what will and will not be delivered (the stories); the 80% is a measurable improvement the business expects, which is a benefit (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Quality covers the characteristics that make products fit for purpose; a target share of compensated journeys is a business improvement, not a product characteristic (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Sustainability concerns the project's impact on the wider environment; the compensation level is a measurable business improvement, so it is the benefits aspect (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

3.q: Forty customer relations staff will join sprint reviews and test the new claim screens during stage 2. Apart from IT, few Larkspur staff have worked in an agile way, and Yusuf Bello reports that his team is unsure what is expected of them. Priyanka Desai, the agile lead, is asked how to raise their agile maturity. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to work?
o: Send each member of staff a guide to Scrum events and invite them to ask the app team when anything is unclear.
Introduce a digital backlog tool to customer relations first, so that staff can see the claim stories on screen before any coaching starts.
Coach Yusuf Bello and his supervisors in depth, and ask them to pass the new ways of working on to their staff.
Combine practical training with on-the-job coaching in real sprint reviews, set out in a training and coaching plan for the stages.
3.w: Agile maturity grows when people receive theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change, so that as many people as possible understand what is changing and why (book 2.7.3).

n.0: Informing people and leaving them to fend for themselves undermines the change and breeds frustration, a leading cause of resistance (book 2.7.3).
n.1: Tools before knowledge and skills do not build maturity; people first need to understand how the change applies to their work through training and coaching (book 2.7.3).
n.2: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why; coaching a few managers and relying on cascade leaves most staff without practical support (book 2.7.3).

3.q: At a board meeting, Dominic Faraday asks why Fair Fares needs organizational change management when the app will do most of the work of paying compensation. Yusuf Bello's 40 staff will move from checking claims by hand to handling unusual cases and possible fraud. Which explanation BEST answers Dominic's question?
o: OCM is a supplier activity that Coinbridge Payments should cover under its fixed-price contract, as its payment service drives the change.
OCM replaces the communication management approach, so that one change plan can hold every message to staff and passengers.
OCM is needed to agree new pay terms with customer relations staff before go-live, as financial reward is what makes a change stick.
The benefits rely on staff adopting new ways of working, so OCM plans the move to the target state and evolves the culture so it lasts.
3.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to a target state (book 4.2.1). Fair Fares only realizes its benefits if customer relations staff work differently, and the change management approach should consider how the culture evolves so changes are not rolled back.

n.0: OCM is how Larkspur itself moves from its current to its target state; it cannot be handed to the payment supplier, whose contract covers building the payment feature (book 4.2.1).
n.1: The communication management approach remains a separate management approach; OCM does not replace it, though communication is one input to how the change is managed (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.2: The book points to evolving the culture, not money, compliance or communication alone, as the way to stop changes being rolled back (book 4.2.1).

3.q: Matteo Ricci wants passengers to trust the one-tap claim and, later, payments made without a claim, so that use of the app grows quickly after each release. He asks who should be engaged as a key influencer to shape how regular passengers see the change. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited?
o: Nigel Ormsby, because as passenger panel chair and a daily commuter he has a network and credibility among regular passengers.
Gemma Lowther, because Coinbridge Payments runs the card payments that passengers will receive under the new service.
Bronwen Hale, because as commercial director she holds the budget for customer-facing services and received the mandate for Fair Fares.
Hollie Brennan, because she checks the stories against their acceptance criteria and knows how the claim screens behave.
3.w: Key influencers are people who, through their network, can shape the perception of the majority affected by a change and so most influence adoption and benefits (book 4.2.2). Among regular passengers, the panel chair who commutes daily has that reach; seniority, technical skill or supplier status do not provide it.

n.1: Gemma commits the supplier's staff and owns its contract; she has no network among passengers through which to shape their view of the change (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Seniority and budget make Bronwen a natural project executive, but they do not give her influence over how regular passengers perceive the change (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Technical knowledge of the screens does not make Hollie someone passengers listen to; a key influencer shapes the majority's perception through a network (book 4.2.2).

3.q: In stage 3, the Coinbridge Payments team works from its own offices in another city and follows its own company's ways of working. Its developers are unsure which decisions about the payment screens they can take themselves and which need Larkspur's agreement, and several small questions have waited days for an answer. What should Rhys Pengelly do to lead this cross-organization team MOST effectively?
o: Ask the Coinbridge developers to send every design question to him, so that he can decide each one quickly for both organizations.
Agree clear decision boundaries with Gemma Lowther and the product owners, such as a delegation matrix, for the Coinbridge developers.
Leave each design decision to Coinbridge, as the fixed-price contract makes the supplier responsible for the design of its work.
Require the Coinbridge team to move into Larkspur's offices for the rest of the project, so that questions can be answered face to face.
3.w: When teams work across organizations and cultures, PRINCE2 Agile advises setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that shows what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3). This lets the Coinbridge developers act quickly within agreed limits.

n.0: Routing every question through the project manager creates a bottleneck and bypasses the product owners; it removes self-management instead of setting boundaries for it (book 4.3.1, 7.3.1).
n.2: Without agreed boundaries, decisions affecting Larkspur's passengers would be made by the supplier alone; the guidance is to define what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1).
n.3: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer; teams across organizations and locations need clear boundaries and planned ways of working together (book 4.3.1, 4.3.3).

3.q: From stage 2, the app team works in Larkspur's head office three days a week, the data team works fully remotely, and the Coinbridge team is based in another city. Fatima Zahra says her team feels cut off and hears about decisions late. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to improve communication across this hybrid set-up?
o: Ask each team to send a weekly written status report to Rhys Pengelly, who will circulate a combined summary to all three teams each Monday.
Require all three teams to work at Larkspur's head office five days a week until Release 3 is live, so questions are answered in person.
Agree how information flows between teams, hold in-person days for key people around planning and reviews, and allow informal time online.
Send the same monthly project newsletter to all three teams, so that everyone receives identical messages at the same time.
3.w: Remote and hybrid teams need a more deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together. Synchronized co-location days for key people help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3, 4.4).

n.0: Periodic reports are not enough on their own and can be biased; they also keep the flow one-way rather than building the relationships a hybrid set-up needs (book 4.4).
n.1: Mandating co-location is not the effective response; hybrid and remote teams need a deliberate, structured approach to working together (book 4.3.3).
n.3: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be two-way and tailored to the groups involved (book 4.4).

3.q: Before stage 2, the app team realizes that none of its members has tested an app with a screen reader, although about 12% of Larkspur's passengers have told it they have a disability or long-term condition. Owen Thackeray wants the team to close this gap without delaying Release 1. Which action follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on building agile teams?
o: Ask Sasha Ellery to move the accessibility stories out of Release 1 until a team member has completed an external course.
Help the team build a skill matrix of current and planned skills, with a training plan for accessibility testing on the team dashboard.
Offer a cash bonus to the first developer who gains an accessibility certificate, to reward the individual effort this will need.
Ask Rhys Pengelly to assign the accessibility testing to one named developer and record the duty in that person's written role description.
3.w: Building agile teams includes empowering them with training plans: the team skill matrix shows current and planned skills and the gaps, and visual management on the team dashboard keeps progress transparent (book 4.5, 7.4.1).

n.0: The app must meet accessibility standards, so deferring the work avoids the gap rather than building the team's capability (book 4.5).
n.2: Value-based incentives in the book are peer-assessed rewards for behaviour that models agile values, balanced with intangible motivators; a race between individuals does not build the team (book 4.5).
n.3: Assigning the work from above sidesteps the team's own planning and leaves a single point of failure; the guidance is to empower the team through training plans (book 4.5).

3.q: At the starting up workshop, Yusuf Bello warns that paying compensation without a claim could make it easier for people to obtain payments they are not owed. Nothing of this kind has happened yet, but he wants the concern managed throughout the project. Which practice is designed to handle this concern, and why?
o: Issues, because it collects and assesses events that are causing a deviation from what has been agreed.
Risk, because it identifies, assesses and controls uncertain events that could affect the project's objectives.
Quality, because it defines the users' requirements and the acceptance criteria the payment feature must meet.
Business case, because it judges whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable.
3.w: The risk practice identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty so that the project is more likely to meet its objectives; it answers 'what if something unexpected happens, and how do we respond?' (book 10.1). A possible rise in fraud has not happened, so it is a risk to be managed, not an issue.

n.0: The issues practice deals with events that have happened or deviations from the baseline; possible future fraud is an uncertainty, not yet an issue (book 11.1).
n.2: Quality documents what users require and how it will be met; Yusuf's concern is an uncertain future event, which the risk practice handles (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: The business case practice keeps the justification under review, and a major risk may appear on the canvas, but identifying, assessing and controlling the uncertainty is the risk practice (book 6.1, 10.1).

3.q: In starting up a project, Bronwen Hale leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate. Release 1, which detects delays and pre-fills a claim for one-tap confirmation, has to be live by the end of month four so that usage data can guide Releases 2 and 3. How should Release 1 be reflected in the project canvas?
o: Show Release 1 as the first benefit of the project, measured by the number of new features passengers can use.
Leave Release 1 out of the canvas and describe it in the team plan that the app team writes for its first sprint.
Record Release 1 as a Could have in the scope section, so that it can be dropped if the budget comes under pressure.
Identify Release 1 as the minimum viable product, so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late.
3.w: Where an MVP is used, the project canvas should identify it so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late (book 6.3.2). Release 1 is described as the MVP and is time-critical because its usage data guides the later releases.

n.0: Features are outputs, not benefits; a benefit is a measurable improvement such as the share of eligible journeys compensated (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.1: A team plan is a detailed plan for the next iteration; the canvas itself should identify the MVP so that a forecast delay can be escalated (book 6.3.2, 8.3.2).
n.2: Release 1 is the MVP whose usage data guides Releases 2 and 3; treating it as a Could have would let the core of the project be dropped, and cost has zero tolerance in any case (book 6.3.2, Table 3.1).

3.q: During initiation, Matteo Ricci wants personas to help the teams understand what different passengers need from Fair Fares. A marketing analyst offers eleven profiles based on age band, income and ticket type, already written from survey data. Which approach to personas follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Write up to five fictional, needs-based personas, such as a commuter who uses a screen reader, in a workshop with team members.
Adopt the eleven profiles as written, because survey data on age, income and ticket type gives the most reliable view of passengers.
Build one persona for each member of the passenger panel, using their real names, so that the teams can test directly with them.
Ask the analyst to merge the profiles into five demographic groups and send them to the teams before the first sprint.
3.w: Personas help identify and articulate benefits for users. PRINCE2 Agile advises writing them in a cross-functional workshop with development team members, keeping them fictional, basing them on needs rather than demographics, and using no more than five for new products or pilots (book 6.4.1).

n.1: Demographics such as age and income no longer predict shared needs, and eleven personas is more than the five the book suggests for new products (book 6.4.1).
n.2: Personas should be fictional, which widens the room for innovation, so real panel members' names and profiles should not be used; one persona for each of the panel's 30 members would also be far above the suggested maximum of five (book 6.4.1).
n.3: The number is right, but the personas would still rest on demographics and be written by one person rather than in a cross-functional workshop with team members (book 6.4.1).

3.q: During initiation, Bronwen Hale refines the project canvas. Under expected benefits she lists 'a new compensation feature in the Larkspur app', 'the delay matching model' and 'personalized journey alerts'. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the canvas has to show the main features of the project product so that the board can see what will be delivered.
Yes, because each item can be released early, which lets the benefits management approach plan for early benefits.
No, because these are outputs; the benefits should be measurable improvements, such as the share of eligible journeys compensated.
No, because benefits belong in the benefits management approach and should be left out of the project canvas.
3.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome; an output such as a feature or a model is never a benefit (Glossary, book 6.3.2). The canvas benefits section should list expected, measurable benefits with tolerance, for example the proportion of eligible journeys compensated or fewer staff hours spent checking claims.

n.0: The canvas does show the project product and main features, but in its scope section; listing them as benefits confuses outputs with benefits (book 6.3.2).
n.1: Frequent releases do enable earlier benefits, but that does not turn the released items into benefits; they remain outputs (book 6.3.2).
n.3: The project canvas does include benefits, expected and measurable with tolerance; the benefits management approach covers how they will be managed and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

3.q: During initiation, Rhys Pengelly and Gemma Lowther agree how the work under Coinbridge's fixed-price contract will support agile delivery: a stable Coinbridge team with a set cost per sprint, an agreed definition of the minimum viable product, and the steps for a formal variation if the supplier's scope changes. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure.
In the role descriptions for the Coinbridge team.
In the commercial management approach.
In the quality management approach.
3.w: The commercial management approach describes how procurement and contracts will support agile product development, for example fixed teams and costs per iteration, a definition of the MVP and tolerances, and an agreed Definition of Done (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: This shows who is involved, how they relate and arrangements such as co-location or remote working; it does not hold procurement and contract terms (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).
n.1: Role descriptions set out each role's responsibilities; the contract model, costs per sprint and variation steps belong elsewhere (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The quality management approach records quality techniques, standards and testing methods, not how the supplier contract supports agile delivery (book 9.3.2).

3.q: Fair Fares has three delivery teams: the in-house app team, the Coinbridge Payments team and the in-house data team. Rhys Pengelly is drafting the project management team structure and wants it to follow PRINCE2 Agile guidance for a project with several teams. Which structure should he propose?
o: One project manager, one chief product owner setting priorities across the teams, and a product owner for each team.
A project manager for each team, with Rhys coordinating the other two and reporting on all three to the project board.
One product owner, Sasha Ellery, prioritizing every story for all three teams, with no chief product owner role.
One project manager who also acts as product owner for all three teams, with a team coach working in each team.
3.w: With multiple teams, PRINCE2 Agile keeps one project manager, possibly several product owners (typically one per team), and a chief product owner who sets priorities across the teams; team coaches work with one or two teams (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

n.1: With several teams PRINCE2 Agile keeps one project manager; the extra roles appear at team level as product owners (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).
n.2: Each team has its own product owner, and a chief product owner sets priorities across teams; one PO for three teams leaves no cross-team user representation (book 7.3.1).
n.3: The project manager has authority over the product owners and agrees work packages with them, so combining the PM with every PO role removes that structure (book 7.3.1).

3.q: Early in stage 2, Rhys Pengelly, who is used to traditional projects, starts assigning daily tasks directly to individual developers in the app and data teams and asks them to report to him each evening. The product owners hear of the changes afterwards. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager runs the project day to day for the board and has to keep each stage within its tolerances.
Yes, because the project manager acts as a servant leader, linking the governance roles with the delivery teams.
No, because daily tasks should be set by the project board through the release map for each stage.
No, because the project manager should agree work with the product owners, who direct their own team members.
3.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, and the product owner, a version of the team manager, is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members. Work is agreed between the PM and the PO as sets of user stories (book 7.3.1).

n.0: This describes the project manager's role correctly, but day-to-day control is exercised by agreeing work packages with the product owners, not by directing developers (book 7.3.1).
n.1: A servant leader supports and enables the teams; assigning their daily tasks and demanding evening reports is the opposite of that stance (Table 7.2).
n.2: The board works at stage level through the release map and tolerances; it does not plan daily tasks, which the team plans for its iteration (book 8.3.2).

3.q: The project board needs someone to represent the user community, own the project backlog and set priorities across the app, Coinbridge and data teams, for example making sure the claim and payment screens follow one consistent style. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the chief product owner role?
o: Sasha Ellery, senior product manager.
Matteo Ricci, head of digital products.
Bronwen Hale, commercial director.
Nigel Ormsby, chair of the passenger panel.
3.w: The chief product owner represents the user community, owns the project backlog, keeps it aligned with the team product backlogs and sets priorities across teams (book Table 7.2). Matteo sets the direction for all digital channels and already works with users and the passenger panel.

n.0: Sasha has prioritized the app team's stories for years, which suits the product owner role for that one team; the CPO prioritizes across all teams (Table 7.2).
n.2: Bronwen received the mandate and holds the budget, which fits the project executive role, accountable for the project, rather than the user-side CPO role (Table 7.2).
n.3: Nigel is a valuable source of passenger feedback and influence, but he advises Larkspur from outside as a passenger; he does not set the direction of its digital channels or prioritize work across the teams (Table 7.2).

3.q: Dominic Faraday, a board member, keeps asking for a Gantt chart and long written reports, and other senior managers outside IT are unsure how agile delivery fits Larkspur's governance. The board wants someone to coach its members, support Rhys Pengelly and remove organization-level blockers to agile working. Who in the scenario is BEST suited to the agile coach role?
o: Owen Thackeray, Scrum master for the app team.
Rhys Pengelly, project manager.
Matteo Ricci, head of digital products.
Priyanka Desai, agile lead in IT.
3.w: The agile coach mentors and facilitates across the organization, removes systemic blockers to agile adoption, such as a board member resisting dashboards, and supports the board, project assurance and the project manager with expert agile knowledge (book Table 7.2). Priyanka has coached departments and senior managers.

n.0: A Scrum master fits the team coach role, working closely with one or two teams on self-management, not coaching the board and removing organization-wide blockers (Table 7.2).
n.1: Rhys is new to agile delivery and is himself someone the agile coach should support; the PM role runs the project day to day (Table 7.2).
n.2: Matteo's user focus and authority over digital channels suit the chief product owner role, not mentoring leaders in agile ways of working (Table 7.2).

3.q: In stage 2, Rhys Pengelly needs to forecast which Release 1 stories the app team can complete by the end of month four. The app team's velocity has ranged from 18 to 34 story points per sprint over its last six sprints, while the Coinbridge team reports a steady 40 points per sprint. How should Rhys forecast the app team's progress?
o: Use the Coinbridge team's steady 40 points per sprint, as it is the more reliable figure and story points are shared across teams.
Use the app team's own average velocity from recent sprints, and update the forecast after each sprint as actual figures come in.
Use the app team's highest figure of 34 points, so that the forecast shows what the team can achieve when it is stretched.
Ask the app team to estimate every Release 1 task in hours now and build a fixed plan from those estimates for the release.
3.w: PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism: start the work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that rate, using the team's own velocity rather than another team's (book 8.3). Velocity is an average rate per timebox and is refined as each sprint adds actual data.

n.0: Velocity should come from the team doing the work; story points are relative to each team, so another team's rate cannot forecast the app team (book 8.3).
n.2: Picking the best sprint produces an optimistic target, not an empirical forecast; velocity is an average rate refined as each sprint adds data (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: Predicting all the work in detail up front is rationalism; PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism, measuring the actual rate of work and forecasting from it (book 8.3).

3.q: In the project initiation workshop, the three teams need to break the Fair Fares epics into user stories, group the stories into the three releases and show that payment to the card in Release 2 depends on the matching model. Rhys Pengelly had started a product breakdown structure. Which technique does PRINCE2 Agile recommend for this?
o: Build a user story map from the passengers' activities and turn it into a release map showing the releases and dependencies.
Finish the product breakdown structure first, then turn it into a Gantt chart listing each team's tasks for the ten months.
Draw a cumulative flow diagram of the epics, so that the teams can see which stories belong in which release.
Ask each team to write a team plan covering all its sprints, then combine the three team plans into the project plan.
3.w: PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, built from user activities and broken into stories. Turning the story map into a release map groups the stories into releases and defines the interdependencies (book 8.3.1, 8.3.1.1).

n.1: The book recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, and a ten-month task list is not how agile plans are built (book 8.3.1).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram tracks work items in each workflow state over time to reveal bottlenecks; it does not group stories into releases (book 12.4.2).
n.3: A team plan is a detailed plan for the next iteration, produced when a work package is accepted, not a long-range plan for every sprint (book 8.3.2).

3.q: To satisfy Dominic Faraday, Rhys Pengelly spends the first two weeks of initiation building a detailed Gantt chart that lists every task for all three teams in every sprint up to December. He asks the teams to follow it and to report any task that slips. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a full baseline of tasks lets the board judge progress against an agreed schedule at each stage boundary.
Yes, because time and cost have zero tolerance, so each task has to be fixed in advance to protect the end date.
No, because task-level planning should be done by each team for the next sprint, under a high-level release map.
No, because a Gantt chart should be prepared by project support rather than by the project manager.
3.w: Planning in PRINCE2 Agile is done just in time: a high-level release map at stage boundaries, and task-level planning for the next iteration in managing product delivery, produced by the team in its team plan (book 8.3, 8.3.2).

n.0: Stage boundaries use a high-level release map; a ten-month task baseline cannot hold when the work is uncertain and would be judged on activity rather than delivered value (book 8.3).
n.1: Zero tolerance on time and cost is protected by flexing lower-priority scope, not by fixing every task in advance (Table 3.1, 8.3).
n.3: Who draws the chart is not the problem; the problem is planning every task months ahead instead of just in time (book 8.3).

3.q: At the end of sprint 4, the app team says the 'confirm claim with one tap' story is almost done. The screens work, but the screen reader checks in the team's Definition of Done have not been run. Hollie Brennan, the test automation engineer, asks how the story should be reported. How should the team treat it?
o: Report it as not done and return it to the product backlog, so that Sasha Ellery can reprioritize the remaining work.
Count it as done for the sprint review, as the screens work, and add the screen reader checks as a new story.
Show it as 90% complete on the team dashboard and give it part of its story points in the velocity figure.
Remove the screen reader checks from the Definition of Done for Release 1, so that the story can be accepted now.
3.w: The Definition of Done is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be complete. An item is either done or not done, with no 'almost done'; unfinished work returns to the backlog for reprioritization (book 9.3.2.2).

n.1: A partly done story may be split only so that the part reported as done meets the Definition of Done; here the screens themselves have not passed the DoD's screen reader checks, so counting them as done hides incomplete work (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: There is no 'almost done' under a Definition of Done: an item is done or not done, and partial credit distorts velocity (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: The app must meet accessibility standards; weakening the team's agreed DoD to pass a story undermines the quality the passengers need (book 9.3.2.2).

3.q: The app team reports that the Larkspur app carries a large amount of technical debt from a rushed redesign two years ago, and that it is slowing work on the claim screens. Sasha Ellery asks how the debt should be handled during Fair Fares. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Pause feature work for two months while the app is rewritten, then start the Release 1 stories once the code has been rebuilt.
Defer work on the debt until Release 3 is live, because refactoring changes how the app behaves for passengers and adds risk before the deadline.
Make the debt visible, set a tolerance for it and plan refactoring into sprints, raising an exception if it is forecast to exceed that.
Record the debt as a Won't have in the product backlog, so that it no longer counts against the team's velocity.
3.w: Technical debt is work owed before a job is truly complete, and it accrues interest. PRINCE2 Agile allows tolerances to be set on it, with an exception if it is forecast to become too significant; refactoring improves internal structure without changing external behaviour (book 9.4.1, 9.4.2).

n.0: A two-month pause would put the fixed Release 1 date and the December end date at risk; the debt should be managed alongside delivery (Table 3.1, 9.4.2).
n.1: Refactoring changes internal structure without changing external behaviour, and leaving debt to grow lets its interest slow every later release (book 9.4.1, 9.4.2).
n.3: Labelling the debt Won't have hides work that is still owed; technical debt should be visible and controlled with tolerances (book 9.4.2).

3.q: During initiation, Rhys Pengelly drafts the quality management approach. It records Larkspur's accessibility standards, the app team's automated testing, the testing methods Coinbridge uses for its payment work, and how the passenger panel will try each release before it goes live. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because agile ways of working and agile testing methods, including suppliers', should be recorded in the approach.
Yes, because recording the testing methods in the approach removes the need for a Definition of Done in each team.
No, because Coinbridge's testing methods belong in its contract and should be kept out of Larkspur's approach.
No, because user testing by the passenger panel should be recorded in the quality register, not in the approach.
3.w: The quality management approach sets out quality techniques, standards, roles and responsibilities. Agile ways of working must be incorporated, documented and assured in it, and agile testing methods, including those of suppliers, should be recorded there (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1).

n.1: The approach and the team Definition of Done do different jobs; each team still needs its own DoD, linked from its product backlog (book 8.3.2.1, 9.3.2.2).
n.2: The book says agile testing methods, including suppliers', should be recorded in the quality management approach (book 9.3.2).
n.3: The quality register records each planned and completed quality activity and its result, but the approach is where the methods and who is involved are described (book 9.3.2).

3.q: In the project initiation workshop, the participants assess the Fair Fares Agilometer. Gemma Lowther confirms that Coinbridge's fixed-price contract was signed before the project started and that any change to its scope will need a formal variation. Which Agilometer slider does this MOST directly affect?
o: Level of collaboration.
Ease of communication.
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally.
Advantageous environmental conditions.
3.w: The 'advantageous environmental conditions' slider assesses whether the overall working environment supports agile, including contracts that do not inhibit agile working (book 10.3.2.2). A fixed-price contract needing formal variations for any scope change pulls this slider down.

n.0: Collaboration concerns how closely the parties work together day to day; the contract terms are part of the wider working environment (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: This slider is about how easily all parties can communicate; a contract variation clause does not change that directly (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: This slider concerns how easily benefit can be delivered through regular partial deliveries; the contract's terms fall under environmental conditions (book 10.3.2.2).

3.q: At a team planning workshop, the Coinbridge team and its product owner agree two responses to the risk that payments made without a claim attract fraud: a check that the card being paid matches the ticket purchase, and a daily limit per account. Both responses need development work in the coming sprints. How should these responses be managed?
o: Add them to the product backlog with the user stories, prioritized alongside them, and keep the risk in the risk register.
Keep them in the risk register and ask the team to fit the work in once its sprint commitments are complete.
Record them in the Agilometer under level of collaboration, so that the board can track them at each agile enablement workshop.
Raise an exception report to the board, as responses to fraud fall outside the tolerances given to the team.
3.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds risk responses and user stories together, so that response work is prioritized and planned like any other item (book 10.4.1). The risk itself stays recorded in the risk register (Table 10.1).

n.1: Response work kept outside the backlog is not prioritized or planned and may never be done; the book puts it in a risk-adjusted product backlog (book 10.4.1).
n.2: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working itself; it is not where responses to a product risk such as fraud are planned (book 10.3.2).
n.3: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; planning risk responses is normal work within the team's delegated authority (Table 12.1).

3.q: Rhys Pengelly runs a full risk workshop during initiation and records the results in the risk register. No, because new risks should be identified by project assurance rather than by the project manager.
No, because risk identification should be a fixed part of every planning session and retrospective.

n.1: Leaving risk out of sprint events does not protect the date; risks found late are more likely to threaten it (book 10.3.1).
n.2: Risks can surface anywhere and are gathered by the teams in their events; it is not a task reserved for project assurance (book 10.3.1).

3.q: In stage 3, Matteo Ricci asks for passengers to be able to receive compensation into a digital wallet as well as to their card. This would add a new epic to the project backlog and change the scope of Coinbridge's fixed-price contract. How should this request be handled?

As a trade, swapping the wallet epic for Coinbridge stories of similar effort so that the project backlog keeps its size.
As a request for change to the project baseline, assessed formally and decided by the board or delegated change authority.
As an off-specification, raised by Hollie Brennan because the payment feature will not meet its original specification.

n.1: Trading absorbs small changes within the existing backlog; a new epic that alters the backlog and the supplier contract needs a formal decision (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).

3.q: During a sprint in stage 2, the passenger panel finds the wording on the claim confirmation screen confusing. No, because changes should wait until the sprint has ended and be raised at the team retrospective.

n.0: The change was not approved by the project manager, and changes to the project baseline need the board or delegated change authority; this one is a team-level detail change (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Changes that do not affect the project backlog are detail changes handled informally at team level; formal board decisions are for baseline changes (book 11.3.2).

n.2: In PRINCE2 Agile the project dashboard replaces the highlight report; a long pushed report adds effort without giving the board a current, visual view (Table 12.1).

3.q: Midway through stage 2, the Release 1 burn-up chart shows that, at the current velocity, the app team will finish all the Must have stories on time, but about a third of the Should and Could have stories will not be done by the end of month four. o: Yes, because the burn-up chart forecasts the finish date, and the board should act on the forecast it shows.

3.w: PRINCE2 Agile fixes time and cost and flexes what is delivered; burn charts track that flexing, and an exception arises only when a tolerance, such as delivering the Must haves, is forecast to be exceeded (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).

n.0: Burn charts do forecast completion, but the right response here is to flex lower-priority stories, not to move a date that has zero tolerance (book 12.3.1).
