No, because the Agilometer is assessed once, by all participants, in the project initiation workshop.
No, because the workshop is for the delivery teams, and board members should attend progress reviews instead.
3.w: The agile enablement workshop, part of directing a project, provides regular Agilometer assessments in initiation and later stages so that agile maturity and agile risks are reviewed; it is meant for the project board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives (book Table 13.5).

n.0: Agilometer trends do appear on the project dashboard, but that is not why the workshop is held; its purpose is regular reassessment of agile maturity and risks (Table 13.5).
n.2: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop, but the book expects regular reassessment in later stages through the agile enablement workshop (Table 13.5, Table 13.7).
n.3: The agile enablement workshop is for the project board, agile coaches and business representatives, not the delivery teams (Table 13.5).

3.q: Fair Fares closes at the end of December. Matteo Ricci already has a list of further ideas, such as support for season tickets and alerts in Welsh, and expects passengers to suggest more once the alerts are in use. How should Larkspur handle these enhancements after the project, following PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Start a new PRINCE2 Agile project for each enhancement, with its own project canvas, project board, release map and closure.
Through agile product management, with a flexible product roadmap and short cycles prioritized by value and passenger feedback.
Add them to the Fair Fares release map and extend the project into next year, as the board is already in place.
Freeze the app for a year after closure, so that customer relations can settle into new ways of working first.
3.w: Agile product management keeps a high-level product vision with a flexible roadmap that is continually adjusted from stakeholder, customer and market feedback, delivering in short, prioritized cycles; enhancements are handled through these iterations rather than a new project each time (book 14.2.2.1).

n.0: The book handles enhancements after a project through product management iterations; a separate project per enhancement adds heavy overhead (book 14.2.2.1).
n.2: The project has a fixed end date with zero time tolerance; work after closure moves into product management rather than stretching the project (Table 3.1, 14.2.2.1).
n.3: Agile product management continually adjusts the roadmap from user and market feedback; freezing the product ignores that feedback loop (book 14.2.2.1).

3.q: The app team currently releases a new version of the app once a month after several days of manual testing. For Release 3, Matteo Ricci wants fixes to the alerts and small improvements to reach passengers within days, and the operations team wants to see how the alerts perform in live use. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to achieve this?
o: Keep the monthly release cycle and add a second week of manual testing, so that each of the larger releases is more reliable.
Hand the alerts to the operations team at closure, so that it can make the fixes once the project team has left.
Release one large version at the end of each stage, after the board has approved every change in the progress review.
Bring development, testing and operations together on an automated pipeline, releasing small changes often and monitoring live use.
3.w: Continuous agile development and operations enable rapid, automated delivery of features and fixes so that the product is always deployable: DevOps removes silos between development, testing and operations, continuous delivery releases small increments, and production monitoring feeds back into development (book 14.2.2.2).

n.0: Longer manual testing makes releases slower, not faster; continuous delivery relies on automation and small, frequent releases (book 14.2.2.2).
n.1: Waiting until closure and keeping development and operations apart is the silo that DevOps removes; fixes would not reach passengers within days (book 14.2.2.2).
n.2: Large stage-end releases with board sign-off for each change slow delivery; continuous delivery ships small increments to production often (book 14.2.2.2).

3.q: Rhys Pengelly has access to an AI assistant approved by Larkspur's IT department. He wants to use it to support the 'learn from experience' principle on Fair Fares. Which use of the assistant would do this?
o: Let the assistant approve or reject requests for change to the project backlog, so that decisions in each stage are faster.
Use the assistant to forecast the Release 2 date from velocity data, so that the board can see whether the business case holds.
Analyse the lessons logs of earlier Larkspur IT projects and give each role a prioritized, searchable list of relevant lessons.
Replace the progress review workshops with summaries written by the assistant and emailed to stakeholders.
3.w: AI can turn large volumes of lessons into searchable, prioritized, role-specific insights and highlight recurring issues and proven solutions, which supports 'learn from experience'. It supports, but does not replace, human decisions and communication with stakeholders (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).

n.0: AI supports but does not replace human decision-making, and approving changes is not about learning from experience (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).
n.1: Forecasting viability and refining stage predictions supports continued business justification and manage by stages, not learn from experience (book 15.4.1).
n.3: AI can automate information sharing, but it does not remove the need to communicate with stakeholders, and this does not draw on past lessons (book 15.4.2).

4.q: At a council meeting, Professor Alison Greer is asked why the Student Support Hub will be delivered with agile ways of working instead of one full design approved at the start. Demand has risen by 60% in four years, the wellbeing service is still working out how it will triage requests, and nobody is sure how students will prefer to ask for help. Which explanation BEST reflects why agile suits this project?
o: Adopting Scrum in both teams will make delivery faster and raise quality, whatever ways of working the wellbeing service keeps.
Agile lets the university fix every feature of the hub now and flex the budget and the go-live date as needs become clearer.
The right solution is uncertain, so short feedback loops with students and staff let the teams adapt quickly and reduce wasted work.
Agile lets the teams start building before the business justification is agreed, which saves time against the Welcome Week deadline.
4.w: Complex situations rarely have one perfect solution known at the start, so it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly. Feedback loops and continual improvement reduce waste and give better solutions to complex problems (book 2.4). Here the triage model and students' preferences are both uncertain.

n.0: This is the classic misconception: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from a change in mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile does the reverse: time and cost are fixed with zero tolerance, and what is delivered is flexed (book Table 3.1). The council has also said the budget is fixed.
n.3: Every PRINCE2 Agile project still needs business justification; it is tailored into a project canvas, not dropped (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).

4.q: To prepare for the new hub, managers in the wellbeing service introduce a daily stand-up and a wall board of sticky notes for the triage redesign. However, every change to a triage step still needs written sign-off from a senior manager, and advisers are told to follow the new routine exactly as set out. Dr Kwame Mensah asks Jamal Hussain how this looks from an agile point of view. Which statement BEST describes the situation?
o: The service is doing agile without being agile: it has adopted agile routines, but staff are not allowed to adapt and decide for themselves.
The service is being agile, because daily stand-ups and a visible wall board show that the agile mindset is already in place among wellbeing staff.
The service is being agile without doing agile, because it has the right mindset but has not yet adopted a framework such as Scrum.
The service is both being and doing agile, because senior sign-off keeps each change within the tolerances agreed with the board.
4.w: Doing agile is the practical use of agile frameworks, techniques and terms; being agile means thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset with suitable self-management (book 2.3.1). Stand-ups and boards with rigid sign-off and fixed routines are doing agile without being agile.

n.1: Stand-ups and boards are visible practices; they do not show the mindset when staff cannot adapt or decide anything for themselves (book 2.3.1, 2.6.1).
n.2: The reverse is true: the service has adopted agile routines (doing) but restricts the freedom to think and act in an agile way (being) (book 2.3.1).
n.3: Tolerances are set for the project, not for every triage step; requiring senior sign-off for each change removes the self-management that being agile needs (book 2.3.1, Table 5.1).

4.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain hears that wellbeing staff have seen three previous systems promised and then dropped. Before planning the initiation stage, he meets Tom Brierley and two other advisers to find out why those systems failed, and records what they say so that the Student Support Hub can act on it. Which principle is Jamal applying, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because he is engaging internal stakeholders who will use the hub.
Ensure continued business justification, because past failures show whether the hub is likely to be worthwhile.
Tailor to suit the project, because he is adapting the method to the culture of the wellbeing service.
Learn from experience, because he is seeking lessons from earlier initiatives at the start and using them in the project.
4.w: Learning from experience means seeking, recording and acting on lessons throughout the project, starting with lessons from previous similar work in starting up (book 5.2, Table 5.1; assess previous lessons, Table 13.1). Jamal is gathering lessons from the three earlier systems.

n.0: Engaging stakeholders is part of defining roles and relationships, but Jamal's purpose here is to capture why earlier systems failed, which is learning from experience (book 5.2.1.3).
n.1: Continued business justification keeps checking that the project is desirable, viable and achievable; the stem describes gathering lessons, not reviewing justification (book 5.2.1.1).
n.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity and context; Jamal has not changed how the method is applied, he has collected lessons (book 5.2.1.7).

4.q: Midway through stage 2, the Release 1 burn-up chart shows that the web team will finish self-referral and booking before Welcome Week, but not the full self-help content library or a live chat option, both rated Should or Could haves. Professor Greer has said self-referral and booking are the minimum for Welcome Week, and the council has fixed the budget. Which response BEST applies PRINCE2 Agile fix and flex?
o: Move Release 1 to two weeks after Welcome Week, so that every planned feature can go live together for new students.
Keep the date and budget, launch self-referral and booking, and move the unfinished Should and Could haves to Release 2.
Drop booking from Release 1 and finish the self-help library instead, as the library costs less to complete in the time left.
Ask the council for extra funding to hire contract developers, so that the full Release 1 scope is ready for Welcome Week.
4.w: PRINCE2 Agile fixes time and cost with zero tolerance and flexes scope: Must haves are fixed and Should and Could haves are flexed (book Table 3.1). Self-referral and booking are the stated minimum, so they go live on time and the lower-priority features move to a later release.

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan; delaying Release 1 past Welcome Week to protect lower-priority scope breaks the fixed date (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Booking is part of the minimum the university must offer, so it is a Must have and fixed; it cannot be traded for a lower-priority feature (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Cost has zero tolerance and the council has fixed the budget; extra funding to protect Should and Could haves flexes the wrong aspect (book Table 3.1).

4.q: Before Release 1, the university plans to send the 45 wellbeing staff a user guide and a recorded webinar on the new triage process, and then let them get on with it. Several staff have already said they feel the change is being done to them, and some have seen earlier systems dropped. Which action is MOST LIKELY to help staff adopt the new ways of working?
o: Send the guide and webinar as planned, and ask managers to report which staff have watched the webinar by the go-live date.
Train the senior managers in depth and ask them to pass the details on to their teams once Release 1 is live.
Combine short training with on-the-job coaching for staff in their own teams, planned to match each release of the hub.
Give staff early access to the case management tool first, so that they learn the new ways of working by using it.
4.w: People need theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching to understand how changes apply to them; informing people and leaving them to cope breeds frustration, a leading cause of resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change (book 2.7.3).

n.0: This is informing people and leaving them to fend for themselves; tracking who watched a webinar measures compliance, not understanding (book 2.7.3).
n.1: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why; limiting training to managers and passing details on later leaves staff unsupported at go-live (book 2.7.3).
n.3: Introducing a tool first does not build the knowledge and skills people need; training and coaching should come first (book 2.7.3).

4.q: At a project board meeting, a council member asks why the Student Support Hub needs organizational change management. In her view, the web team and Northmere will build the hub, and once it is live the wellbeing staff will simply have to use it. Which explanation BEST answers her question?
o: OCM gives the board a way to instruct staff to use the hub by a set date, and clear instructions with a deadline are what make staff comply.
OCM is needed because the change management approach cannot be used outside a project, so another discipline must cover the wellbeing service's 45 staff.
OCM is mostly a record of the training given, because frequent releases of the hub are what make staff adopt the new ways of working.
The service must move from its current way of triaging to a new target state, and the change lasts if the culture adopts it rather than rolling back.
4.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to the target state (book 4.2.1). Building the hub does not change how 45 staff triage requests; the culture has to evolve so that the change is not rolled back once the project ends (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: Making change stick depends on evolving the culture, not on compliance with instructions; staff who have seen three systems dropped are unlikely to adopt the hub because of a deadline (book 4.2.1).
n.1: The change management approach can be tailored for use outside a project, for example to describe the target state for the business (book 4.2.1, Table 4.1).
n.2: Frequent releases support adoption, but OCM is the whole transition from current to target state, including culture and communication, not a training record (book 4.2.1, 4.2.4).

4.q: Dr Kwame Mensah wants the wellbeing staff to adopt the new triage process before Welcome Week. Many staff fear that a digital route will make support feel impersonal, and some doubt the hub will last. Jamal Hussain asks who should be engaged as a key influencer to shape how the staff see the change. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited, and why?
o: Dr Kwame Mensah, because as director of the service he has the authority to require staff to use the new process.
Tom Brierley, because he is respected by his colleagues, so his views can shape how many staff see the hub.
Ian Prothero, because Northmere supplies the records system and can explain how the link to the hub will work.
Dr Ruth Sefton, because she must approve the handling of health data and can reassure staff that it is secure.
4.w: A key influencer is someone who can shape the perception of the majority and, through their network, most affect the adoption of the change (book 4.2.2). Tom Brierley is respected by the staff who must change, and his open doubts mean his support would carry weight with colleagues who share them.

n.0: Formal authority is not the same as influence over colleagues' perceptions; the key influencer is the person with network and credibility among those affected (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Ian Prothero is the supplier's account manager; he has no network among the wellbeing staff whose adoption matters (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Dr Sefton is a specialist approver; reassurance on data is useful, but she does not have the peer network that shapes how staff see the change (book 4.2.2).

4.q: In stage 2, the Northmere developers work from their own offices under their company's rules, while the university web team works on campus. The two teams must agree how the hub exchanges data with the records system, but they have never met, and misunderstandings over the shared data fields have already cost a sprint. Which action BEST builds the working relationship between the two teams?
o: Agree regular days when key people from both teams work together in person, and set aside online time for less structured conversation.
Require all the Northmere developers to work on campus every day until Release 1 is live, so that the teams can share one room.
Limit contact between the teams to written requests passed through Jamal Hussain, so that the per-iteration agreement with Northmere is protected.
Leave the two teams to build their own relationship, as self-managing teams decide for themselves how they will work together.
4.w: Teams that work apart need a plan for how they will use their time together and build social cohesion. Sync co-location days for key people and teams, plus time for less structured conversation online, are the aids PRINCE2 Agile suggests (book 4.3.3).

n.1: Mandating full co-location for another organization's staff is not the effective answer; planned co-location days for key people build cohesion without it (book 4.3.3).
n.2: Channelling all contact through the project manager reduces collaboration and rich communication, which is what caused the misunderstandings (book 4.3.3, 4.4).
n.3: Self-management works within clear boundaries; leading teams across organizations means planning how people work together, not leaving it to chance (book 4.3.1, 4.3.3).

4.q: The wellbeing staff work across both campuses, and many work part-time or remotely, so they often miss face-to-face meetings about the new triage process. Jamal Hussain is drafting the communication management approach and asks how communication should be handled for this group. Which explanation BEST fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Hold all briefings in person on the main campus, because rich communication needs people to be in the same room together.
Send one weekly email to all 45 staff, because a single message for everyone keeps the information on the change consistent.
Plan a deliberate structure: agreed formats and channels, the key relationships, and set times for structured and informal contact.
Rely on a formal monthly report to the service, because informal conversations about the change cannot be controlled by the project.
4.w: Remote and hybrid working need a more deliberate, structured approach to communication: clarity on how information flows and in which formats, the key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together (book 4.4). This group works in a hybrid way across two campuses.

n.0: Rich communication is not limited to face-to-face meetings, and in-person briefings would keep excluding the part-time and remote staff who already miss meetings (book 4.4).
n.1: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be bidirectional and tailored to groups, with listening as well as broadcasting (book 4.4).
n.3: Most communication happens outside formal channels and should be accepted and supported; periodic reports on their own are not enough (book 4.4).

4.q: For Release 1, Dr Kwame Mensah forms a triage team of eight advisers from both campuses to handle self-referrals. They have not worked together before, and several are unsure which changes to the triage questions they may make themselves and which need his approval. Which action BEST helps build this into an agile team?
o: Kwame writes the team's values and decision rules himself and circulates them, so that the advisers can start triaging without delay.
Pay a monthly bonus to the advisers who close the most self-referral requests, so that the team is motivated to work quickly.
Ask each adviser to email Kwame a daily summary, so that he can approve any change to the triage questions before it is made.
Hold a session where the team co-decides its values and agrees which decisions it can take and which must be escalated.
4.w: Building agile teams starts with co-deciding team values and accountabilities, so that the team knows the boundaries of its self-management and when decisions must be escalated (book 4.5).

n.0: Values and accountabilities should be co-decided by the team; values written by a manager do not build shared ownership (book 4.5).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile suggests value-based incentives that reward behaviour modelling agile values, balanced with intangible motivators; a bonus for volume can reward rushing urgent cases (book 4.5).
n.2: Approving every change centrally removes self-management; the team needs agreed boundaries, not daily approval (book 4.5).

4.q: During initiation, the university's quality team asks for evidence that each release of the Student Support Hub has been tested with real students, and the hub must work with screen readers. Jamal Hussain wants to settle what the users will accept and how that will be checked. Which practice addresses this concern, and why?
o: Quality, because it documents the users' requirements of the project products and how they will be met.
Progress, because it monitors actual achievements against those planned and forecasts the project's objectives.
Risk, because failing an accessibility check is an uncertain event that could affect the project's objectives.
Issues, because a release that has not been tested with students will deviate from the agreed baseline.
4.w: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes how they will be met; it answers 'what is acceptable to users and how is it measured?' (book 9.1). Accessibility standards and testing with students are quality requirements and quality methods.

n.1: Progress compares actual achievements with plans and forecasts objectives; it does not define what users will accept or how products are checked (book 12.1).
n.2: A failed check is a possible threat, but defining acceptable quality and how it is verified is the quality practice, not the risk practice (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: Nothing has deviated yet; the issues practice controls changes to the baseline, while the quality team's request is about defining and meeting requirements (book 9.1, 11.1).

4.q: Jamal Hussain is drafting the benefits management approach. Professor Greer wants evidence of benefits, such as fewer paper forms printed and shorter waits for a first appointment, well before the project closes in month 14. How should the approach reflect this?
o: Plan a single benefits review after the project closes, because benefits cannot be realized until all three releases are live.
Treat the on-time go-live of each release as the benefit, because meeting each date shows that value has been delivered.
Leave benefits out of the approach until Release 3, because the early-warning feature is expected to bring the largest benefit to students.
Use the releases to deliver benefits early, and set out when and how each benefit will be measured and reviewed after each release.
4.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases so that benefits can be delivered early, and it sets out how benefits will be measured, reviewed and by whom (book 6.3.2). Iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project, not only after closure (book 6.3.1).

n.0: Most benefit confirmation happens after closure, but iterative releases let some benefits be realized and measured during the project (book 6.3.1).
n.1: A go-live date is a time target and a release is an output; a benefit is a measurable improvement such as shorter waiting times (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.2: Release 3 may not be built at all, subject to ethics review; Releases 1 and 2 already bring measurable benefits that the approach should plan for (book 6.3.2).

4.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain assembles the project brief for the Student Support Hub. Professor Greer wants the brief to show clearly how the agile approach will shape the project, as most university leaders are used to annual plans. Which content is MOST appropriate to add to the brief?
o: A fixed list of every feature in all three releases, so that the council can approve the whole scope before initiation starts.
The scope and quality areas that can flex by priority, the agile techniques chosen and their benefits, and how releases affect operations.
The web team's task plans for its first three sprints, so that the board can approve the work each developer will do on the hub in stage 2.
The design of the web team's online dashboard, so that the board can see how sprint progress will be reported to it each week.
4.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project brief outlines the flexible areas of scope and quality criteria based on prioritization, the agile techniques and approaches chosen with their expected benefits, and, because of incremental delivery, more detail on the impact on operations and maintenance (book 6.3.2).

n.0: Fixing every feature in advance removes the flexibility on scope that agile relies on; Must haves are fixed but Should and Could haves flex (book 6.3.2, Table 3.1).
n.2: Task-level plans are produced by the team for the next iteration in managing product delivery, not by the board in starting up (book 8.3.2).
n.3: Team dashboards are co-created by each team in the project kickoff workshop; the board pulls information from the project dashboard (book Table 13.8, Table 12.1).

4.q: During initiation, Professor Greer refines the project canvas. It shows one cost figure of £950,000 and one forecast of benefits, which assumes that all three releases, including the early-warning feature, will be delivered. The ethics committee has not yet reviewed the early-warning feature. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the budget is fixed, so a single cost figure and a single benefits forecast give the board all it needs.
Yes, because the canvas is a one-page summary, so alternative outcomes should be kept for the full business case.
No, because the canvas should show best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios, such as benefits without Release 3.
No, because benefits belong in the benefits management approach and should not be forecast on the project canvas.
4.w: When the business case is tailored into a project canvas, the canvas should outline best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios (book Table 5.2). Release 3 depends on an ethics review, so the board needs to see whether the hub is still justified if it is not built.

n.0: A fixed budget does not remove uncertainty about benefits; the forecast depends on a feature that may never be approved (book Table 5.2).
n.1: The canvas is a one-page visual business justification, and in PRINCE2 Agile it is the business case; it should still outline the different scenarios (book 6.3.2, Table 5.2).
n.3: The project canvas includes expected, measurable benefits with tolerance; the benefits management approach covers how they will be managed and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

4.q: Early in stage 2, Northmere developers change two shared data fields without telling the web team, while web developers wait for approvals they do not need. Jamal Hussain wants to make clear, for each type of decision about the link to the records system, who decides and who must be involved, such as Rebecca Lyle or Dr Ruth Sefton. Which technique should he use?
o: A team skill matrix, showing each developer's strengths and gaps on the two team dashboards.
The commercial management approach, setting out the delivery model for Northmere's work.
A delegation matrix, showing for each decision area who decides and who is involved.
A user story map, showing the order in which the integration stories will be delivered.
4.w: A delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision authority transparent: for each decision area it shows who decides and who is involved (book 7.4.3). Here both teams are unsure which decisions they can take.

n.0: A team skill matrix shows capabilities, strengths and gaps to assign people and plan training; it does not set decision authority (book 7.4.1).
n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contract arrangements, such as the per-iteration payment, not who decides each technical question (book 7.3.2).
n.3: A story map breaks products into user stories and orders them; it does not make decision rights clear (book 8.3.2.4).

4.q: During initiation, Jamal Hussain records how the people working on the hub will work together: the days when key people from the web team, Northmere and the wellbeing service meet in person, and the shared online boards that keep each team's work visible to the others. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure.
In the commercial management approach.
In the role descriptions for each team member.
In the quality management approach.
4.w: The project management team structure shows who is involved and how they work together, including working practices that reflect agile and the arrangements for co-located or remote teams, with the tools used for transparency and rich communication (book 7.3.2).

n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and the form of contract, such as Northmere's per-iteration payment, not day-to-day working arrangements (book 7.3.2).
n.2: Role descriptions set out each role's specific responsibilities; working practices and co-location arrangements sit in the team structure (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The quality management approach covers quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, including agile testing, not how teams meet and share their work (book 9.3.2).

4.q: During stage 2, Professor Greer and Peter Langley start emailing two web team developers directly with new tasks for the current sprint, including early work on the early-warning feature. The developers begin the work without telling Rebecca Lyle, the web team's product owner. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project executive is accountable for the project and can direct the work of any team member.
Yes, because self-managing developers may take on work from any senior stakeholder who supports the project.
No, because the project manager is the role that should assign each task to the individual developers.
No, because the product owner directs the team's work, so new requests should go through her and the product backlog.
4.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the product owner is a version of the team manager and the only role with direct authority over the delivery team members; the project manager agrees work with the PO as sets of user stories (book 7.3.1). New work should reach the team through the PO's product backlog.

n.0: The executive is accountable for the project, but direct authority over delivery team members sits with the product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.1: Self-management works within the tolerances and work agreed through the product owner, not on requests from any senior stakeholder (book 7.3.1).
n.2: The project manager has direct authority over the product owner, not over individual developers; the PO directs the team (book 7.3.1).

4.q: The Student Support Hub needs a chief product owner to represent its users, who include students and the wellbeing staff who will use the case view, to own the project backlog and to set priorities across the web team and the Northmere team. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the chief product owner role?
o: Rebecca Lyle, senior digital product manager.
Dr Kwame Mensah, director of student wellbeing.
Maya Kowalczyk, students' union vice-president for welfare.
Professor Alison Greer, pro vice-chancellor.
4.w: The CPO represents the user community, owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams (book Table 7.2). Kwame Mensah knows students' needs in detail and leads the wellbeing staff who will use the case view, so he can speak for both user groups.

n.0: Rebecca Lyle has managed the web team's backlog for two years, which suits the product owner role for that one team rather than representing users across teams (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Maya Kowalczyk represents students, but not the wellbeing staff who will also use the hub; she is better placed to help recruit and voice the student design panel (book Table 7.2, 4.2.2).
n.3: Professor Greer received the mandate and holds the budget, which fits the project executive role accountable for the project (book Table 7.2).

4.q: The project board wants someone independent of the delivery teams and of the wellbeing service to monitor whether agile practices and governance checks are being followed, and to advise the board and Jamal Hussain on risks, exception reports and their impact on the project canvas. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the project assurance role?
o: Chloe Hartley, Scrum master for the web team.
Rebecca Lyle, senior digital product manager.
Daniel Ferreira, head of the web team.
Sinead Walsh, quality and enhancement manager.
4.w: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, builds quality and governance checks into delivery, and advises the board and project manager on issues, risks, exception reports and impacts on the canvas (book Table 7.2). Sinead Walsh reviews services against standards and is independent of the wellbeing service and the teams.

n.0: Chloe Hartley works inside the web team as its Scrum master, which fits the team coach role; she is not independent of a delivery team (book Table 7.2).
n.1: Rebecca Lyle manages the web team's backlog and fits the product owner role, so she would be assuring her own team's work (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Daniel Ferreira heads the web team that builds the hub, so he is on the supplier side and not independent of the delivery teams (book Table 7.2).

4.q: During initiation, Rebecca Lyle and the web team need to size about 120 user stories for the hub so that Jamal Hussain can draft a first release map. Time is short, and Daniel Ferreira does not want the team to spend days debating each story. Which estimating approach is MOST suitable?
o: Magic estimation, with the whole team quickly placing the stories in order of relative size with little discussion of each.
Ask Daniel Ferreira to estimate all 120 stories himself in story points, so that the developers' time is kept for building.
Use the Northmere team's past velocity to size the web team's stories, as Northmere has delivered similar integration work.
Estimate each story in hours with the most experienced developer, then add up the hours to fix the Release 1 end date.
4.w: Agile estimation is relative and draws on the whole team. Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for early planning that sizes many stories without lengthy discussion (book 8.4.3), which fits sizing 120 stories for a first release map.

n.1: Agile estimates should harness the whole team so that everyone contributes; one person's estimates lose the team's knowledge and shared commitment (book 8.4.3).
n.2: Velocity is a team's rate of delivery used for forecasting, not a way to size stories, and forecasts should use the team's own figures (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile uses relative estimates from the whole team, not hour-by-hour estimates from one person, and time is already fixed by Welcome Week (book 8.4.3, Table 3.1).

4.q: Daniel Ferreira says his team will not commit to any feature more than one sprint ahead. Jamal Hussain accepts this and decides that the plan for Release 1 will be the web team's current sprint plan, with no release map, until each new sprint begins. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because detailed task-level planning should be done for the next iteration and not further ahead.
Yes, because empiricism means that no forecast for the release can be made until the work itself is finished.
No, because a high-level release map is still needed for the releases, with detailed planning kept to the next sprint.
No, because the web team should commit during initiation to a detailed plan for every Release 1 sprint.
4.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans just in time: a high-level release map serves as the project and stage plan, showing how many releases there are, when, and which features they contain, while task-level planning is done for the next iteration (book 8.3.2, Table 8.1). Ferreira's point is valid for team plans, but the board still needs a release map.

n.0: This is true for team plans, but it does not justify having no release map; the higher-level plan is still needed (book 8.3.2).
n.1: Empiricism means starting work, measuring how much gets done and forecasting from that rate; it supports forecasts during the work (book 8.3).
n.3: Detailed plans for every sprint in advance go against planning just in time; task-level planning belongs to the next iteration (book 8.3.2).

4.q: The university's quality team wants evidence that each release has been tested with real students. For Release 1, Maya Kowalczyk's student design panel takes part in three planned test sessions on phones and with screen readers, and the result of each session is recorded. Where should the planned sessions and their results be recorded?
o: In the product register, with the current status of each product.
In the quality register, with planned and actual dates and results.
On the web team's team dashboard, beside the sprint burn-down.
In the lessons log, with what the team learned from each session.
4.w: The quality register holds all planned and completed quality activities, with their method, planned and actual dates, responsibilities, results and records (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1). The student test sessions are quality activities, so they and their results go there.

n.0: The product register lists the products required by a plan and their status; it is not the record of quality activities and results (book 9.3.2).
n.2: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and shows the team's progress; it is not the record of planned and completed quality activities (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The lessons log captures lessons; the planned test sessions and their pass or fail results belong in the quality register (book 9.3.2, Table 12.1).

4.q: Members of the student design panel disagree about two designs for the first screen of self-referral: one asks students to choose a category of need, the other asks them to describe their concern in their own words. Rebecca Lyle wants evidence of which design more students complete. Which quality technique BEST fits this situation?
o: Refactoring, changing the internal structure of the screen while keeping its behaviour the same for students.
Test-driven development, writing unit tests for each design before the code for that design is written.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many stories for each design are in progress and how many are done.
A/B testing, releasing both versions to groups of students and comparing how many complete each one.
4.w: A/B testing compares two versions of a product with users to see which performs better (book 9.4.3). It gives Rebecca evidence from students instead of opinions from the panel.

n.0: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing external behaviour; it cannot show which design students prefer (book 9.4.1).
n.1: Test-driven development checks that code works at unit level; it does not compare how real users respond to two designs (book 9.4.3, Glossary).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram is a progress technique that shows work in each workflow state; it says nothing about which design students complete (book 12.4.2).

4.q: The web team's definition of done does not include testing with assistive technology, which an external auditor has carried out once a year. Rebecca Lyle proposes keeping the definition of done as it is for Release 1 and booking the auditor's annual check for August, a few weeks before Welcome Week. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because an external auditor gives more independent evidence of accessibility than the team's own checks.
Yes, because the definition of done belongs to the team, so the project should leave it unchanged.
No, because accessibility should be checked by project assurance at each stage boundary instead.
No, because assistive-technology testing should be part of done for each story, so faults are found as work is built.
4.w: The definition of done is the shared agreement of what makes an item complete; work that has defects is not done (book 9.3.2.2). PRINCE2 Agile advises deciding early how much can be tested first or tested as the work goes (book 9.4.3). For a hub used by many disabled students, accessibility is part of done, not a late check.

n.0: An external audit may still be useful, but a single check weeks before go-live finds faults too late to fix, and stories would count as done while untested (book 9.3.2.2, 9.4.3).
n.1: The definition of done is a shared agreement that the team and product owner should keep fit for the product's quality needs, which here include accessibility (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Project assurance monitors adherence to practices and governance; it does not test products, and a check at stage boundaries is still late (book Table 7.2, 9.4.3).

4.q: In the project initiation workshop, the participants assess the Agilometer for the hub. Peter Langley insists that the early-warning feature must be in Release 1, and several senior staff describe every requested feature as essential for Welcome Week. The group rates the related slider low. Which action is MOST LIKELY to improve that slider?
o: Hold more frequent stand-ups with the wellbeing staff on both campuses, to raise the level of collaboration.
Move the Northmere agreement to one fixed price for the whole project, to protect the scope already agreed.
Challenge with the board and stakeholders whether so many features really are Must haves, using Greer's stated minimum.
Ask the council for extra budget for more web developers, so that every requested feature can fit into Release 1 before Welcome Week.
4.w: Stakeholders treating every feature as essential lowers the 'flexibility on what is delivered' slider. One way to raise it is to challenge whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them (book 10.3.2.2, 10.3.2.3). Greer's statement that self-referral and booking are the minimum gives a basis for that conversation.

n.0: More stand-ups might help collaboration, but the low reading here comes from stakeholders' unwillingness to flex scope, which is a different slider (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: A fixed-price contract for all the scope would make flexing what is delivered harder, and contracts that inhibit agile lower another slider (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: Cost has zero tolerance and the council has fixed the budget; adding money avoids, rather than improves, flexibility on what is delivered (book Table 3.1, 10.3.2.3).

4.q: Professor Greer, whose council has a very low appetite for risks to student data, asks Jamal Hussain to show whether the total exposure from the data security risks that the web team is tracking is falling from sprint to sprint during stage 2. Which technique BEST meets her request?
o: A cumulative risk burn-down chart, with the team updating the likelihood of each tracked risk at every planning session.
A release burn-up chart, showing the story points completed against the scope of Release 1 over the sprints of the stage.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many data security stories sit in each workflow state over the weeks of the stage.
An Agilometer, with its sliders reassessed at each agile enablement workshop held by the board during the stage.
4.w: In a cumulative risk burn-down chart the team sets the likelihood of each tracked risk at the first planning meeting and updates it at each planning session; the chart shows total risk exposure across iterations, which should fall over time (book 10.4.2).

n.1: A burn-up chart tracks completed work against scope; it does not show risk exposure (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows work in each workflow state and reveals bottlenecks; it does not measure risk exposure (book 12.4.2).
n.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working itself, such as flexibility and collaboration, not the exposure from specific data security risks (book 10.3.2).

4.q: Dr Ruth Sefton requires two responses to the risk of a breach of student health data: encryption of stored case notes, and access to notes limited by staff role. Both need development work. Rebecca Lyle adds them as stories to the web team's product backlog, prioritized alongside the user stories, and the risk stays in the risk register. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because placing risk responses in the product backlog lets them be prioritized and tracked alongside the stories.
Yes, because once the responses are in the product backlog, the risk no longer needs to be held in the risk register.
No, because responses to data risks should be planned by the board in the agile enablement workshop, not by the team.
No, because data protection risks fall outside the team's tolerances and must be reported in an exception report.
4.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds risk responses together with the user stories, so that the work to manage risk is prioritized and delivered like any other work (book 10.4.1). The risk register still records the risk and its status (book 10.3.2).

n.1: The risk register is the record of identified risks with their status and history; adding responses to the backlog does not replace it (book 10.3.2, Table 10.1).
n.2: The agile enablement workshop deals with risks to agile adoption found through the Agilometer, not with planning responses to specific product risks (book Table 13.5).
n.3: An exception report is needed when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; nothing suggests that, and the responses can be planned within the team's work (book Table 12.1).

4.q: In stage 2, Peter Langley asks again for the early-warning feature to be moved from Release 3 into Release 1 as a Must have. Professor Greer has said that self-referral and booking are the minimum for Welcome Week, and the ethics committee has asked to review any use of predictive analytics before it is built. How should Langley's request be handled?
o: As a detail change, agreed by Rebecca Lyle with the web team at the next team planning workshop in stage 2.
As a request for change to the baseline, assessed formally and decided by the board or delegated change authority.
As a trade, swapping the early-warning epic for Release 1 stories of similar effort within the web team.
As an off-specification, because Release 1 will not include a feature that a senior stakeholder expects.
4.w: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline. Making a whole epic a Must have for Release 1 changes the approved scope in the project backlog and the release map, so it is handled formally and decided by the project board or whoever holds delegated change authority (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2). The ethics review would also have to come first.

n.0: A detail change does not affect the project backlog; moving an epic into Release 1 changes the agreed scope, so the product owner cannot decide it at team level (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort inside a team's work; it is not a way to bring a new epic into a release without a baseline decision (book 11.4.1, 11.3.2).
n.3: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; the early-warning feature was never part of Release 1's scope (book 11.3.1).

4.q: Late in stage 2, testing with screen readers shows that the appointment booking screens will not meet the university's accessibility standard, which forms part of their quality criteria. The fix will not be ready before Welcome Week. What type of issue is this, and why?
o: A request for change, because the accessibility standard will have to be changed for Release 1.
An off-specification, because a product will not meet its quality specification.
A business opportunity, because the fault shows where the booking screens can be improved.
A problem, because the fault has an immediate effect on the web team's velocity this sprint.
4.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification (book 11.3.1). The booking screens are forecast to miss the accessibility standard set in their quality criteria.

n.0: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline; nobody has proposed changing the standard, and the facts are that the product will fall short of it (book 11.3.1).
n.2: A business opportunity is an unexpected positive consequence; a failure to meet a quality standard is not (book 11.3.1).
n.3: The problem type covers issues with a negative impact that are not a product failing its specification; this issue is specifically about the screens missing their quality criteria (book 11.3.1).

4.q: In sprint 5, the link between the hub's booking screens and the student records system fails testing, blocking three of the Northmere team's stories. Before the team has looked at it together, its product owner reports it to Jamal Hussain, who writes an issue report and asks the project board how to proceed. Release 1 is still forecast to be on time. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a fault that blocks stories should be recorded in an issue report for the board to decide on.
Yes, because faults in a supplier's work under the per-iteration agreement need a decision from the board.
No, because the blocked stories should be traded for other Northmere stories of similar effort instead.
No, because the team should first swarm on the blocker together and escalate it if it cannot resolve it.
4.w: Swarming means the team focuses together on a stuck task or blocker, and it should be tried before an issue is escalated to the project manager (book 11.4.2). The board is involved when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, and Release 1 is still on time (book Table 12.1).

n.0: Formal issue handling is for matters the team cannot resolve or that affect the baseline; a blocker should be swarmed first (book 11.4.2).
n.1: The per-iteration agreement does not turn every technical fault into a board decision; the team should try to resolve it first (book 11.4.2, Table 12.1).
n.2: Trading absorbs change by swapping requirements of similar effort; it is not a way to remove a blocker (book 11.4.1).

4.q: Midway through stage 2, the web team's cumulative flow diagram shows the 'waiting for data protection sign-off' band growing wider each week, while the 'done' band rises slowly. Chloe Hartley asks the team what the chart is telling them. Which reading is correct?
o: The team is ahead of plan, because more stories are moving through the workflow each week than before.
Work is queuing at data protection sign-off, a bottleneck the team should address before starting more stories.
Total risk exposure is rising, so the data protection risks in the risk register should be reassessed.
The team's velocity is falling because its data stories were underestimated, so the remaining stories should be re-estimated.
4.w: A cumulative flow diagram shows how many items are in each workflow state over time and reveals bottlenecks; a band that keeps widening shows work queuing at that state (book 12.4.2).

n.0: A widening waiting band with a slowly rising 'done' band shows work piling up, not faster delivery (book 12.4.2).
n.2: Total risk exposure is shown by a cumulative risk burn-down chart, not by a cumulative flow diagram (book 10.4.2, 12.4.2).
n.3: The chart shows where work is waiting, not that estimates were wrong; velocity and estimates are read from burn charts and story points (book 12.4.2, 12.4.3).

4.q: Professor Greer asks Jamal Hussain for a detailed weekly written report. To produce it, Jamal asks the web team to stop updating its online team dashboard and instead email him a status note every Friday, which he will rewrite into a report for her. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project executive decides the format and frequency of the reports that she receives.
Yes, because written reports give the board a more reliable record of progress than visual dashboards.
No, because the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report, and Greer should pull from a project dashboard.
No, because the web team should send its weekly status note directly to Greer rather than through Jamal.
4.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and the project manager pulls information from it; the project dashboard replaces the highlight report and the board pulls information from it (book Table 12.1). Replacing the team dashboard with emailed notes removes the team's visual management and pushes reports instead.

n.0: The board's information needs matter, but in PRINCE2 Agile they are met through a project dashboard it can pull from, not by dismantling the team's dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.1: Written reports are not more reliable; people tend to adjust what they report to what seems acceptable, while dashboards keep progress visible (book 4.4, 12.3.1).
n.3: Sending status notes to the executive bypasses the project manager and still pushes reports; the board should pull from the project dashboard (book Table 12.1).

4.q: In starting up a project, Professor Greer brings key stakeholders together to define the core elements of the Student Support Hub in line with the university's goals. In which workshop, and under which topic, should this be discussed?
o: The project initiation workshop, under persona definition
The project canvas workshop, under user group definition
The project canvas workshop, under benefits analysis
The starting up workshop, under project roles
4.w: The project canvas workshop in starting up builds a shared understanding of the project's core elements in line with organizational goals. Its user group definition topic identifies one to three key user groups and prioritizes them (book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

n.0: Persona definition is a topic of the project initiation workshop in initiating a project, where fictional needs-based personas are written; choosing and ranking the key user groups comes earlier, in the canvas workshop (book Table 13.7, Table 13.2).
n.2: Benefits analysis is a canvas workshop topic, but it identifies benefits and dis-benefits and their tolerances, not which user groups matter most (book Table 13.2).
n.3: The project roles topic of the starting up workshop aligns the team on role descriptions; it does not identify the hub's key user groups (book Table 13.3).

4.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain confirms the hub's objectives, scope and exclusions, its tolerances, and the constraints and assumptions. He also notes that the hub depends on Northmere's planned upgrade of the student records system and on the ethics committee's review of predictive analytics. Which starting up activity is he carrying out?
o: Select the project approach, because it decides how the hub will be delivered and what tailoring it needs.
Plan the initiation stage, because the dependencies will shape the release map for the initiation stage.
Prepare the outline business case, because the dependencies affect whether the hub is viable.
Assemble the project brief, because it confirms the objectives, scope, tolerances and dependencies.
4.w: Assembling the project brief confirms the objectives, outcomes, scope, exclusions, tolerances, constraints, assumptions and dependencies, for example on other initiatives (book Table 13.1).

n.0: Selecting the project approach evaluates delivery solutions and defines tailoring needs; it does not confirm objectives, tolerances and dependencies (book Table 13.1).
n.1: Planning the initiation stage sets time and cost constraints, a high-level release map and controls for initiation; the dependencies Jamal records are part of the project brief (book Table 13.1).
n.2: Preparing the outline business case is where the executive leads the project canvas from the mandate; confirming scope, tolerances and dependencies is assembling the project brief (book Table 13.1).

4.q: At the end of stage 2, after Release 1 has gone live, the project board reviews the updated project dashboard and the updated release map for stage 3, which plans request tracking and the staff case view for Release 2. The board approves the release map so that the next stage can begin. Which directing a project activity is the board carrying out?
o: Authorize a stage or exception plan, because it approves the updated release map for the next stage.
Give ongoing direction, because it responds to the updated project dashboard at any point in a stage.
Authorize the project, because Release 2 commits significant further resources to the hub.
Authorize project closure, because Release 1 has been accepted and handed over to its users.

n.2: Authorizing the project happens once, at the end of initiation, when the board approves the PID and commits resources for the project (book Table 13.4).
n.3: Authorizing project closure happens at the end of the whole project and approves the end project report; Release 1 going live does not close the project (book Table 13.4).

4.q: In the project initiation workshop, Dr Kwame Mensah and the teams agree that the hub as a whole will be acceptable to its users when it works with screen readers, has been tried by the student design panel and has data handling approved by Dr Ruth Sefton. o: Project Definition of Ready
Management approaches
Project Definition of Done
Persona definition

o: Team values and norms
Psychological safety
Team delegation matrix
Icebreaker, project intro and team intro

4.q: During stage 2, Jamal Hussain gathers the latest information from the web team's and Northmere's team dashboards, the project log and recent changes to the release map, and uses it to update the project dashboard so that Professor Greer and the board can see the stage's status when they need it. Evaluate stage status, because it reviews the progress of the stage as a whole during a progress review.
Escalate issues and risks, because it informs the board of the stage's status and any deviation.
Report highlights, because it updates the project dashboard so that the board can pull information.

n.1: Evaluating stage status reviews progress, decides on actions and updates release map forecasts; assembling information into the project dashboard for the board is reporting highlights (book Table 13.9).
n.2: Escalating issues and risks recommends options to the board in an exception report when a deviation threatens tolerance; nothing here is forecast to exceed tolerance (book Table 13.9).

4.q: Near the end of stage 2, Jamal Hussain holds a workshop with the board and key stakeholders to assess the stage's status, celebrate what has been achieved and deal with challenges. They agree who will follow up each point. In which workshop, and under which topic, is this discussed?
o: The progress review workshop, under current risks and issues
The progress review workshop, under project highlights
The agile enablement workshop, under risk identification
The project retrospective workshop, under the learning
4.w: The progress review workshop in controlling a stage assesses status, celebrates achievements and addresses challenges; its current risks and issues topic is where open risks and issues are discussed and actions agreed (book 13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

n.2: The agile enablement workshop in directing a project deals with risks to agile adoption found through the Agilometer, not product risks and issues in a stage (book Table 13.5).
n.3: The project retrospective workshop reflects on what went well and what was learned; it is not the workshop for reviewing stage status and open risks and issues (book Table 13.11).

4.q: At the web team's team planning workshop, Chloe Hartley helps the team and Rebecca Lyle rewrite the acceptance criteria for the 'cancel an appointment' story so that each criterion is clear and testable, and they agree what will count as done for that story. User story refinement
Iteration planning

The learning
The good
Team building

n.2: The good covers what went well and what to celebrate, not problems and their causes (book Table 13.14).

4.q: At the end of stage 2, the teams meet to align with the hub's vision and plan stage 3, reviewing the project canvas, the project backlog and the release map. The team planning workshop, under iteration planning
The team planning workshop, under user story refinement

n.1: The team planning workshop prepares a team for its next iteration in managing product delivery; iteration planning selects stories for that iteration, not the stage's release map (book Table 13.13).

4.w: The project closure workshop formally concludes the project; its final handover planning topic agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and the actions for benefits after the project (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19).

n.0: The final product demo shows the product for user acceptance and readiness for handover; it does not agree support responsibilities and benefits actions (book Table 13.19).
n.2: The progress review topic of the closure workshop updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer, not the support and benefits arrangements (book Table 13.19).
n.3: The release planning workshop is held at stage boundaries to plan the next stage; at the end of the project the handover is planned in the closure workshop (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.19).

4.q: Most of the university's leaders are used to annual plans and committee approvals. The project board decides to hold an agile enablement workshop in each stage with an agile coach from the IT department and two business representatives, to reassess the Agilometer and agree practical steps to reduce risks to agile adoption. Is this an appropriate application of the directing a project process, and why?
o: Yes, because the agile enablement workshop is where the agile transformation plan for the whole university is produced.
Yes, because regular Agilometer reassessment with the board, coaches and business representatives keeps agile risks under review.
No, because the Agilometer is assessed once in the project initiation workshop and is not revisited in later stages.
No, because risks to agile adoption are a progress matter and belong in the progress review workshop instead.
4.w: The agile enablement workshop in directing a project provides regular Agilometer assessments in initiation and later stages, so that agile maturity and agile risks are reviewed; it is for the project board, agile coaches and business representatives (book Table 13.5). That suits a university with leaders new to agile.

n.0: The agile transformation plan, where needed, is produced in initiation through the project initiation workshop, not in the agile enablement workshop (book Table 13.7).
n.2: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop, but it is reassessed regularly in later stages through agile enablement workshops (book 10.3.2, Table 13.5).
n.3: The Agilometer is a risk tool, and reviewing risks to agile adoption with the board is the purpose of the agile enablement workshop (book 10.3.2, Table 13.5).

4.q: At the release planning workshop at the end of stage 2, Jamal Hussain asks the web team and the Northmere team to plan every task for all the sprints of Release 2 in detail, with named developers and hours, so that the board can approve the stage 3 plan at task level. Is this an appropriate application of the managing a stage boundary process, and why?
o: Yes, because the board approves the next stage plan, so it needs the full detail of each task to authorize the stage.
Yes, because time is fixed for Release 2, so every task has to be planned before the stage begins to protect the date.
No, because the stage boundary updates the release map at a high level, and task planning is done before each sprint.
No, because the release planning workshop is for the project board, and the delivery teams should not take part in it.
4.w: At a stage boundary the release map is updated at a high level for the next stage; detailed task planning is done for the next iteration in managing product delivery, through the team planning workshop (book 13.7.4.1, 8.3.2).

n.0: The board approves the next stage plan as an updated release map; it does not need task-level detail, which the teams plan each sprint (book Table 13.4, 8.3.2).
n.1: Time is fixed, but it is protected by flexing what is delivered, not by planning every task in advance (book Table 3.1, 8.3.2).
n.3: The release planning workshop aligns the teams with the vision and plans the next stage, so the teams take part (book 13.7.4.1).

4.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain learns that the university council usually expects a long written business case before it backs a project. He must produce the business justification for the hub in a way that fits PRINCE2 Agile while keeping the council's confidence. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Professor Greer leads a project canvas workshop with key stakeholders, adding supporting detail where the council needs it.
Jamal writes a 40-page business case on his own, because the council's committees expect a full written document before approval.
The business justification is postponed until Release 1 has shown value, because agile projects learn as they go along.
The web team defines the hub's business value in its first sprint review, using the feedback it gathers from students.
4.w: In starting up, the executive leads development of the project canvas from the mandate, and the project canvas workshop builds a shared understanding of the project's core elements (book Table 13.1, 13.2.4.1). Tailoring to suit the project allows extra detail where the organization's governance needs it (book 5.2.1.7).

n.1: The executive should lead the canvas with stakeholders; a long document written by one person loses the shared understanding the canvas workshop builds (book Table 13.1, 13.2.4.1).
n.2: Every project needs business justification from the start; agile tailors the business case into a canvas rather than postponing it (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).
n.3: Business value is defined in the project canvas workshop in starting up, before delivery begins, not by a delivery team in its first sprint (book Table 13.2).

4.q: To save time before Welcome Week, Daniel Ferreira suggests that the web team hold its team planning workshop and team retrospective once per release rather than every sprint. Jamal Hussain wants to tailor managing product delivery without losing the purpose of these workshops. Which tailoring is MOST appropriate?
o: Hold both workshops once per release as suggested, since a release of two to four sprints is a natural point to plan and reflect.
Replace the team retrospective with a written review by Jamal at the end of each stage, and keep team planning once per release.
Plan all the Release 1 sprints in one team planning workshop in initiation, and hold one retrospective after Welcome Week.
Keep a short team planning workshop before each sprint and a team retrospective at the end of each sprint, sized to two weeks.
4.w: The team planning workshop prepares for the next iteration and the team retrospective reflects on the last one (book 13.6.4.1, 13.6.4.2). Both are tied to the iteration, and risks are also identified in every planning session and retrospective (book 10.3.1); they can be kept short to suit two-week sprints.

n.0: Planning and reflecting once per release loses the iteration-by-iteration planning, feedback and risk identification these workshops exist for (book 13.6.4.1, 13.6.4.2, 10.3.1).
n.1: A retrospective is the team's own reflection on its last iteration; a project manager's written stage review cannot replace it (book 13.6.4.2).
n.2: Task-level planning is done for the next iteration only, and retrospectives happen at the end of each iteration (book 8.3.2, 5.6.3.3).

4.q: Release 2 hands the staff case view over to the wellbeing service, whose 45 staff work across two campuses and often part-time. Dr Kwame Mensah asks Jamal Hussain what the transition to operations should include so that the service can run and keep improving the hub. Which approach BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Send the full technical documentation to every member of staff, and close the teams' dashboards and backlogs at handover.
Keep the web team handling triage until staff feel confident, and begin training the staff once the project has closed.
Hand over the backlog, dashboards and tools, give tailored training with quick guides, and set up regular feedback loops.
Leave feedback from staff until the post-project benefits review, so that they have time to get used to the hub first.
4.w: Transition to operations hands over agile artifacts and tools so agile practices continue, provides tailored end-user training with guides and videos, sets out operational procedures and escalation paths, and creates regular feedback loops such as surveys and check-ins (book 14.2.1).

n.0: Closing the artifacts and tools stops agile practices continuing after handover, and technical documentation is no substitute for tailored training (book 14.2.1).
n.1: Training should help staff adopt the product at handover; delaying it leaves the service unable to run the hub (book 14.2.1).
n.3: Regular feedback loops should start at transition so that actionable insights are collected early (book 14.2.1).

4.q: The project will close in the spring term. Dr Kwame Mensah already has more ideas, such as text reminders before appointments and a live chat with advisers, and the web team will keep working on the hub as part of normal business. How should these further enhancements BEST be handled after the project closes?
o: Manage the hub as a product, with a vision and a flexible roadmap adjusted from feedback, prioritizing work in short cycles.
Start a new PRINCE2 Agile project for each enhancement, so that each has its own business justification and board.
Freeze the hub for a year after closure so that it stays stable, then gather all the ideas into one large upgrade.
Fix a detailed three-year roadmap of enhancements now, so that the web team knows what it will build each term.
4.w: Agile product management keeps a high-level product vision with a flexible roadmap that is adjusted from stakeholder and customer feedback, and works in short cycles prioritized by value (book 14.2.2.1). Enhancements after a project are handled through product management iterations.

n.1: Enhancements after the project are handled through agile product management iterations, not by starting a new project for each one (book 14.2.2.1).
n.2: Agile product management delivers value in short cycles from feedback; holding ideas back for one large upgrade loses that (book 14.2.2.1).
n.3: A detailed fixed roadmap cannot be continually adjusted from feedback, which agile product management relies on (book 14.2.2.1).

4.q: Jamal Hussain can use an AI assistant approved by the university. Staff keep asking him the same questions about how the hub will work, and he wants more time for conversations with doubtful staff such as Tom Brierley. Separately, Peter Langley suggests that AI could pick out students who need support. Which statement BEST describes how AI can support the project?
o: AI could decide which students are at risk for Release 3, removing the need for the ethics committee's review of the early-warning feature.
A project chatbot could answer staff's common questions, freeing Jamal for key conversations, while decisions stay with people.
AI could replace the communication management approach by writing and sending every project update to staff each week.
AI could approve the release map at each stage boundary, because it forecasts time and cost more accurately than the board.
4.w: AI can support people by automating the collection and sharing of information and by running a project chatbot for common questions, freeing leaders for strategic communication. It supports, but does not remove, human decision-making or the need to communicate with stakeholders (book 15.4.2).

n.0: AI does not remove human decision-making; the ethics committee's review and the decision on the feature stay with people (book 15.4.2).
n.2: AI can help spread information, but it does not remove the need to communicate with stakeholders, which the communication management approach plans (book 15.4.2, 4.4).
n.3: AI can refine forecasts for time, cost and benefits, but approving the next stage plan stays with the project board (book 15.4.1, Table 13.4).

5.q: At an early board meeting, the finance director asks Gwen Tallowby why Pinewick is using an agile approach for click and collect rather than specifying every website feature and store process in full before any work starts. The board accepts that customer behaviour in the pilot stores is hard to predict, and that the spring peak leaves no room to move the date. Which explanation BEST describes the benefit of working this way on this project?
o: Using Scrum and Kanban means the project will be delivered faster and at higher quality, because adopting an agile framework brings these gains with it.
Agile working allows the date and budget to move later on if feedback from the pilot stores shows that more features are needed before Easter.
Short feedback loops from Release 1 and the pilot stores let the teams learn what customers and staff need and adapt, reducing effort wasted on unused features.
An agile approach removes the need for the board to authorize each stage, so the teams can respond to customer feedback from the pilot stores without waiting for decisions.
5.w: Where a situation is complex and uncertain there is rarely one perfect solution, so it is better to stay adaptable. Feedback loops and continual improvement reduce waste and lead to better solutions, which is the responsiveness and innovation benefit described in book 2.4. Pinewick cannot predict how customers and stores will respond, so learning from each release and the pilot is the main gain.

n.0: This is the classic misconception the book warns against: adopting a framework does not by itself make delivery faster or better; the value comes from a change of mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: Time and cost have zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile by default, and the board has said neither can move; it is what is delivered that flexes (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Manage by stages still applies: the board authorizes one stage at a time and delegates day-to-day control within tolerances (book 5.2.1.4).

5.q: Six weeks into Stage 2, Nikhil Rao visits the store operations team. The team has set up a Kanban board, holds a short stand-up every morning and uses agile terms in its meetings. However, members wait for Sophie Draper to tell them which card to move next, and nobody questions the order of work even when a store is clearly blocked. Using the Agile Onion, which diagnosis is MOST accurate?
o: The team has taken on practices, the most visible layer, but the mindset at the core has not yet changed, so it looks agile without thinking in an agile way.
The team has taken on processes, the most visible layer, and now needs to add the practices layer by introducing more agile events such as retrospectives.
The team has reached the values layer, the innermost part of the onion, so the remaining gap is a lack of formal process from a framework such as Scrum.
The team has taken on principles, the layer that explains the why, so the problem lies in Sophie Draper's leadership style rather than in the team's understanding.
5.w: In the Agile Onion, practices (techniques and activities such as boards and stand-ups) are the most visible part of agile adoption, and teams that stop there can look agile without the mindset. The mindset is the innermost layer that drives everything (book 2.6.1). A team that waits to be told what to do and never questions priorities is doing agile without yet being agile (book 2.3.1).

n.1: Practices, not processes, are the most visible layer, and adding more events would add more doing rather than change the way the team thinks (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Mindset, not values, is the innermost layer, and nothing in the team's behaviour shows that it has absorbed agile values; more framework process would not close the gap (book 2.6.1).
n.3: A team that has taken on the principles understands the why behind its work; members who never question the order of work have not reached that layer (book 2.6.1).

5.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne, who is new to agile, asks Nikhil Rao to bring two e-commerce team members and a manager from another department that has adopted agile to a session with the store operations team. They describe what helped and what went wrong in their first agile work. Patrick also agrees that the store team will hold a retrospective after each pilot store goes live and change its checklist before the next store. Which principle is Patrick applying, and why?
o: Tailor to suit the project, because he is deciding which agile frameworks and workshops the store operations team will use on the project.
Manage by stages, because the retrospectives divide the pilot into short periods that the board can review and authorize one at a time.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because he is bringing people from other departments into contact with the project team.
Learn from experience, because he is seeking lessons from earlier agile work and building inspect-and-adapt loops into the store roll-out.
