5.w: Learn from experience means seeking and applying lessons from previous work at the start and throughout the project. Many agile concepts support it, such as short feedback loops, inspect and adapt, and retrospectives (book Table 5.1). Patrick gathers lessons from earlier agile adopters and builds a retrospective after each pilot store into the plan.

n.0: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity and context; the purpose here is to gather and apply lessons, not to choose frameworks (book 5.2.1.7).
n.1: Manage by stages concerns the board authorizing one management stage at a time; a retrospective after each store is a team learning loop, not a stage (book 5.2.1.4).
n.2: The visitors share their experience; they are not given roles, and nothing in the stem defines responsibilities or relationships in the project (book 5.2.1.3).

5.q: In Stage 4, the release map shows the project is forecast to finish £60,000 over budget. A packaging supplier offers single-use cardboard boxes that would save £45,000 compared with the reusable crates, which the board set as the minimum sustainability criterion for all collection orders. Installing lockers at 14 stores instead of 20 would save £70,000, and the board has agreed that fewer lockers are acceptable. What should Patrick Dunne recommend?
o: Switch to cardboard boxes and install lockers at slightly fewer stores, because cost has zero tolerance and must be protected before the other aspects of the project.
Keep the reusable crates and install lockers at 14 stores, because sustainability is fixed at its minimum criteria while lower-priority scope can flex.
Keep the crates and all 20 lockers, and move the last stores' go-live to after Easter, so that the extra weeks spread the cost into the next year.
Keep the crates and all 20 lockers, and ask the board to raise the budget by £60,000, because the sustainability strategy has priority over cost.
5.w: PRINCE2 Agile fixes time and cost with zero tolerance, fixes sustainability at its minimum criteria and flexes above them, and fixes scope for Must haves while flexing Should and Could haves (book Table 3.1). Reusable crates are the minimum sustainability criterion, and the board has said lockers can flex, so reducing lockers keeps the project within budget and on time.

n.0: Cardboard boxes would breach the minimum sustainability criterion, which is fixed; protecting cost does not justify falling below it (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Time has zero tolerance, and the board has said the service must be live in every store before Easter; delaying does not reduce cost either (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Cost has zero tolerance by default; the agile response is to flex what is delivered, here the lockers, rather than ask for more money (book Table 3.1, Table 5.1).

5.q: In the store operations team's retrospectives, Sophie Draper answers most suggestions from the two trainers by explaining why the stores' current way of working is better. The trainers say they feel part of the team and enjoy working with Sophie, but they have stopped putting forward ideas. Nikhil Rao is asked for advice. Which action is MOST LIKELY to improve the situation?
o: Raise inclusion safety by holding a team social event so that the trainers feel accepted, while Sophie continues to decide which ideas are worth discussing.
Raise the team's agile maturity by sending the trainers on a Kanban course, as their suggestions show that they do not yet understand how flow works.
Build contributor safety by coaching Sophie to invite everyone's ideas first and to let the team agree which suggestions to try in the next cycle.
Ask Patrick Dunne to chair the retrospectives and rule on each suggestion, so that the trainers' ideas are judged by someone from outside the stores.
5.w: Psychological safety lets people speak up and challenge ideas without fear (book 2.7.4). Contributor safety means people are encouraged to share ideas and skills and their contributions are respected. The trainers already feel accepted, so the gap is in how their contributions are received, which Nikhil can address by coaching Sophie.

n.0: The trainers already feel part of the team, which is inclusion safety; the problem is that their contributions are dismissed, and this option leaves that unchanged (book 2.7.4).
n.1: Nothing suggests the trainers lack knowledge; training would not change the way their ideas are received in retrospectives (book 2.7.3, 2.7.4).
n.3: Having the project manager rule on ideas takes the retrospective away from the team and weakens self-management rather than building contributor safety (book 2.7.4, 13.6.4.2).

5.q: At the starting up workshop, Gwen Tallowby asks why the project needs organizational change management (OCM). In her view the project will deliver the website features, the collection points and the staff training, and store managers can then be told to use them. Bill Rowntree points out that store managers are already worried about extra work at the busiest time of year. Which explanation BEST answers Gwen's question?
o: OCM is a communication activity, so Lucy Fenn's national campaign in February will give store managers and customers the information they need to adopt the service.
OCM moves Pinewick from its current way of working to the target state and helps the culture evolve, so stores keep running collections after the project ends.
OCM is needed to secure compliance, so area managers should audit each store and record any that fail to use the new collection process correctly.
OCM begins once the project closes and the stores take over the service, so it should be planned by Bill Rowntree's team as part of business as usual.
5.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to the target state. When deciding how much of it to plan, the book asks the project to consider the evolving culture and how to make sure changes are not rolled back once the transformation is over (book 4.2.1). Delivering the products is not enough; store managers have to adopt and keep the new way of working.

n.0: Communication is part of OCM, but a national campaign aimed at customers does not address store managers' concerns, and making change stick depends on evolving the culture rather than on messaging (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.2: Audit and compliance may show who is not using the process, but they do not make the change last; the book points to evolving the culture (book 4.2.1).
n.3: OCM covers the transition from current to target state, which runs alongside delivery; frequent releases and user involvement during the project support adoption (book 4.2.1, 4.2.4).

5.q: Patrick Dunne wants a key influencer to help the 85 store managers accept click and collect before the pilot begins. He learns that Sophie Draper has run the store managers' peer forum for five years and is widely trusted by other managers, who often copy changes she makes at the Wrexham store. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to be the key influencer for store managers?
o: Bill Rowntree, because as head of store operations he has the formal authority to instruct area managers and store managers to adopt the new process.
Gwen Tallowby, because as retail operations director she received the mandate and is accountable to the board for the performance of the stores.
Elena Marsh, because Tallis supplies the stock system that store managers rely on, and she can explain how live stock levels will work in stores.
Sophie Draper, because she is a store manager with a trusted network among her peers, whose views shape how other managers see the change.
5.w: Key influencers are people who can shape how the majority perceive a change and who, through their network, most influence its adoption and the realization of benefits (book 4.2.2). Sophie is a fellow store manager, runs the managers' peer forum and is copied by others, so her view will shape how store managers see click and collect.

n.0: Formal authority can secure compliance, but a key influencer is chosen for network and credibility among the people adopting the change, not for position (book 4.2.2).
n.1: Gwen is senior and accountable, which suits governance, but nothing suggests store managers look to her as a peer whose example they follow (book 4.2.2).
n.2: A supplier can explain the system, but the key influencer is the person whose network shapes store managers' perception, not a technical specialist outside Pinewick (book 4.2.2).

5.q: Two Tallis developers join the e-commerce team's refinement sessions and sprint reviews to advise on the new stock interface. After a few weeks there is friction: the e-commerce developers expect Tallis to accept their design choices, while the Tallis developers believe they should decide the interface's data format and update frequency. Tallis works to its own quarterly release cycle. What should Patrick Dunne do to lead this cross-organization team MOST effectively?
o: Agree with Elena Marsh and both teams a delegation matrix showing which interface decisions Tallis makes, which it advises on and which the e-commerce team makes.
Ask Elena Marsh to move the Tallis developers onto the e-commerce team's two-week sprints, so that both organizations follow one framework and timetable.
Route all questions about the interface through himself and Elena Marsh, so that developers in the two organizations no longer need to negotiate the design directly.
Ask the two Tallis developers to work at Pinewick's head office every day until Release 1, so that the teams resolve their differences face to face.
5.w: When people work across organizations and cultures, the book advises setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that makes clear what external specialists decide and what they advise on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3). The friction here is about who decides, so making decision rights transparent addresses its cause.

n.1: Tallis has said it cannot change its cycle for one customer, and putting everyone on one framework would not settle who decides what about the interface (book 4.3.1).
n.2: Funnelling questions through two managers slows communication and reduces collaboration, and it still leaves decision boundaries unclear (book 4.3.1, 2.6.2).
n.3: Requiring daily co-location is not the effective answer; planned co-location days can help, but the friction comes from unclear decision rights (book 4.3.3).

5.q: Three members of the store operations team work from their own stores in Cardiff, Leeds and Exeter, while the two trainers are based at head office. The team has always reported progress by email, and Patrick Dunne notices that the store-based members often learn about decisions days after the trainers. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to improve communication in this hybrid team?
o: Ask each member to send Sophie Draper a fuller weekly email report, so that she can pass a single summary on to everyone at the end of each week.
Ask the three store-based members to relocate to head office for the whole of Stage 3, so that the team can work together in one place every day.
Agree how information will flow, keep the Kanban board online for all, hold structured and informal video time, and plan in-person days for key events.
Let the two head office trainers make day-to-day decisions, as they share an office, and ask the store-based members to concentrate on preparing their own stores.
5.w: Remote and hybrid teams need a more deliberate, structured approach to communication: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, identifying key relationships and agreeing both structured and unstructured time together (book 4.4). Planned co-location days for key people and moments help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3).

n.0: Periodic written reporting is not enough on its own and keeps information flowing one way and late, which is the problem the team already has (book 4.4).
n.1: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer for a team spread across stores; the book suggests planned co-location days instead (book 4.3.3).
n.3: Splitting decisions by location creates a two-tier team and damages the social cohesion and collaboration a hybrid team needs (book 4.3.3, 2.6.2).

5.q: Bill Rowntree wants to keep the store operations team motivated through the busy Stage 4 roll-out. He proposes a cash bonus for each member based on how many stores they personally take live, ranked in a league table that he will publish to all store managers. Nikhil Rao is asked for advice. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on building and leading agile teams?
o: Keep Bill's individual bonus but show the league table to the team rather than to all store managers, to reduce the public pressure on members.
Replace the bonus with a personal target for each member, set by Sophie Draper and reviewed against each member's results at the end of the stage.
Avoid incentives, because motivation in an agile team comes from personal values and is best left to each member to manage for themselves.
Use peer-assessed recognition for behaviour that reflects the team's agreed values, balanced with purpose and recognition, instead of individual targets.
5.w: The book suggests motivating agile teams through value-based incentives, such as peer-assessed points for behaviour that models agile values, balanced with intangible motivators such as purpose and recognition and with personal values. Team values can be used in peer-based assessments in retrospectives (book 4.5).

n.0: Rewarding individual go-live counts still sets members against each other, which works against collaboration; hiding the table does not make the incentive value-based (book 4.5).
n.1: Manager-set individual targets do not reflect values the team has agreed or peer assessment, which the book recommends (book 4.5).
n.2: The book does not leave motivation to chance; it recommends value-based incentives balanced with intangible motivators and personal values (book 4.5).

5.q: At the starting up workshop, Bill Rowntree says that no store should offer click and collect until its stock accuracy is at least 97%, because customers would otherwise arrive to find items missing. Patrick Dunne wants this requirement defined, together with how it will be measured in each store, by the practice designed for that purpose. Which practice should handle it, and why?
o: Risk, because it identifies, assesses and controls uncertain events, such as stock accuracy failing to improve, that would affect the project's objectives.
Progress, because it compares actual achievements in each store against those planned and controls any deviations that would cause an exception.
Business case, because it judges whether the investment in each store is and remains desirable, viable and achievable for Pinewick.
Quality, because it documents the users' requirements for the project's products and establishes the means by which they will be met.
5.w: The quality practice documents what users require of the project's products and sets up how those requirements will be met; it answers what is acceptable to users and how that is measured (book 9.1). A minimum stock accuracy of 97% before a store goes live is an acceptance requirement of that kind.

n.0: The chance that accuracy will not improve in time is a risk, but defining the 97% requirement and how it is measured is the job of the quality practice (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.1: Progress monitors achievement against plan and handles exceptions; it does not define what is acceptable to users (book 12.1).
n.2: The business case practice keeps the justification for the investment under review; it does not set the acceptance criteria a store must meet (book 6.1).

5.q: In starting up a project, Gwen Tallowby leads the project canvas workshop. The finance director has said he will support the project if there is evidence that click and collect increases total sales, rather than moving existing sales from home delivery into stores. How should the benefits section of the project canvas reflect his concern?
o: List the click and collect service in all 85 stores as the main benefit, because it is the product the finance director is being asked to fund.
State a measurable benefit, such as the net rise in total sales at stores offering collection compared with similar stores, with a tolerance.
Record the number of reservations made through the website as the benefit, because each reservation represents an extra sale for Pinewick.
Leave the benefits section blank until after closure, because benefits are confirmed once the service has run through a full spring peak.
5.w: The benefits section of the project canvas sets out expected benefits that are measurable and have a tolerance (book 6.3.2). A benefit is a measurable improvement that the investing organization sees as an advantage, so a net increase in sales, measured against comparable stores, answers the finance director directly.

n.0: The service in 85 stores is the project's output, part of its scope; an output is not a benefit (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.2: Reservations could simply move sales from home delivery into stores, so counting them does not measure the net improvement the finance director asked about (book 6.3.2).
n.3: The canvas must show expected benefits now to justify the investment; benefits are confirmed later, but they must be defined from the start (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2).

5.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne drafts the benefits management approach. Release 1, live stock levels by store on the website, is due in month 3, long before the full service is live in all stores. Market research shows that a third of customers have travelled to a store and found an item out of stock. How should the benefits management approach treat Release 1?
o: Measure no benefits until Release 3 is complete, because the benefits of click and collect come from the full service operating in all 85 stores.
Treat Release 1 as an output for the e-commerce team to accept, because the benefits of each release are reported in the end project report.
Plan to measure early benefits from Release 1, such as fewer wasted trips to stores, because frequent releases are planned to deliver benefits early.
Plan to measure Release 1 benefits in the post-project benefits review, because benefits are realized once products are in use by customers after the project.
5.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases so that benefits can be delivered early (book 6.3.2), and iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project rather than after it (book 6.3.1). Release 1 goes live in month 3 and addresses wasted trips, so its benefits can be measured from then on.

n.0: Waiting for the full service throws away the early benefits that frequent releases are planned to deliver (book 6.3.2).
n.1: The end project report compares performance with the PID; benefits are measured as set out in the benefits management approach, and Release 1 can start delivering them during the project (book 6.3.2, Table 12.1).
n.3: Release 1 is in live use from month 3, so its benefits can be measured during the project; leaving them to the post-project review loses early evidence (book 6.3.1).

5.q: At the end of Stage 3, sales data from the 10 pilot stores show that about half of the collection orders came from customers who would otherwise have bought online for home delivery. Patrick Dunne updates the project canvas with the pilot results and a revised expected case, and asks the board to confirm that Release 3 is still justified before it authorizes Stage 4. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the business justification must remain valid throughout, so the canvas is updated with real results for the board to review at the stage boundary.
Yes, because the revised canvas allows Patrick to raise the budget for Stage 4 to pay for the extra marketing needed to attract new customers to stores.
No, because the budget and date cannot change, so the business case was settled when the board authorized the project and does not need revisiting.
No, because benefits are measured after the project closes, so the pilot results should be held back for the post-project benefits review.
5.w: Ensure continued business justification requires a valid justification throughout the project (book 5.2.1.1). At a stage boundary the board reviews the current stage and confirms continued business justification before approving the next stage (book 13.7.1). Updating the canvas with real pilot results gives the board the evidence it needs.

n.1: Cost has zero tolerance by default; the canvas is updated to test the justification, not to increase the budget (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Fixed time and cost do not remove the need to check justification; the board confirms it at every stage boundary (book 5.2.1.1, 13.7.1).
n.3: The pilot results are real evidence about viability, and checking viability at the stage boundary depends on them; some benefits can be realized during the project (book 6.3.1, 13.7.1).

5.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne and Elena Marsh agree how Tallis will work with the project. The new stock interface will be delivered in Tallis's quarterly releases, both parties will use an agreed Definition of Done for the interface, and Tallis will report its progress through the project dashboard. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure, because it describes who is involved in the project and how the teams and people work together.
In the commercial management approach, because it sets out how the supplier arrangement will support agile delivery and how progress is tracked.
In the role descriptions, because they describe the specific responsibilities that Elena Marsh and the Tallis developers have in the project.
In the risk register, because the dependency on Tallis's quarterly release cycle is the main uncertainty that could affect Release 1.
5.w: The commercial management approach makes sure procurement and contracts support agile product development, for example through an agreed Definition of Done, the delivery model, and guidelines for tracking and reporting (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3). The agreed working terms with Tallis belong there.

n.0: The project management team structure covers who is involved, their relationships and arrangements such as co-location; the terms of the supplier arrangement belong in the commercial management approach (book 7.3.2).
n.2: Role descriptions set out the responsibilities of roles in the project management team; they do not hold the terms on which a supplier delivers (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The dependency may also be logged as a risk, but the agreed way of working with the supplier is a commercial arrangement, not a risk record (book 7.3.2, 10.3.2).

5.q: At the start of Stage 3, the store operations team and Patrick Dunne disagree about who should decide matters such as the order in which the pilot stores are prepared, changes to collection-point signage and the timing of staff training sessions. Sophie Draper says her team keeps waiting for approvals it may not need. Which technique should Patrick use with the team?
o: A team skill matrix, completed with the team, showing which members have the skills needed to make each type of decision about the pilot stores.
A product flow diagram, showing the order in which pilot stores, signage and training must be completed and who signs off each step.
A responsibility chart drawn up by Patrick and Bill Rowntree and issued to the team, setting out which decisions each member may take.
Delegation poker, so that Patrick and the team agree the level of delegation for each decision area and record it in a delegation matrix.
5.w: Delegation poker is a collaborative technique for defining how decisions are made within teams (book 7.4.2), and a delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision authority transparent, showing who decides and who is involved for each decision area (book 7.4.3). The dispute is about decision rights, so these techniques address it.

n.0: A team skill matrix shows capabilities, strengths and gaps; it does not settle who has authority to decide (book 7.4.1).
n.1: A product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products, not who makes which decisions (book 8.4.2).
n.2: A chart imposed by managers does not involve the team; delegation poker agrees decision levels collaboratively, which supports self-management (book 7.4.2).

5.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne proposes that Fran Okonedo, the e-commerce team's Scrum master, also act as team coach for the store operations team. Fran has coached a Kanban team before and will facilitate the store team's workshops and help it manage itself, while Sophie Draper looks after the team's work and backlog. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the team coach is accountable for delivering the work packages of both teams, which keeps the two teams' work aligned.
Yes, because a team coach works closely with one or two teams, helping them to self-manage and facilitating their workshops.
No, because each delivery team must have its own dedicated team coach, so the store operations team needs a separate coach.
No, because coaching a team that is new to agile is the agile coach's role, so Nikhil Rao should coach the store operations team.
5.w: A team coach works closely with one or two specific teams, helping them self-manage, facilitating team workshops and coaching agile practices; a Scrum master fits this role (book Table 7.2, 7.3). Coaching both teams is within that span, and the team's work stays with its own lead.

n.0: Delivering allocated work within agreed tolerances is the product owner's responsibility, not the team coach's (book Table 7.2).
n.2: The book says a team coach can work with one or two teams, so a coach shared by two teams is acceptable (book 7.3, Figure 7.2).
n.3: The agile coach works across the organization on systemic blockers and supports leaders; team-level coaching is the team coach's role (book Table 7.2).

5.q: Pinewick's board asks Patrick Dunne to propose who should take the project executive role. The person must be accountable for the project, approve the tolerances within which the teams make agile decisions, and act as a role model for agile adoption across the business. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the project executive role?
o: Marcus Lindell, because as head of e-commerce he owns the website and app roadmap and represents online customers' needs.
George Ahmed, because as head of internal audit he can give the board independent assurance that the project is controlled.
Gwen Tallowby, because she received the mandate and is accountable to the board for the store performance the project must improve.
Bill Rowntree, because as head of store operations he manages the area managers and store standards that the roll-out will change.
5.w: The project executive is accountable for the project and its strategic alignment, approves the tolerances for agile decision-making and acts as a role model for agile adoption (book Table 7.2). Gwen was given the mandate by the board and answers to it for store performance, which the project exists to improve, so she is the natural person to hold that accountability.

n.0: Marcus represents online customers' needs and owns the roadmap, which suits a user-facing role such as chief product owner rather than overall accountability (book Table 7.2).
n.1: George's independent audit view suits a project assurance contribution, which checks how the project is run on the board's behalf; he was not given the mandate and is not accountable for the project's outcome (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Bill speaks for store operations, an important user and stakeholder group, but he was not given the mandate or the accountability for the project's success (book Table 7.2).

5.q: Patrick Dunne needs a product owner for the e-commerce team. The person will own the team's product backlog, keep it aligned with the project backlog and agree sets of user stories with Patrick as work packages. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the product owner role for the e-commerce team?
o: Anita Shah, because she already manages the e-commerce team's backlog and works day to day with the team that will build the features.
Fran Okonedo, because as the team's Scrum master she runs its sprint events and knows how the team plans and estimates its work.
Marcus Lindell, because he owns the roadmap for the website and app and represents online customers' needs across Pinewick.
Nikhil Rao, because he helped the e-commerce team adopt agile and understands how it turns customer needs into new features.
5.w: The product owner is a version of the team manager role: they own one team's product backlog, keep it aligned with the project backlog, prepare user stories and agree work package descriptions with the project manager (book Table 7.2). Anita already manages the e-commerce team's backlog.

n.1: A Scrum master fits the team coach role, which helps the team self-manage and facilitates its workshops (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Marcus owns the roadmap across channels and represents customers, which fits the chief product owner role, prioritizing across teams, rather than one team's backlog (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Nikhil is an agile coach, a role that works across the organization on systemic blockers rather than owning a team's backlog (book Table 7.2).

5.q: Four weeks into Stage 4, the store operations team's Kanban board shows that, in addition to the 10 pilot stores, it has taken 24 stores live, a steady rate of about six stores a week. Patrick Dunne must forecast whether the remaining 51 stores will be ready before Easter. Bill Rowntree suggests using the rate of ten stores a week that a contractor achieved in last year's store refit programme. How should Patrick forecast the roll-out?
o: Use the store operations team's own measured rate of about six stores a week to forecast the finish, and update the release map with the result.
Use the contractor's rate of ten stores a week, because it comes from a larger programme and so gives a more reliable basis for the forecast.
Ask each area manager to estimate a go-live date for each remaining store, and combine their estimates into a detailed schedule for the stage.
Work back from the Easter deadline to set the rate needed each week, and plan the remaining stores so that this rate is met.
5.w: PRINCE2 Agile planning is empirical: start the work, measure how much gets done and use that to forecast (book 8.3). The rate should be the team's own, not another person's or team's. The store operations team has a steady measured rate, so it is the right basis, and the release map is updated with the forecast.

n.1: Another organization's rate on different work is not evidence of what this team can do; forecasts should use the team's own measured rate (book 8.3).
n.2: Estimates from people outside the team are reasoned predictions rather than measured experience, and they ignore the data the team already has (book 8.3).
n.3: Working back from the deadline sets a target; it does not forecast what the team will actually achieve from its measured rate (book 8.3).

5.q: During initiation, the teams turn their user story map into a release map. Live stock levels on the website depend on Tallis's new interface, and Tallis's quarterly releases fall in months 2, 5 and 8. Elena Marsh has confirmed that Tallis will not change these dates for Pinewick. How should Patrick Dunne and the teams reflect this in the release map?
o: Leave the Tallis dates out of the release map and record them in the risk register, because they are outside the project's control.
Plan every sprint for both teams in detail for the full nine months, so that each task linked to the Tallis interface can be scheduled exactly.
Ask Elena Marsh to bring forward Tallis's month 5 release, so that the interface work for Release 2 arrives earlier in the stage.
Show the dependency on each Tallis release and place the features that need the interface in releases that follow the matching Tallis date.
5.w: Turning a story map into a release map also defines the interdependencies, and releases are planned around them (book 8.3.1.1). The release map shows how many releases there are, when they happen and which features they contain (book 8.3.2), so it should show the Tallis dates and sequence the dependent features after them.

n.0: The dependency may also be a risk, but release planning must take known interdependencies into account rather than leave them out (book 8.3.1.1).
n.1: Detailed task-level planning is done just in time for the next iteration in a team plan, not for the whole project in advance (book 8.3.2).
n.2: Tallis has confirmed that its dates will not change, so the plan has to work around them rather than depend on a request already refused.

5.q: In initiation, Patrick Dunne builds a release map with both teams from their story map, showing the three releases with their epics and main user stories. Detailed plans for each sprint and each store are left to the teams' planning workshops. Gwen Tallowby asks for a day-by-day plan of every task for the nine months because the date cannot move, but Patrick keeps his approach. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the release map is owned by the chief product owner, so the project manager is not the right person to produce detailed plans.
Yes, because plans are made just in time: the release map stays high level and the teams make task-level plans for the next iteration.
No, because zero tolerance on time means the board must approve a detailed baseline of every task before the project can start.
No, because a release map covers a single release, so Patrick needs a separate stage plan for each of the three releases as well.
5.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the release map is kept at a high level and updated at stage boundaries, while task-level planning is done by the delivery team in a team plan for the next iteration (book 8.3.2). Planning every task for nine months would rest on guesses; the plan is refined empirically as the teams learn (book 8.3).

n.0: The chief product owner owns the project backlog; the release map is the project plan, which the project manager prepares with the teams (book 8.3.2, Table 7.2).
n.2: With time fixed, PRINCE2 Agile flexes what is delivered; a detailed baseline of every task is not needed and would not stay accurate (book Table 3.1, 8.3).
n.3: The release map serves as both the project plan and the stage plan, with the stage view covering a shorter horizon (book 8.3.2).

5.q: In Stage 2, the e-commerce team twice pulls stories about showing stock levels into a sprint and then finds that the field names and test data for the Tallis interface are not yet available. Both stories stall and roll over to the next sprint. Anita Shah asks how to stop this happening again. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on quality?
o: Add 'interface tested with Tallis data' to the Definition of Done, so that the stories cannot be counted as complete until the data is available.
Agree a Definition of Ready requiring the interface details and test data to be available before a story that needs them enters a sprint.
Let the team start the stories anyway and swarm on them once the data arrives, so that the sprint can still finish with them complete.
Ask Elena Marsh to set the order of the stories that use the interface, so that Tallis decides when the work is pulled into a sprint.
5.w: A Definition of Ready is a shared team agreement on the criteria an item must meet before work begins, such as clear information, resources and dependencies being in place (book 9.3.2.1). The stories stalled because they entered sprints before their dependency was met.

n.0: The Definition of Done sets the criteria for an item to be complete; the problem is that work started before the story was ready (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Swarming helps a team clear a blocker, but starting stories that cannot progress would repeat the stalls; readiness should be checked first (book 11.4.2, 9.3.2.1).
n.3: The product owner owns and orders the team's product backlog; handing that to the supplier would not ensure stories are ready (book Table 7.2).

5.q: In Stage 3, the e-commerce team cannot agree whether customers are more likely to complete a reservation if the 'reserve and collect' button appears above or below the delivery options on the product page. Marcus Lindell prefers it above, while Anita Shah prefers it below. Both layouts are quick to build. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Ask Marcus Lindell to decide, because he represents online customers' needs and owns the roadmap for the website and app.
Refactor the product page so that both layouts are coded cleanly, then choose one of them at the next sprint review.
Run an A/B test, showing each layout to a share of real customers and comparing how many go on to complete a reservation.
Survey the 85 store managers on which layout they think customers would prefer, and build the one the majority favours.
5.w: A/B testing compares two versions of a product with real users to see which performs better (book 9.4.3). It replaces opinion with evidence about which layout leads more customers to complete a reservation.

n.0: Marcus's preference is still an opinion; testing with users gives evidence of what customers actually do (book 9.4.3).
n.1: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour; it does not tell the team which layout customers respond to (book 9.4.1).
n.3: Store managers are not the users of the product page, and a survey of opinions is not a test with customers (book 9.4.3).

5.q: Early in Stage 4, Bill Rowntree proposes that the store operations team marks a store's card as done once staff are trained and the collection point works, and that stock accuracy is checked in the weeks after the store goes live, to save time during the peak. Patrick Dunne agrees and updates the quality management approach accordingly. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the quality management approach can record the organization's own procedures, and Bill is responsible for store standards.
Yes, because stock accuracy is a risk rather than a quality criterion, so it belongs in the risk register instead of the Definition of Done.
No, because the Definition of Done must be set by the project board, so Patrick cannot change it through the quality management approach.
No, because a store is done once every agreed criterion is met, including 97% stock accuracy, and there is no such state as almost done.
5.w: The Definition of Done is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be complete, and an item is either done or not done, with no almost done (book 9.3.2.2). The go-live condition for each store includes stock accuracy of at least 97%, so a store cannot be counted as done before that is met.

n.0: An organization's own procedures can be recorded as a tailoring decision, but this change removes an agreed acceptance criterion from the meaning of done (book 9.3.1, 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Whether accuracy will reach 97% in time is a risk, but the 97% threshold itself is a go-live criterion that each store must meet (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: A Definition of Done is a shared agreement among those doing and accepting the work; it is not reserved to the board, and the reason the change fails is that it drops a criterion (book 9.3.2.2).

5.q: In the agile enablement workshop at the start of Stage 3, the participants review the Agilometer. Lucy Fenn has insisted that every feature to be advertised in February must be in Release 3, and the board has started to treat almost every item in the project backlog as a Must have. Which slider does this MOST directly affect, and how could it be improved?
o: Level of collaboration; it could be improved by inviting Lucy Fenn to the e-commerce team's sprint reviews so that she sees progress first-hand.
Ease of communication; it could be improved by sending the board a summary of the project backlog at the end of each sprint.
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally; it could be improved by moving the national campaign to after Easter.
Flexibility on what is delivered; it could be improved by challenging whether so many requirements are really Must haves.
5.w: The flexibility on what is delivered slider reflects how comfortable stakeholders are with flexing scope and with their role in prioritizing work (book 10.3.2.2). One way to raise it is to challenge whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them (book 10.3.2.3).

n.0: Collaboration concerns how closely people work together; treating everything as a Must have is about willingness to flex scope (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: Ease of communication is about how easily all parties communicate; more summaries would not change the board's view of what must be delivered (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: This slider concerns delivering benefit through regular partial deliveries; the issue here is stakeholders' unwillingness to flex scope, and moving the campaign does not change that (book 10.3.2.2).

5.q: George Ahmed asks how the e-commerce team can show whether its overall exposure to the main delivery risks, such as payment security weaknesses and interface delays, is falling from one sprint to the next. Patrick Dunne wants a technique that the team can keep up to date itself as part of its normal planning. Which technique should the team use?
o: A cumulative risk burn-down chart, with the team rating the likelihood of each tracked risk at every sprint planning session.
The Agilometer, reassessed at every sprint planning session, so that the board can see how the team's delivery risks change.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many risk responses are in each state of the team's workflow at the end of each day.
A burn-up chart of the risk responses completed in each sprint, plotted against the total number of responses planned.
5.w: In a cumulative risk burn-down chart the team rates the likelihood of each tracked risk at the first planning meeting and updates it at each planning session; the chart shows total risk exposure across iterations, which should fall over time (book 10.4.2).

n.1: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, not the project's delivery risks such as payment security (book 10.3.2).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows how many items are in each workflow state over time and reveals bottlenecks; it does not show risk exposure (book 12.4.2).
n.3: Counting completed responses shows work done, not whether the likelihood of the risks, and so the exposure, is falling (book 10.4.2, 12.4.3).

5.q: In the project initiation workshop, all participants assess the Agilometer and the results are combined into a single project view. Patrick Dunne then files it with the PID and tells the board that it will not need to be repeated, because the e-commerce team has used agile for three years. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the Agilometer is a progress tool, and progress against the release map is reported through the project dashboard instead.
Yes, because a team with several years of agile experience already understands the risks that agile working brings to its projects.
No, because the Agilometer should be reassessed regularly in later stages, and this project adds a store team new to agile and a supplier.
No, because the Agilometer should be completed by Nikhil Rao as agile coach rather than by the participants of the workshop.
5.w: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working (book 10.3.1, 10.3.2). It is first assessed in the project initiation workshop and then reassessed regularly in later stages, for example in the agile enablement workshop, with trends shown on the project dashboard (book Table 13.5). Pinewick has never run a project combining technology, store operations and an external supplier, and the store team is new to agile.

n.0: The Agilometer belongs to the risk practice; it assesses risks of agile working, not progress (book 10.3.2).
n.1: One team's experience does not cover the store operations team or the supplier, and the book expects regular reassessment (book Table 13.5).
n.3: In the project initiation workshop all participants assess the Agilometer and the results are combined, so the workshop assessment is the intended approach (book Table 13.7).

5.q: During a Stage 3 sprint, staff in the pilot stores say the reservation confirmation email confuses customers because the collection point is described at the bottom. They ask for the store's collection point details to appear at the top. The change does not alter any epic or requirement in the project backlog. How should this change be handled?
o: As a request for change, recorded in an issue report and sent to the project board for a decision before the email is altered.
As an off-specification, because the email does not meet its quality specification and must be reported to Patrick Dunne.
As a detail change, agreed informally between the team and Anita Shah and handled within the team's product backlog.
As an exception, because changing a feature already released to the pilot stores means the stage is forecast to exceed tolerance.
5.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change. It is seen as making the final product more accurate and is handled informally at team level (book 11.3.2), here between the team and its product owner, Anita Shah.

n.0: Formal handling by the board or change authority is for changes to the project baseline, which in PRINCE2 Agile means the project backlog; this change does not affect it (book 11.3.2).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; the email works as specified, and staff are suggesting an improvement (book 11.3.1).
n.3: An exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; nothing suggests a small wording change threatens any tolerance (book Table 12.1).

5.q: In Stage 4, the collection point at one large store is stuck in the preparation column because the store's handheld scanners cannot connect to the new stock system. Rather than raising an issue straight away, the store operations team stops starting new stores for a day and works on the problem together with one e-commerce developer. They agree to tell Patrick Dunne if it is still unresolved by the end of the week. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because swarming focuses the team on a blocker together, and it should be tried before an issue is escalated to the project manager.
Yes, because trading lets the team swap the blocked store for another store of similar effort, which keeps the roll-out on schedule.
No, because every problem should be captured in the issue register and reported to the project board before the team acts on it.
No, because pausing new work for a day breaks the team's work-in-progress limits, so the blocked store should go back to the backlog.
5.w: Swarming is when the team focuses together on a stuck task or blocker, which can also speed up time-critical work; the book suggests trying it before escalating an issue to the project manager (book 11.4.2). The team escalates if it cannot resolve the problem.

n.1: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort to absorb a change; the team has not swapped anything, and trading is not a way to remove a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Swarming comes first; a problem is escalated as an issue if the team cannot resolve it, and the board is involved for decisions beyond the project manager's tolerance (book 11.4.2).
n.3: Stopping new work to clear a blocker keeps work in progress down, which is consistent with limiting it; moving the store back would leave the problem unsolved (book 11.4.2).

5.q: George Ahmed asks how the board will know, between stage boundaries, whether the project is still on track. Patrick Dunne, used to sending weekly written reports on construction projects, wants to meet this need while following PRINCE2 Agile guidance on the progress practice. What should Patrick propose?
o: A highlight report emailed to each board member every Friday, summarizing both teams' progress in the same format he used for construction projects.
Board members taking turns to attend the e-commerce team's daily stand-ups, so that they hear about progress directly from the developers.
An end stage report at each stage boundary, with a detailed list of the tasks completed and the costs incurred in that stage.
A project dashboard, built from the team dashboards and showing release status, burn charts and current risks, that the board can view at any time.
5.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project dashboard replaces the highlight report and end stage report. The board pulls information from it rather than having reports pushed to it, and it shows items such as release status, burn charts, current risks and issues, and Agilometer trends (book Table 12.1, 12.3.2.1). It is updated from the team dashboards and reviewed in progress review workshops.

n.0: A pushed weekly report is what the project dashboard replaces in PRINCE2 Agile; the board pulls the information it needs (book Table 12.1).
n.1: Stand-ups are the team's own events, which even the project manager attends with the team's agreement, and they do not give the board a project-level view (book Table 12.1).
n.2: George asked about the period between stage boundaries; an end stage report comes at the boundary itself (book Table 12.1).

5.q: In Stage 2, Patrick Dunne sets up progress control as he did in construction. Each week he measures the percentage of the budget spent and the percentage of the nine months used, and reports the project as on track while both figures stay below 100%. He does not track which user stories or store tasks have been completed. Which is the MAIN weakness of this approach?
o: Spend should be tracked monthly rather than weekly, because weekly figures on an agile project change too often to show a reliable trend.
With zero tolerance on time and cost, the aspect of interest is how much is being delivered, which burn charts of completed work would show.
The board should receive these figures in an exception report each week, because the stage plan has no tolerance for time or cost.
The time measure should be replaced by velocity, because the date can move if the teams' velocity shows that more time is needed.
5.w: Because time and cost have zero tolerance, flexibility in what is delivered is the main aspect of interest, and burn charts suit every level; tracking spend against a budget or time tolerance adds little when both are fixed (book 12.3.1). Patrick's measures cannot show whether the Must haves will be delivered.

n.0: The frequency is not the problem; whatever the interval, budget and time used say nothing about how much has been delivered (book 12.3.1).
n.2: An exception report is raised when a plan is forecast to exceed its tolerances, not as a routine weekly report (book Table 12.1).
n.3: Time has zero tolerance; velocity is used to forecast what can be delivered in the fixed time, not to move the date (book Table 3.1, 12.4.3).

5.q: In starting up a project, Gwen Tallowby runs the project canvas workshop. The group compares doing nothing, building click and collect in-house with Tallis exposing stock levels, buying a ready-made module from a retail platform, and selling through a third-party marketplace that offers collection. They agree which of these to take forward. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop is this discussed?
o: Business option selection.
Business value definition.
Scope definition.
Benefits analysis.
5.w: Business option selection is the project canvas workshop topic in which the group weighs the alternative ways of meeting the need, including doing nothing, and chooses the one to pursue (book Table 13.2).

n.1: Business value definition sets out the value the project should bring to the organization; it does not compare alternative solutions (book Table 13.2).
n.2: Scope definition covers the timeline and tolerance, the scope as epics prioritized with MoSCoW, and dependencies, once an option has been chosen (book Table 13.2).
n.3: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits, usually in small groups, and their tolerances; it does not choose between options (book Table 13.2).

5.q: Near the end of starting up a project, Patrick Dunne confirms the project's objectives, scope, tolerances and constraints. He also records that Release 1 depends on Tallis's quarterly release in month 2, and that Lucy Fenn's February campaign depends on the service being ready in the stores it will advertise. Which activity of the 'starting up a project' process is Patrick carrying out?
o: Select the project approach.
Assemble the project brief.
Plan the initiation stage.
Prepare the outline business case.
5.w: In assembling the project brief, the project manager confirms the objectives, outcomes, scope, exclusions, tolerances, constraints, assumptions and dependencies, including dependencies on other initiatives (book Table 13.1).

n.0: Selecting the project approach evaluates delivery solutions, decides the approach and defines any known tailoring requirements (book Table 13.1).
n.2: Planning the initiation stage sets the time and cost constraints for initiation and produces a high-level release map for it (book Table 13.1).
n.3: Preparing the outline business case is where the executive leads the project canvas and the project backlog is created (book Table 13.1).

5.q: At the start of Stage 3, the board, Nikhil Rao and several area managers hold an agile enablement workshop. After reviewing the latest Agilometer results, they list further threats to agile working that the Agilometer does not cover, such as area managers asking stores for weekly written reports instead of using the team dashboard. Under which topic of the workshop does this listing take place?
o: Agilometer assessment review.
Risk identification.
Risk assessment.
Risk planning.
5.w: In the agile enablement workshop, the risk identification topic looks for additional threats and opportunities to agile adoption that the Agilometer does not capture (book Table 13.5).

n.0: The Agilometer assessment review links the Agilometer's risk areas to agile values and transformation objectives and builds a shared view of them; the threats here lie outside the Agilometer (book Table 13.5).
n.2: Risk assessment estimates the probability and impact of risks already identified and prioritizes them (book Table 13.5).
n.3: Risk planning agrees practical steps to mitigate the risks; the group is still listing them (book Table 13.5).

5.q: At the end of starting up a project, the board reviews the project brief and the high-level release map for the one-month initiation stage. Gwen Tallowby confirms that the board is content, lets the store managers and Tallis know that initiation is beginning, and asks Patrick Dunne to start work. Which activity of the 'directing a project' process is the board carrying out?
o: Authorize the project.
Give ongoing direction.
Authorize a stage or exception plan.
Authorize initiation.
5.w: In authorizing initiation, the board approves the project brief and the release map for initiation, informs stakeholders and authorizes the project manager to initiate the project (book Table 13.4).

n.0: Authorizing the project comes after initiation, when the board approves the PID and commits resources for delivery (book Table 13.4).
n.1: Ongoing direction is informal guidance given at any time in response to requests, issues or reports, not the formal start of initiation (book Table 13.4).
n.2: Authorizing a stage or exception plan approves an updated release map at a stage boundary or after an exception (book Table 13.4).

5.q: In the project initiation workshop, the teams, Elena Marsh and Bill Rowntree agree criteria that any epic must meet before a team starts work on it, such as the interface details being confirmed with Tallis and the store's current stock accuracy figure being available. Under which topic of the project initiation workshop should this be agreed?
o: Management approaches.
Project Definition of Done.
Project Definition of Ready.
High-level release planning.
5.w: The project Definition of Ready topic of the project initiation workshop agrees the product-wide criteria that work must meet before it starts (book Table 13.7).

n.0: The management approaches topic co-creates approaches such as risk and quality; criteria for starting work belong to the project Definition of Ready (book Table 13.7).
n.1: The project Definition of Done sets the criteria for work to be acceptable to users, not the conditions for starting it (book Table 13.7).
n.3: High-level release planning develops or updates the release map; it does not set entry criteria for epics (book Table 13.7).

5.q: At the project kickoff workshop, the store operations team lists who can train staff on the handheld scanners, who has designed store signage before and who knows the stock system. They find that one trainer is the sole person able to teach the scanner process, and plan for a second member to learn it. Under which topic of the project kickoff workshop does this take place?
o: Team delegation matrix.
Team values and norms.
Psychological safety.
Team skill matrix.
5.w: The team skill matrix topic of the project kickoff workshop maps the team's skills, gaps and overlaps (book Table 13.8), giving an overview of capabilities and training needs (book 7.4.1).

n.0: The team delegation matrix clarifies who decides what, to simplify decisions and support self-management; it does not map skills (book Table 13.8).
n.1: Team values and norms build an agile culture and shared expectations of behaviour (book Table 13.8).
n.2: The psychological safety topic assesses whether people feel safe to speak up and take risks (book Table 13.8).

5.q: Midway through Stage 3, Patrick Dunne holds a progress review workshop with the board, Marcus Lindell and Sophie Draper. After the welcome, they look at the project dashboard metrics, including the burn-up chart for Release 2 and the number of pilot stores live, and celebrate the first four stores taking collection orders. Under which topic of the workshop does this take place?
o: Product demo.
Current risks and issues.
Project highlights.
Welcome.
5.w: In the progress review workshop, the project highlights topic reviews the project dashboard metrics and achievements, which supports the workshop's aim of assessing status and celebrating success (book Table 13.10).

n.0: The product demo shows completed features to gather user acceptance and feedback; the group is reviewing dashboard metrics, not using the product (book Table 13.10).
n.1: Current risks and issues looks at open risks and issues and how to address them (book Table 13.10).
n.3: The welcome opens the session; the stem says the review of metrics comes after it (book Table 13.10).

5.q: At the e-commerce team's team planning workshop for sprint 9, the stories at the top of the product backlog have already been refined and estimated. The team now selects stories in priority order until the total matches its recent velocity of about 30 points, and agrees a team plan for the sprint. Under which topic of the team planning workshop does this take place?
o: Iteration planning.
Product backlog refinement.
Effort estimation.
User story refinement.
5.w: Iteration planning is the team planning workshop topic in which the team selects stories by priority and estimate and agrees a realistic team plan for the next iteration (book Table 13.13).

n.1: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes backlog items, for example with MoSCoW; the stem says this is already done (book Table 13.13).
n.2: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's effort; the stories are already estimated (book Table 13.13).
n.3: User story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable; that has already happened (book Table 13.13).

5.q: At the store operations team's retrospective after the first pilot stores go live, the team notes that two stores missed their go-live date because stock counts started late. The team then proposes running a stock count a week before staff training at every remaining pilot store, and agrees to try this in the next cycle. Under which topic of the team retrospective workshop is the proposal captured?
o: The good.
The bad.
The learning.
Team building.
5.w: The learning topic of the team retrospective workshop captures lessons, improvement suggestions and actionable insights (book Table 13.14). The proposal to start stock counts earlier is an improvement the team will act on.

n.0: The good covers positives and celebrating success, not improvement proposals (book Table 13.14).
n.1: The bad captures issues, risks and challenges and their causes, such as the late stock counts; the proposal that follows belongs under the learning (book Table 13.14).
n.3: Team building uses a game or food to strengthen bonds within the team (book Table 13.14).

5.q: At the end of Stage 3, Patrick Dunne holds a release planning workshop for Stage 4. After the introduction, the teams agree an objective of making click and collect part of everyday store life, with key results such as all 85 stores live with stock accuracy of at least 97% and 90% of orders ready within two hours. Under which topic of the workshop is this agreed?
o: Release planning.
OKR definition.
Introduction.
Wrap-up.
5.w: The OKR definition topic of the release planning workshop defines or updates the teams' objectives and key results (book Table 13.16). OKRs pair a clear, aspirational objective with specific, measurable key results (book 12.3.2.3).

n.0: The release planning topic breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map (book Table 13.16).
n.2: The introduction opens the workshop and sets the context; the stem says the OKRs were agreed after it (book Table 13.16).
n.3: The wrap-up closes the workshop; objectives and key results are agreed under their own topic, OKR definition (book Table 13.16).

5.q: In closing the project, Patrick Dunne holds the project closure workshop. Store staff and a group of regular customers use the locker collection process at one of the largest stores, and the users' representatives confirm that it meets the agreed requirements and is ready to be handed over. Under which topic of the project closure workshop does this take place?
o: Final product demo.
Final handover planning.
Project lessons.
Progress review.
5.w: The final product demo topic of the project closure workshop shows the final product so that users can confirm acceptance and that it is ready for handover (book Table 13.19).

n.1: Final handover planning agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and benefits actions after the product is accepted (book Table 13.19).
n.2: Project lessons is where participants share insights from the project (book Table 13.19).
n.3: The progress review topic updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer (book Table 13.19).

5.q: Before the project kickoff workshop, Patrick Dunne designs a team dashboard for each team himself, using the same layout and measures for both, so that he can combine them easily into the project dashboard. At the workshop he presents the finished dashboards and asks the teams to start updating them. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager pulls information from the team dashboards, so the project manager should decide what they contain.
Yes, because both teams must report in the same format so that the board can compare them in the progress review workshops.
No, because team dashboards are created in the team planning workshop for each iteration, not in the project kickoff workshop.
No, because the kickoff aims to build self-management, and each team should co-create its own dashboard rather than have one dictated.
5.w: The project kickoff workshop aims to create an agile culture of openness and self-management, and its team dashboards topic has each team co-create its own dashboard rather than have one imposed (book Table 13.8). Designing them for the teams undermines that purpose.

n.0: The project manager does pull information from team dashboards, but that does not make the project manager their designer; teams co-create them (book Table 13.8, Table 12.1).
n.1: The board pulls information from the project dashboard, which the project manager assembles; the teams' dashboards do not need an identical format (book Table 12.1, Table 13.8).
n.2: Team dashboards are created in the project kickoff workshop and later updated in team planning and retrospective workshops (book Table 13.8, Table 12.1).

5.q: In starting up a project, Gwen Tallowby is busy with the spring peak, so she asks Patrick Dunne to write the project canvas on his own from the mandate and send it to her for approval. Patrick does so without holding a project canvas workshop or involving the user, supplier or finance representatives. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the fixed budget and date in the mandate mean that the content of the canvas has in effect already been decided.
Yes, because a project canvas is a one-page summary, so there is little to gain from involving other people in writing it.
No, because the executive should lead the canvas from the mandate, working with others so that they share an understanding of the project.
No, because the project canvas is prepared in initiating a project, so it should not be written while the project is still starting up.
5.w: In starting up a project the executive leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate (book Table 13.1), and the project canvas workshop exists to build a shared understanding of the project's core elements in line with organizational goals (book 13.2.4.1). A canvas written alone by the project manager loses both.

n.0: Budget and date are only part of the canvas, which also covers vision, users, business options, scope, benefits and major risks (book 6.3.2).
n.1: The canvas is short, but its value comes from the shared understanding built by defining it together (book 13.2.4.1).
n.3: The canvas is first developed in starting up a project and then refined in initiation; writing it in starting up is correct (book Table 13.1, Table 13.6).

5.q: As Stage 2 nears its end, Patrick Dunne holds a release planning workshop with both teams, Marcus Lindell and Elena Marsh. They review the project canvas and project backlog, break the Release 2 features into user stories and update the release map for Stage 3. Sprint-level and store-level task planning is left to the teams. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the stage boundary updates the release map for the next stage, while detailed task plans are made in managing product delivery.
Yes, because the release map produced at the stage boundary removes the need for team plans in the managing product delivery process.
No, because the release map should be updated in the team planning workshop, where each team plans the work for its next sprint.
No, because the board approves the next stage plan, so the board rather than the teams should plan Release 2 in this workshop.
5.w: At a stage boundary the release planning workshop reviews the project canvas, project backlog and release map, breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map for the next stage (book Table 13.16). Detailed task-level plans are made by the teams in managing product delivery (book Table 13.12, 8.3.2).

n.1: Team plans are still needed; the delivery team produces one when it accepts a work package, at task level for the next iteration (book Table 13.12).
n.2: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration; the stage-level release map update belongs to the release planning workshop (book Table 13.13, Table 13.16).
n.3: The board approves the updated release map in directing a project, but the project manager prepares it with the teams at the stage boundary (book 13.7.1, Table 13.4).

5.q: In Stage 4, Patrick Dunne begins attending the store operations team's daily stand-up every morning without asking the team, and uses it to tell members which stores to prepare next. He says this saves time compared with agreeing work packages with Sophie Draper, the team's product owner. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'managing product delivery' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager runs the project day to day for the board and can therefore direct the delivery team members.
Yes, because attending stand-ups lets the project manager pull progress information without asking the team for a report.
No, because stand-ups belong to the Scrum framework, and a Kanban team such as the store operations team should not hold them.
No, because the project manager attends stand-ups with the team's agreement and agrees work with the product owner as work packages.
5.w: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups only with the delivery team's agreement (book Table 12.1). Work reaches the team through work packages, sets of user stories agreed between the project manager and the product owner, who is the role with direct authority over delivery team members (book 7.3.1, Table 13.9).

n.0: The project manager runs the project day to day, but the product owner is the role with direct authority over delivery team members (book 7.3.1).
n.1: Pulling information from the team dashboard is encouraged, but joining stand-ups without agreement and directing the team is not (book Table 12.1, Table 13.9).
n.2: Kanban teams can hold short daily stand-ups; the problem is the project manager attending uninvited and bypassing the product owner (book Table 12.1).

5.q: As Release 3 nears completion, Bill Rowntree's area managers will take over the daily running of click and collect in all 85 stores, and the store operations team will disband at closure. Bill asks what the handover should include so that the stores keep running the service well. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on transition to operations?
o: Give each store a printed manual of the collection process and close the project, so that store managers can adapt the process locally as they see fit.
Hand over the team's Kanban board and dashboards, tailored training and quick guides, clear procedures, escalation routes and regular feedback loops.
Keep the store operations team in place for a year after closure, so that it can run the service in each store until staff feel confident.
Transfer responsibility for the stores' collection process to Kieran Walsh's IT operations team, as it already supports the website.
5.w: For transition to operations the book recommends handing over agile artifacts and tools, tailored end-user training with guides and other aids, explicit operational procedures, escalation pathways, and regular feedback loops such as surveys and retrospectives (book 14.2.1).

n.0: A manual alone gives no training, escalation routes or feedback loops, which the book recommends to support adoption after handover (book 14.2.1).
n.2: The project is temporary; keeping the project team running the service delays handover to the business rather than preparing operations to take it on (book 1.3.1, 14.2.1).
n.3: IT operations supports the website, but the daily collection process is run by the stores, which need the training, procedures and feedback loops themselves (book 14.2.1).

5.q: The e-commerce team deploys small website changes several times a week. Kieran Walsh, who is responsible for keeping the website running, wants every change to go through his weekly change board, especially during the spring peak. After the project, the team will keep improving the service. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to keep the website stable while keeping the benefits of frequent releases?
o: Bring Kieran's team into the e-commerce team's work, with automated testing and deployment, and live monitoring that feeds back into development.
Group all changes into a single weekly release approved by the change board, so that IT operations reviews each change before it goes live.
Let the e-commerce team deploy without involving IT operations, because frequent small changes carry little risk to the website.
Freeze changes to the website from February until after Easter, and release the remaining features in one deployment after the peak.
5.w: Continuous agile development and operations aims for rapid, automated delivery so the product is always deployable. In DevOps, development, testing and operations work closely together without silos, small releases go to production often, and monitoring of the live service feeds back into development (book 14.2.2.2).

n.1: Batching changes into a weekly release slows feedback and keeps development and operations apart, which is what DevOps seeks to avoid (book 14.2.2.2).
n.2: Leaving operations out creates the silo that DevOps removes and ignores the person responsible for website stability (book 14.2.2.2).
n.3: A freeze stops feedback from live use, and holding features until after Easter would break the fixed date for the service (book 14.2.2.2, Table 3.1).

5.q: Patrick Dunne wants to use an AI assistant to reduce the load on the store operations team during the Stage 4 roll-out, when store managers are sending many questions about the new collection process. Which use of AI is consistent with PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Set up a project chatbot that answers common store questions, so that Sophie Draper's team has more time to talk to store managers about concerns.
Let the assistant decide whether each store meets the go-live conditions and send its manager the go-live date, to save the store operations team's time.
Upload customer orders, including payment details, to a public AI tool so that it can predict which stores will be busiest at Easter.
Use the assistant to write and send all messages to store managers, so that the team no longer needs to hold meetings with them.
5.w: AI can support people by automating the collection and sharing of information, for example a project chatbot answering frequent questions, which frees leaders for more important communication. It supports human judgement and does not remove the need to make decisions or to communicate with stakeholders (book 15.4.2).

n.1: Go-live decisions remain human decisions; AI supports decision-making but does not replace it (book 15.4.2).
n.2: Sharing customer payment data with a public tool ignores data care set out in the digital and data management approach, and the board has a very low appetite for payment security risks (book 15.4, Table 12.1).
n.3: AI does not remove the need to communicate with stakeholders; store managers' concerns need direct conversation (book 15.4.2).

6.q: During initiation, Joan Whitaker agrees that the Care Online digital team may work in two-week sprints, hold daily stand-ups and keep a backlog. However, she asks that her programme board approve every user story before it enters a sprint, and that the team follow the corporate project office's sprint checklist step by step without changing it. Which statement BEST describes the council's position?
o: The council is being agile without doing agile: its leaders think in an agile way, but the team has not yet adopted agile events or tools.
The council is doing agile without being agile: the team uses agile events and terms but is not allowed to apply an agile mindset.
The council is both doing and being agile, because the board keeps governance control while the team runs sprints, stand-ups and a backlog.
The council is being agile, because following a sprint checklist exactly is how a new team builds an agile mindset in its first stages.
6.w: Doing agile is the practical use of agile frameworks, processes, techniques and terminology; being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset with appropriate self-management. Sprints and stand-ups are in place, but approval of every story and a fixed checklist leave the team no room to adapt or decide, so this is doing without being (book 2.3, 2.3.1).

n.0: The reverse is true here: the agile events and tools are in place, but the leadership does not allow the mindset to be applied (book 2.3.1).
n.2: Governance and agile can coexist, but approving every story and fixing the routine removes the self-management that being agile needs (book 2.3, 2.3.1).
n.3: Following a framework rigidly without understanding why is the routine side of the being versus doing contrast; being agile means adapting and thinking critically (book 2.3.1).

6.q: In the sprint 3 review, two occupational therapists explain that the self-assessment's timed pages will be hard for people with sensory impairments to complete. Two developers reply that therapists are not designers and that the pages follow the council's standard template, and the team moves on to the next item. Amy Fletcher wants to raise this at the retrospective. Which characteristic of the agile mindset is the team MOST in need of?
o: Empowerment, because the developers need more freedom to decide the page design without waiting for the therapists' approval.
Adaptability, because the team should inspect its release plan and adapt the sprint length to the therapists' availability.
Transparency and rich communication, because the review should have been recorded so that the therapists' points could be reread later.
Respect, because the team needs the empathy and open-mindedness to value every voice, including views from outside the digital team.
6.w: Respect in the agile mindset is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness: every voice is valued and diverse perspectives are welcomed. Dismissing the therapists because they are not designers shows a lack of respect, and their knowledge of users with sensory impairments is exactly what the team needs (book 2.6.2).

n.0: Empowerment is about autonomy and self-management; the developers already acted on their own view, and the problem is that they dismissed others (book 2.6.2).
n.1: Adaptability is inspecting and adapting in response to change; changing the sprint length does not address the developers brushing aside the therapists' views (book 2.6.2).
n.2: The therapists' points were raised openly in the review, so information did flow; what was missing was the willingness to value them (book 2.6.2).

6.q: In starting up a project, Simon Archer asks Gita Bhatt what went well and what went badly when her two previous councils adopted agile, and he reviews the lessons from the council's last digital project with Helen Crowther. Later, every Care Online sprint ends with a retrospective, and the improvements agreed are carried into the next sprint. Which principle is being applied?
o: Learn from experience, because lessons are sought at the start and the short feedback loops of retrospectives turn them into improvements.
Tailor to suit the project, because Simon is adapting the method and its workshops to the council's low agile maturity before the project begins.
