Manage by stages, because the retrospectives divide the project into short sprints that the board can review one at a time.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Gita's experience will shape the description of the agile coach role.
6.w: Learn from experience means seeking and applying lessons at the start, during and at the end of the project. In agile it is supported by retrospectives, inspect and adapt, and short feedback loops (book Table 5.1). Simon seeks lessons from Gita and from an earlier project, and the teams apply lessons sprint by sprint.

n.1: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity and context, for example by choosing frameworks and workshops; seeking and applying lessons is a different principle (book 5.2.1.7).
n.2: Manage by stages concerns the board authorizing one management stage at a time; retrospectives are learning events, not stage controls (book 5.2.1.4).
n.3: Nothing in the situation concerns who is accountable for what; Simon is gathering lessons and the teams are applying them (book 5.2.1.3).

6.q: At the project canvas workshop, Sarah Pennington explains that, under the council's climate pledge, every project must meet minimum environmental criteria. For Care Online these are that the paper carers' assessment form is withdrawn and that first conversations no longer need a car journey to the person's home. Further measures to cut printing and travel are welcome if they fit the budget and timescale. Which aspect of project performance is being described, and how should PRINCE2 Agile treat it?
o: Benefits, fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it, because fewer home visits is the improvement the council expects to gain.
Scope, fixed for Must have features and flexed for Should and Could haves, because withdrawing the paper form is a feature.
Sustainability, fixed for the minimum criteria and flexed above them, because the pledge concerns the project's impact on the environment.
Sustainability, flexed in full like Should and Could scope, because zero tolerance applies to time and cost rather than to sustainability.
6.w: Sustainability is how the project affects the wider environment. PRINCE2 Agile fixes sustainability at its minimum criteria and flexes it above them (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1). The climate pledge sets the minimum; any extra measures are the flexible part.

n.0: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability, but the stem sets minimum environmental criteria from a climate pledge, which is the sustainability aspect (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).
n.1: MoSCoW scope treatment applies to features by priority; the statement here sets environmental criteria, which is the sustainability aspect (Table 3.1).
n.3: Table 3.1 fixes sustainability for its minimum criteria, so withdrawing the paper form and removing the first-visit journey cannot be traded away; the flexible part is above that minimum.

6.q: The council has agreed to train ten social workers as Care Online product champions. The learning and development team proposes a two-day agile theory course for them in month one, after which the champions would go back to their teams and apply what they learned on their own. Gita Bhatt is asked for her view. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to build the agile maturity the council needs?
o: Run the two-day course as proposed, then measure each champion's agile maturity in the project closure workshop at month twelve.
Replace the course with a set of agile reading materials and videos, so that champions can learn at their own pace around caseloads.
Delay all training until Release 1 is live, so that the champions can learn agile from the finished product rather than from theory.
Combine the course with on-the-job coaching from Gita, set out in a training and coaching plan that follows the stages of the change.
6.w: People need both theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching to apply a change; leaving them to fend for themselves breeds frustration and resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the agile change (book 2.7.3).

n.0: This leaves the champions on their own after the course, which the book warns undermines the change, and assessing maturity at closure is too late to help (book 2.7.3, 12.4.1).
n.1: Self-study is still theory with no practical coaching; the book pairs training with on-the-job coaching (book 2.7.3).
n.2: Champions need to understand the change while it is happening; delaying training until after Release 1 leaves them unprepared throughout stage 2 (book 2.7.3).

6.q: At an early board meeting, Joan Whitaker asks why Care Online needs organizational change management at all. In her view, once the online service works and the interface to the case system is live, staff and the public will simply use it. Simon Archer notes that Paul Henshaw has said the change will create more work for the front door team, and that many social workers fear their judgement will be bypassed. Which explanation BEST answers Joan?
o: OCM is needed because it controls changes to the project's baseline, so that requests from front door staff and social workers are assessed formally.
OCM is needed because it replaces the communication management approach with a single plan for training social workers and front door staff.
OCM is needed because the benefits depend on staff and the public adopting new ways of working, and the culture must change for that to last.
OCM is needed because the grant conditions require a separate change management team to report on the project's outcomes every quarter.
6.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to the target state. Working software does not deliver benefits on its own: people must adopt the change, and culture decides whether it is adopted and whether it is rolled back later (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice, not of OCM (book 11.1, 4.2.1).
n.1: The communication management approach is part of the people guidance that supports OCM; OCM does not replace it (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.3: The grant needs a quarterly report of spend and outcomes, but nothing in the scenario calls for a separate team; the reason for OCM is adoption of the change (book 4.2.1).

6.q: Simon Archer wants front-line social workers to see online self-assessment as support for their professional judgement rather than a threat to it, so that they follow up online assessments promptly. He wants to work with one key influencer who can shape how social workers across the county see the change. Using the Additional information (People), who is the BEST choice?
o: Dr Rajesh Iyer, because he leads practice standards for all social workers and is trusted by front-line staff across the county.
Joan Whitaker, because as assistant director she chairs the department's programme board and has formal authority over the service.
Bev Lomax, because she chairs the carers' network and can explain to others how carers will benefit from the online assessment.
Amy Fletcher, because she has run user research with carers and older people and understands how the service will be used.
6.w: Key influencers are people who, through their network and credibility, most shape how the majority see a change and so drive its adoption and benefits (book 4.2.2). Rajesh leads practice standards for all social workers and is trusted by front-line staff, so his view will carry with the group Simon needs to reach.

n.1: Formal seniority is not the same as influence; Joan prefers traditional reporting and is not described as trusted by front-line social workers (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Bev is a strong influencer for carers, but the group to reach here is social workers, and she is not part of their network (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Amy understands users, but she sits in the digital team and has no described standing among front-line social workers (book 4.2.2).

6.q: In stage 3, the Abacus Care Software developers build the case system interface from their own offices in another region, while the council's digital team works in county hall. The two teams have so far met only on formal calls about change requests, and integration problems are taking days to resolve. Which action is MOST LIKELY to build the social cohesion the two teams need?
o: Require the Abacus developers to work from county hall every day until Release 2 is live, so that both teams sit together.
Agree co-location days for key people from both teams around integration points, and make time for less structured conversation online.
Route all contact between the teams through Martin Sallis and Simon Archer, so that technical discussions stay within the fixed-price contract terms.
Ask both teams to send each other a weekly written status note, so that each team knows what the other has finished and what is next.
6.w: Leading teams across organizations and locations means planning how people work together and building social cohesion, for example by syncing co-location days for key people and teams and allowing time for less structured conversation online (book 4.3.3).

n.0: Mandating full-time co-location is not the effective answer; planned co-location days and good hybrid working build cohesion without it (book 4.3.3).
n.2: Funnelling contact through two managers cuts the direct, rich communication between the teams that integration work needs (book 4.3.3, 4.4).
n.3: Periodic written reports are not enough to build trust and cohesion, and they can be biased towards what seems acceptable (book 4.4).

6.q: The Care Online digital team works together in county hall, while the social workers and occupational therapists who help with research and testing join from offices and home visits across a rural county, with little spare time. Oliver Grant notices that decisions made in quick office conversations are not reaching the practitioners. Which statement BEST explains how communication should be handled in this hybrid team?
o: Office conversations should stay the main channel, because most communication happens outside formal channels and cannot be planned.
The practitioners should receive the monthly highlight report, because periodic reporting keeps remote members informed without taking their time.
Each update should go to all practitioners in one identical message, because consistent wording makes sure nobody receives a different account.
The remote part needs a deliberate approach: agree how information flows and in which formats, and set structured and unstructured time together.
6.w: Remote working needs a more deliberate, structured approach than co-location: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, the key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together. A hybrid team combines co-located and remote working, so its remote members need this structure (book 4.4).

n.0: Informal communication should be accepted, but relying on office conversations is exactly what is leaving the remote practitioners out (book 4.4).
n.1: Periodic reporting alone is insufficient and can be biased; it does not give remote members a two-way flow of information (book 4.4).
n.2: Generic messaging is rarely effective; messages should be tailored to each group and the flow should be two-way (book 4.4).

6.q: Helen Crowther wants to motivate the digital team and the practitioners who work with it during stage 2. She proposes a monthly gift voucher for the developer who completes the most story points. Oliver Grant is concerned that this could damage the collaboration the team has built. Which approach BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on motivating agile teams?
o: Keep the voucher but base it on story points per hour worked, so that part-time practitioners can compete fairly with full-time developers.
Let team members award points to colleagues whose behaviour models the team's agreed values, alongside recognition and a clear sense of purpose.
Replace the voucher with a bonus for the whole team if Release 1 is live by month four, with progress shown on the project dashboard.
Ask Helen to rate each person's contribution at the end of every release and show the resulting ranking on the team dashboard for everyone to see.
6.w: PRINCE2 Agile suggests value-based incentives, such as peer-assessed points or a fictional currency for behaviour that models agile values, balanced with intangible motivators such as purpose and recognition, and with personal values (book 4.5).

n.0: Rewarding individual output still sets team members against each other; the book points to peer-assessed rewards for behaviour that models agile values (book 4.5).
n.2: A deadline bonus rewards output against a date rather than behaviour that models the team's values, and leaves out intangible motivators (book 4.5).
n.3: A manager's ranking is neither peer-based nor tied to the team's agreed values, and it works against self-management (book 4.5).

6.q: Early in stage 2, Sarah Pennington asks Simon Archer how the board will see, month by month, whether the work completed so far puts Care Online on course to finish by the grant deadline, and what will happen if it starts to look as though the agreed tolerances will be exceeded. Which practice is designed to answer Sarah's question?
o: Plans, because it defines the products to be delivered and the means of delivering them, with estimates of when and at what cost.
Risk, because it identifies, assesses and controls the uncertain events that could stop the project from meeting its grant deadline and budget.
Progress, because it compares actual achievement with the plan, forecasts the objectives and controls deviations causing an exception.
Issues, because it collects and assesses deviations from what was agreed and controls any changes to the project's baseline.
6.w: The progress practice establishes mechanisms to monitor and compare actual achievements against those planned, to forecast the project's objectives and continued viability, and to control any deviation that would cause an exception (book 12.1).

n.0: Plans set out what will be delivered and estimate when and how much; comparing actual work with the plan and forecasting is the progress practice (book 8.1, 12.1).
n.1: Risk handles uncertain events; Sarah wants a regular comparison of actual with planned work and a forecast, which is progress (book 10.1, 12.1).
n.3: Issues controls changes to the baseline; controlling deviations that would cause an exception belongs to progress (book 11.1, 12.1).

6.q: At the project canvas workshop, the group lists possible entries for the benefits section of the Care Online project canvas: the online carers' self-assessment form; the community support directory; text message updates for people tracking their case; and a fall in the average wait for a first assessment from eight weeks to four. Which entry should be recorded as a benefit, and why?
o: The online carers' self-assessment, because it is the minimum the council must deliver to respond to the inspection findings.
The community support directory, because carers and the public will start using it as soon as Release 1 goes live in month four.
Text message updates, because a feature that people use to track their case counts as a benefit once it has been delivered.
The fall in the average wait for a first assessment, because it is a measurable improvement that the council sees as an advantage.
6.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that the investing organization sees as an advantage; an output such as a form, directory or feature is never a benefit in itself (Glossary, book 6.3.2). The canvas benefits section holds expected, measurable benefits with their tolerance.

n.0: The carers' self-assessment is an output, even though it is the minimum to deliver; it would be identified as the MVP, not as a benefit (Glossary, book 6.3.2).
n.1: The directory is an output; its use may lead to benefits, but the directory itself is not a measurable improvement (Glossary).
n.2: A delivered feature is an output; any benefit would be the measurable improvement that the feature leads to (Glossary, book 6.3.2).

6.q: The grant conditions require the council to report outcomes to the government department every quarter, and Sarah Pennington wants some benefits to be visible well before month twelve. During initiation, Simon Archer is preparing the benefits management approach for Care Online. What should it include?
o: Plans for frequent releases so that benefits start early, with measures, tolerances and reviews of those benefits from Release 1 onwards.
A single measurement of benefits in a post-project review after month twelve, since benefits are confirmed after the project closes.
A count of features delivered each quarter as the outcome measure, since the features are what the grant is paying for.
A cross-reference to the project canvas in place of its own content, as the canvas already lists the expected benefits and tolerances.
6.w: The benefits management approach defines the actions and reviews for realizing and measuring benefits. In agile, frequent releases are planned so that benefits arrive early, and some benefits can be confirmed during the project rather than all after closure (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2).

n.1: Benefits are mostly confirmed after closure, but iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project, which is what the grant and Sarah need (book 6.3.1).
n.2: Features are outputs, not outcomes or benefits; the measures should track the improvements the features bring (Glossary, book 6.3.2).
n.3: The canvas states the expected benefits, but the benefits management approach is still needed to set out how they will be realized, measured and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

6.q: During initiation, Simon Archer points out that the £1.1 million grant has already been awarded and the cabinet has approved the spend. He proposes that the Care Online project canvas be finalized at the end of initiation and not reviewed again, so that the board can concentrate on delivery. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the investment decision was made when the grant was awarded, so the board's remaining role is to oversee delivery of the releases.
Yes, because the project canvas is a one-page artifact that replaces the detailed business case and so needs little upkeep.
No, because a publicly funded project should replace the project canvas with a full written business case before delivery starts.
No, because the justification must stay valid throughout, so the canvas should be checked and updated as releases deliver and learning grows.
6.w: Ensure continued business justification requires the project to remain desirable, viable and achievable throughout its life. In PRINCE2 Agile the project canvas is the business case, and it should be checked and maintained, for example at stage boundaries when the board confirms continued justification (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1, 13.7.1).

n.0: Approved funding does not remove the need to keep checking that the project is still worthwhile; every project needs continued justification (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).
n.1: The canvas is a suitable replacement for the business case, but being concise does not exempt it from being checked and kept up to date (book 6.3.2).
n.2: The verdict is right, but the project canvas is a suitable business case for an agile project; the fault is freezing it, not its format (book 6.3.2).

6.q: During initiation, Simon Archer and Martin Sallis discuss how Abacus will work on the case system interface. Abacus normally quotes for each fixed-price change request, which takes about six weeks. They agree instead on a fixed Abacus team and cost for each two-week sprint, a shared Definition of Done, and tolerances around the Release 2 interface. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure, because it describes who is involved in the project and how the people will work together.
In the commercial management approach, because it sets out procurement and contract arrangements that support agile product development.
In the role descriptions, because Martin Sallis's responsibilities as the supplier's account manager need to be defined for the project.
In the risk register, because the six-week quoting time is a threat to the Release 2 date that needs a planned response.
6.w: The commercial management approach sets out how procurement and contracts will support agile delivery, for example fixed delivery teams and costs per iteration, the MVP and tolerances, and an agreed Definition of Done (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: The team structure covers who is involved, their relationships and working arrangements such as co-location; contract form and payment per sprint belong in the commercial management approach (Table 7.3).
n.2: Role descriptions set out project roles and their responsibilities, not the contract terms under which a supplier works (Table 7.3).
n.3: The old quoting time might have been recorded as a risk, but the agreed contract arrangements themselves belong in the commercial management approach (Table 7.3, Table 10.1).

6.q: Care Online has two delivery teams: the council's digital team and the Abacus team building the case system interface. Simon Archer is drafting the project management team structure and wants it to be clear who decides priorities when the two teams' work competes for the same release. Which structure follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: A project manager for each team, both reporting to the board, with the chief product owner deciding priorities within each team's backlog.
One project manager who prioritizes the user stories across both teams' backlogs, supported by a team coach working in each team.
One project manager; a product owner per team who owns its backlog; and a chief product owner setting priorities across both teams.
One product owner covering both teams' backlogs, who also represents the user community on the board in place of a chief product owner.
6.w: With several teams there is one project manager, a product owner for each team (a version of the team manager role, owning that team's product backlog), and a chief product owner who represents the users and sets priorities across the teams (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

n.0: A multi-team project still has one project manager, and each team's product backlog is owned by its product owner rather than the CPO (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).
n.1: Setting priorities across teams is the chief product owner's job, not the project manager's (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.3: The product owner is a team-level role; representing the user community and prioritizing across teams belong to the chief product owner (Table 7.2).

6.q: Social workers have high caseloads and work across a rural county. During initiation, Simon Archer records in the project management team structure that practitioners will join the digital team remotely for fixed two-hour slots in each sprint, using video calls and a shared online team dashboard, with a co-located session at the start of each release. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the team structure should record co-location and remote arrangements, with tools for transparency and rich communication.
Yes, because practitioners are not members of the delivery team, so their involvement can be arranged outside the project's governance.
No, because practitioners should be co-located with the digital team for every sprint if agile ways of working are to succeed.
No, because remote working arrangements belong in the communication management approach rather than in the team structure.
6.w: The project management team structure records who is involved and how they work together, including arrangements for co-located or remote teams and the agile techniques and tools that keep work transparent and communication rich (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3). Planned remote slots, a shared dashboard and periodic co-location suit busy practitioners.

n.1: The practitioners take part in the team's research and testing, so their involvement sits within the project's structure; this reason does not explain why the arrangement is sound (book 7.3.1, Table 7.3).
n.2: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer for people spread across a county; planned remote and hybrid arrangements are recognized (book 4.3.3, Table 7.3).
n.3: Co-location and remote arrangements are part of the project management team structure in Table 7.3; the communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication (book 4.4).

6.q: Care Online needs a project executive who will be accountable for the project and for the grant that funds it, keep it aligned with the council's strategy, and approve the tolerances within which the teams make agile decisions. Using the Additional information (People), which person is BEST suited to the project executive role?
o: Joan Whitaker, because she chairs the department's programme board and is used to approving detailed plans in advance.
Sarah Pennington, because she received the mandate for Care Online and is accountable for the government grant that funds it.
Helen Crowther, because she manages the digital team that will build most of the online service and knows its capacity.
Simon Archer, because he is an experienced project manager from the corporate project office and knows PRINCE2 7 well.
6.w: The project executive is accountable for the project, keeps it aligned with strategy and approves the tolerances for agile decision-making (Table 7.2, Table B.1). Sarah received the mandate and is accountable for the grant, so she holds the business accountability the role needs.

n.0: Joan chairs a departmental programme board, but she is not described as accountable for this project or the grant, and a liking for detailed advance plans is no reason to hold the role (Table 7.2).
n.2: Helen manages the people who will build the service, which points to the supplier side rather than to accountability for the investment (Table 7.2).
n.3: Simon is the project manager, who runs the project day to day for the board within tolerances; the executive role sits above him (Table 7.2).

6.q: The Care Online digital team needs a team coach who will work closely with it, help it manage itself, facilitate its team workshops, improve communication and help it write user stories. Using the Additional information (People), which person is BEST suited to the team coach role for the digital team?
o: Gita Bhatt, because she has led agile adoption in two other councils and will support the council's leaders and teams for six months.
Helen Crowther, because as head of customer and digital services she line manages the digital team and can direct its work.
Amy Fletcher, because she has led research with carers and older people and can make sure the team builds what users need.
Oliver Grant, because as the digital team's delivery manager he already runs its sprint planning sessions and retrospectives.
6.w: The team coach works closely with one or two teams, helps them self-manage, facilitates team workshops such as planning and retrospectives, and coaches agile practice; a Scrum master fits this role (Table 7.2, Table B.1). Oliver already runs the digital team's sprint planning and retrospectives.

n.0: Gita's background fits the agile coach role, which works across the organization on systemic blockers rather than inside one team (Table 7.2).
n.1: Line managing and directing the team's work does not fit a role whose purpose is to help the team manage itself (Table 7.2).
n.2: Amy's research skills suit work on user needs and testing, but she is not described as facilitating the team's workshops or ways of working (Table 7.2).

6.q: After three sprints in stage 2, the Care Online digital team has completed 21, 25 and 23 story points. Joan Whitaker wants to know which Release 1 stories will be ready by month four. Gita Bhatt mentions that a team at one of her previous councils averaged 35 points a sprint on similar work. How should Simon Archer forecast the Release 1 scope?
o: Use the team's own average of 23 points a sprint to forecast how many remaining stories, in priority order, fit by month four.
Use the 35-point average from Gita's previous council, as it comes from a more experienced team that delivered similar work.
Ask each developer to estimate in hours every task of every remaining Release 1 story, and fix the release scope from the total.
Average the digital team's figures with the 35-point figure, so that the forecast reflects both experience and the team's current rate.
6.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans empirically: start work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that rate (calibration, or calculating velocity). The forecast should use the team's own velocity, not another team's (book 8.3). Here that is (21 + 25 + 23) / 3 = 23 points a sprint.

n.1: A team forecasts from its own measured velocity; another council's figure, however experienced that team was, does not show what this team will deliver (book 8.3).
n.2: Detailed task estimates for a whole release are rationalist planning; agile planning is empirical, and task-level plans are made for the next iteration (book 8.3, 8.4.3).
n.3: Mixing in another team's velocity still distorts the forecast; empiricism uses the rate this team has actually achieved (book 8.3).

6.q: Early in initiation, the digital team, Amy Fletcher and two practitioners have written about 140 user stories across the three Care Online releases. Before the project initiation workshop, they need a rough relative size for every story so that a first release map can be drafted, and they have one short session in which to do it. Which estimating technique fits BEST?
o: Planning-poker style estimation, with each person revealing a card for every story at the same time and discussing any differences.
A product flow diagram, which shows the sequence of and dependencies between the stories across the three releases.
Magic estimation, a quick collaborative technique for sizing a large number of stories early in planning without long debate on each.
Task-level estimation in hours for each story, so that the release map is built from actual rather than relative effort.
6.w: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for early planning, for example at project product level, that sizes many stories relative to one another without lengthy discussion (book 8.4.3).

n.0: Simultaneous card estimation is a valid relative technique, but revealing and discussing cards for each of 140 stories takes far longer than one short session allows (book 8.4.3).
n.1: A product flow diagram shows sequence and dependencies, not the size of each story (book 8.4.2).
n.3: Agile estimation is relative rather than in actual hours, and task-level estimates belong to planning the next iteration (book 8.4.3, 8.3).

6.q: During initiation, Simon Archer runs a session with the digital team, Amy Fletcher, two practitioners and Bev Lomax. Starting from the personas, they set out in order what carers and people who may need care do, break those activities into user stories, and then group the stories into the three releases. Simon does not draw up a separate product breakdown structure. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because product-based planning is not part of PRINCE2 Agile, so the team is free to plan from what users do instead of from products.
Yes, because PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map that breaks products into stories.
No, because a product breakdown structure is still needed to show the board which products will be delivered in each stage.
No, because the product owner should group the stories into releases on their own before users and practitioners see the story map.
6.w: Product-based planning still applies in PRINCE2 Agile, but the product breakdown structure is recommended to be replaced by a user story map: start from personas, set out user activities in order, break them into stories, then turn the story map into the release map (book 8.3.1, 8.3.2.4).

n.0: Product-based planning is still part of PRINCE2 Agile; it is carried out through story mapping rather than dropped (book 8.3.1).
n.2: The story map removes the need for a separate PBS, and the release map shows the board what each release and stage will deliver (book 8.3.1, 8.3.2.5).
n.3: Story mapping is collaborative and starts from users and their activities, so involving users and practitioners is a strength here (book 8.3.2.4).

6.q: Carol Mbeki must approve how personal data flows between the online service and the case system. She asks Simon Archer where she can see which information governance reviews of the interface have been planned and held, who carried them out, on what dates and whether each one passed. Which artifact holds this information?
o: The product register, because it records every product the plan requires and the current status of each of those products.
The issue register, because a failed review of personal data flows is an issue that must be captured and assessed.
The team dashboard, because the Abacus team updates it every sprint and the project manager pulls progress from it.
The quality register, because it records planned and completed quality activities with dates, responsibilities and results.
6.w: The quality register records all planned and completed quality activities, with identifiers, method, planned and actual dates, responsibilities, pass or fail results and references to quality records (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1).

n.0: The product register tracks products and their status; the reviews, dates, reviewers and results belong in the quality register (Table 9.1).
n.1: A failed review could lead to an issue being raised, but the record of planned and completed reviews and their results is the quality register (Table 9.1, 11.3.1).
n.2: The team dashboard shows a team's progress through the iteration; it is not the formal record of quality activities and results (Table 12.1, Table 9.1).

6.q: During initiation, Simon Archer drafts the Care Online quality management approach. It records the council's document standards and the accessibility checks for the online pages, and names Carol Mbeki as the reviewer for personal data. It does not say how the digital team or Abacus will test their work within sprints, as Simon expects each team to use its usual methods. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because Abacus works on fixed-price change requests, so its testing methods are covered by its contract rather than by the project.
Yes, because the quality management approach describes standards and responsibilities, while testing belongs in each team plan.
No, because the agile ways of working and the agile testing methods to be used, including the supplier's, should be recorded in the approach.
No, because in PRINCE2 Agile the team Definition of Done takes the place of a quality management approach, so none should be drafted.
6.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the quality management approach must incorporate, document and assure agile ways of working and behaviours, and should record the agile testing methods to be used, including those of suppliers (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1).

n.0: A supplier's contract terms do not take its testing outside the project's quality approach; suppliers' agile testing methods should be recorded there (Table 9.1).
n.1: Standards and responsibilities belong in the approach, but so do the agile testing methods; a team plan sets out the work for the next iteration (Table 9.1, Table 8.1).
n.3: The quality management approach is kept and tailored in PRINCE2 Agile; the Definition of Done sits alongside it (Table 9.1, 9.3.2.2).

6.q: In the project initiation workshop, the participants assess the Care Online Agilometer. The 'flexibility on what is delivered' slider is rated low: senior managers have marked 92 of the 100 user stories as Must haves, because they expect every feature named in the mandate to be delivered. Which action is MOST LIKELY to improve this slider?
o: Ask the cabinet to add time tolerance to the twelve-month deadline, so that all of the Must haves can still be delivered.
Challenge whether so many stories are really Must haves, and test the assumptions behind each one with the senior managers.
Arrange co-location days for the digital team and practitioners, so that collaboration between them improves before stage 2.
Record the low rating as an issue in the issue register and report it to the board on the next project dashboard.
6.w: The Agilometer is a risk tool that assesses the areas where agile working could cause problems. Flexibility on what is delivered can be raised by challenging whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them (book 10.3.2.2, 10.3.2.3).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance and the cabinet has said the date cannot move; extending time does not make stakeholders more comfortable flexing scope (Table 3.1, 10.3.2).
n.2: Co-location may help the level of collaboration and the ease of communication, but those are different sliders (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: A low Agilometer rating is a risk to agile working to be managed, not an issue that has already happened, and reporting it does not raise the rating (book 10.3.2, 11.3.1).

6.q: The council has a very low appetite for any risk to the safeguarding of adults at risk. In stage 3, the digital team adds risk responses to its product backlog as stories, such as 'flag answers that suggest a safeguarding concern to the duty social worker on the same day', and its product owner prioritizes them alongside the features. The risks stay in the risk register. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a risk-adjusted product backlog keeps stories and risk responses together, so responses are prioritized and built in sprints.
Yes, because once the responses are held in the product backlog, the risk register no longer needs to be updated for these safeguarding risks.
No, because responses to safeguarding risks should be held in the risk register and kept apart from the team's user stories and features.
No, because a risk with a very low appetite has to be escalated to the board as an exception rather than handled by the team.
6.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds user stories and risk responses together, so that responses are prioritized and built within the iteration cycle, while the risk register still records the risks and their status (book 10.4.1, Table 10.1). With a very low appetite for safeguarding risk, building responses into the product is sound.

n.1: The risk register remains the record of identified risks with their status and history, so it continues to be updated (Table 10.1).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile recommends combining stories and risk responses in a risk-adjusted product backlog (book 10.4.1).
n.3: An exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; planning responses in the backlog is normal risk management (Table 12.1, 10.4.1).

6.q: In sprint 4, carers testing the online assessment through the carers' network say that the question 'Do you provide substantial care?' is confusing. Amy Fletcher suggests plainer wording that asks how many hours a week they spend caring. The change fits within the existing user story and does not affect the project backlog. How should this change be handled?
o: As a request for change to the project baseline, raised in an issue report and decided by the project board.
As an off-specification, because the question as written does not meet the quality criteria agreed for the carers' assessment story.
As an exception, because the story will now take longer than planned and the sprint may not deliver its forecast.
As a detail change, handled informally by the team with its product owner, as it makes the final product more accurate.
6.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change. It is seen as making the final product more accurate and is handled informally at team level rather than through formal baseline change control (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Formal handling by the board or change authority is for changes to the project baseline, and this change leaves the project backlog untouched (book 11.3.2).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; this is a refinement found in testing, within the story as agreed (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2).
n.2: An exception means tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; a small wording change within one story does not do that (Table 12.1).

6.q: In sprint 9, the story that sends a completed self-assessment into the Abacus test environment has been stuck for three days. One developer has tried several fixes alone while the rest of the digital team carries on with other stories. The sprint ends in four days. What should the team do FIRST?
o: Swarm on the blocked story, with the whole team focusing on it together until the work can move again.
Trade the blocked story for another story of similar effort, so that the sprint's scope stays the same size.
Raise an issue report to Simon Archer, so that he can escalate the blocker to the project board for a decision.
Ask Simon Archer to prepare an exception report, as the sprint goal is now at risk of being missed.
6.w: Swarming means the team focusing together on a stuck task or blocker, and it also speeds up time-critical work. The team should try swarming before escalating an issue to the project manager (book 11.4.2).

n.1: Trading or swapping absorbs a change by replacing requirements of similar effort; it is not a tool for removing a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Escalation comes after the team has tried to resolve the blocker itself by swarming (book 11.4.2).
n.3: An exception report is for a stage or project plan forecast to exceed tolerance, not for a sprint goal at risk (Table 12.1).

6.q: In stage 2, Paul Henshaw asks for a staff screen in Release 1 so that the front door team can triage online carers' assessments. Amy Fletcher, acting as the digital team's product owner, adds a new epic for it to the team's backlog. To keep the month four date, she removes the easy-read versions of the carers' assessment, which are Must haves in the project backlog, without referring the change to anyone. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because trading lets the product owner swap requirements of similar effort so that the release date can still be met.
Yes, because the product owner owns the product backlog and can reprioritize it to absorb change requested by users.
No, because removing Must haves from the project backlog changes the baseline, so it needs formal handling by the board or change authority.
No, because requests for change are considered at stage boundaries, so Paul's request should have waited until the end of stage 2.
6.w: A change that alters the project backlog, here removing Must haves agreed in it, is a change to the project baseline and must be handled formally by the project board or whoever holds delegated change authority. Detail changes inside the backlog can be handled at team level, but this is not one (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Trading swaps items of similar effort within agreed scope; it cannot be used to drop Must haves from the project backlog without formal approval (book 11.4.1, 11.3.2).
n.1: The product owner owns the team's product backlog, but the project backlog is the baseline, owned by the chief product owner, and changes to it go formal (book 8.3.2.1, 11.3.2).
n.3: Issues and changes are captured and assessed as they arise during a stage, not held back to its end; what makes this inappropriate is that a baseline change was made informally (Table 13.9, book 11.3.2).

6.q: On day 7 of a ten-day sprint in stage 2, the digital team's burn-down chart shows 30 story points still outstanding. The ideal line stands at 9 points for day 7, and the actual line has been above the ideal line since day 3. What does the chart show, and what should the team do?
o: The team is behind and will not finish every story at this rate, so it should focus on the highest-priority stories for the rest of the sprint.
The team is ahead, because more points remain in hand than the ideal line shows, so it can pull further stories into the sprint.
The team is behind, so the product owner should extend the sprint by three days to give the team enough time to finish every story it chose.
The chart shows completed work against the release date, so Simon Archer should update the release map before the team changes its plans.
6.w: A burn-down shows outstanding work over time. An actual line above the ideal line means not enough work has been done, so the team cannot finish everything at this rate and should concentrate on the highest-priority items (book 12.4.3).

n.1: Points remaining above the ideal line mean less work has been burned than planned, which is behind, not ahead (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A sprint is a timebox and time has zero tolerance; the content flexes rather than the end date (Table 3.1, Glossary).
n.3: That describes a burn-up at project or product level; this team-level chart shows remaining work over the days of one sprint (book 12.4.3).

6.q: Midway through stage 3, the Release 2 burn-up chart shows that, at the current velocity, about 80% of the Release 2 Must haves will be complete by month eight. Time and cost have zero tolerance, and the forecast is outside the scope tolerance agreed for the stage. What should Simon Archer do NEXT?
o: Move the Release 2 date to month nine, using the time tolerance in the stage plan to protect delivery of all the Release 2 Must haves.
Record the forecast on the next monthly project dashboard and let the board decide what to do about it at the end of stage 3.
Ask the digital team to work longer hours, including weekends, until its velocity rises enough to deliver every Release 2 Must have by month eight.
Hold an immediate meeting with the product owners and teams to explore options, then raise an exception report if tolerance will be breached.
6.w: An exception occurs when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, and an updated burn chart can trigger it. The book suggests holding an immediate meeting to discuss options before escalating to the board in an exception report with options and a recommendation (Table 12.1).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, and the cabinet has said the end date cannot move (Table 3.1).
n.1: A forecast breach of tolerance should be raised promptly as an exception rather than left to routine reporting at the end of the stage (Table 12.1).
n.2: Pushing the team to work longer hours does not deal with a forecast tolerance breach; the board needs to see the options in an exception report (Table 12.1).

6.q: Simon Archer, who is new to agile, asks the digital team whether he may attend its daily stand-ups. The team agrees that he can listen in to two stand-ups a week. On other days he takes progress information from the team dashboard, and he updates the project dashboard for the board after each progress review. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager is responsible for running the stand-ups so that he can assign the day's tasks to developers.
Yes, because the project manager may attend stand-ups with the team's agreement, and he pulls progress from the team dashboard.
No, because the project manager should receive a written checkpoint report from the product owner instead of using the team dashboard.
No, because the delivery team, rather than the project manager, should update the project dashboard for the board to pull from.
6.w: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups only with the delivery team's agreement. The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and the project manager pulls information from it; the project dashboard is updated in progress reviews so that the board can pull from it (Table 12.1).

n.0: Stand-ups belong to the delivery team, and the project manager attends with its agreement; assigning daily tasks would undermine self-management (Table 12.1).
n.2: In PRINCE2 Agile the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report, and the project manager pulls information from it (Table 12.1).
n.3: In reporting highlights, the project manager assembles the team dashboards and updates the project dashboard so that the board can pull information from it (Table 13.9).

6.q: In starting up a project, Sarah Pennington runs the project canvas workshop for Care Online. The group agrees that carers, people who may need care, and social care staff are the three groups the service must serve, and it ranks carers first because Release 1 is built for them. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop is this agreed?
o: User group definition
Project vision definition
Benefits analysis
Scope definition
6.w: The user group definition topic of the project canvas workshop identifies one to three key user groups and prioritizes them (book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

n.1: Project vision definition sets out the long-term outcomes and aligns the project with business value and sustainability objectives, not the user groups (Table 13.2).
n.2: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits and their tolerances, not who the users are (Table 13.2).
n.3: Scope definition sets the timeline, tolerance and the epics prioritized with MoSCoW, not the user groups (Table 13.2).

6.q: Once Sarah Pennington has led the development of the project canvas from the mandate, Simon Archer meets her, the chief product owner and Martin Sallis to define what Care Online will deliver. They agree high-level epics for online self-assessment, eligibility checking, the community directory and case tracking. In the 'prepare the outline business case' activity, what are they creating?
o: The release map for initiation, which sets out the time and cost constraints and controls for the initiation stage.
The product backlog for the digital team, which holds the team Definition of Done and the team's user stories.
The project backlog, which replaces the project product description and holds mainly epic user stories.
The work package descriptions, which set out the sets of user stories that each team will deliver.
6.w: In starting up a project, the executive leads the project canvas, and the project manager, with the CPO, senior supplier and executive, defines what is to be delivered and creates the project backlog. The project backlog replaces the project product description and holds mostly epic user stories (Table 13.1, book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: The release map for initiation is produced when planning the initiation stage, not when defining what the project will deliver (Table 13.1).
n.1: A product backlog is a team-level backlog of user stories owned by a product owner; high-level epics for the whole project form the project backlog (book 8.3.2.1).
n.3: Work package descriptions are agreed between the project manager and product owners when work is authorized in controlling a stage (Table 13.9).

6.q: Midway through stage 2, Simon Archer phones Sarah Pennington. Social workers are struggling to find time for testing sessions, and he asks whether she will support a request to their team managers to release two practitioners for half a day each sprint. Sarah agrees and speaks to the managers that afternoon. Which activity of the 'directing a project' process is this?
o: Authorize the project
Authorize a stage or exception plan
Authorize initiation
Give ongoing direction
6.w: Give ongoing direction covers informal guidance and responses from the board at any time, for example to informal requests, requests for advice and escalated issues (Table 13.4).

n.0: Authorize the project approves the PID and commits resources at the end of initiation; this is an informal request in the middle of stage 2 (Table 13.4).
n.1: Authorizing a stage or exception plan happens at a stage boundary or an exception, when the board reviews the project dashboard and approves the updated release map (Table 13.4).
n.2: Authorize initiation approves the project brief and the release map for initiation at the end of starting up (Table 13.4).

6.q: In the project initiation workshop, Dr Rajesh Iyer, Carol Mbeki and the chief product owner agree the criteria that any part of Care Online must meet before it is acceptable to users, including an easy-read version, approval of the personal data flows and a route to a practitioner assessment where eligibility is likely. Under which topic of the workshop is this agreed?
o: Project Definition of Ready
Project Definition of Done
Management approaches
Project canvas refinement
6.w: The project Definition of Done topic of the project initiation workshop agrees the criteria that work must meet to be acceptable to the users and the chief product owner (book 13.4.4.1, Table 13.7).

n.0: The project Definition of Ready sets product-wide criteria that must be met before work starts, not before it is accepted (Table 13.7).
n.2: The management approaches topic co-creates approaches such as quality and risk; the criteria for accepting products are the project Definition of Done (Table 13.7).
n.3: Project canvas refinement updates the business justification, not the criteria for accepting products (Table 13.7).

6.q: At the project kickoff workshop, Oliver Grant asks the digital team and the practitioners who will join it to complete a short anonymous survey on whether they feel able to raise concerns, admit mistakes and challenge ideas without fear. The results will be compared with later surveys during the project. Under which topic of the kickoff workshop does this belong?
o: Team values and norms
Team skill matrix
Psychological safety
Team delegation matrix
6.w: The project kickoff workshop includes a psychological safety topic, which assesses whether people feel safe to speak up, take risks and challenge ideas without fear (book 13.4.4.2, Table 13.8, 2.7.4).

n.0: Team values and norms build the team's agile culture and shared expectations; assessing how safe people feel to speak up is a topic of its own (Table 13.8).
n.1: The team skill matrix maps skills, gaps and overlaps, not how safe people feel (Table 13.8, 7.4.1).
n.3: The team delegation matrix clarifies who decides what, to simplify decisions and support self-management (Table 13.8, 7.4.3).

6.q: Near the end of stage 2, Simon Archer holds a progress review workshop. Twelve members of the carers' network, invited by Bev Lomax, try the finished carers' self-assessment and community directory on their own phones and tell the team what works for them and what does not. Under which topic of the progress review workshop does this take place?
o: Product demo
Project highlights
Current risks and issues
Final product demo
6.w: The product demo topic of the progress review workshop shows completed features and gathers user acceptance and feedback (book 13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

n.1: Project highlights reviews the project dashboard metrics and achievements, not users trying the product (Table 13.10).
n.2: Current risks and issues reviews the open risks and issues, not user feedback on completed features (Table 13.10).
n.3: The final product demo is a topic of the project closure workshop at the end of the project, not of a progress review in stage 2 (Table 13.19).

6.q: During stage 3, Simon Archer has short conversations with the Abacus team's product owner about risks and issues, pulls progress from the Abacus team dashboard, and updates the release map with actuals and forecasts for the interface work. Which activity of the 'controlling a stage' process is he carrying out?
o: Report highlights
Authorize a work package
Receive completed work package
Evaluate work package status
6.w: In evaluate work package status, the project manager holds informal conversations with the product owner about issues and risks, pulls progress from the updated team dashboard and updates the release map with actuals, forecasts and adjustments (Table 13.9).

n.0: Report highlights assembles the team dashboards, project log and release map changes into an updated project dashboard for the board (Table 13.9).
n.1: Authorize a work package co-creates and agrees the work package description with the product owner and team before work starts (Table 13.9).
n.2: Receive completed work package confirms that the set of user stories was delivered at the end of the work package (Table 13.9).

6.q: In the digital team's team planning workshop for sprint 8, the team finds that the story 'show the person their likely eligibility' has no testable acceptance criteria. With Amy Fletcher and an occupational therapist, the team agrees what the page must show for each possible outcome and what will count as done. Under which topic of the team planning workshop is this work done?
o: Product backlog refinement
Effort estimation
User story refinement
Iteration planning
6.w: User story refinement makes each story's acceptance criteria clear and testable and agrees what counts as done (book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.0: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes the backlog, for example with MoSCoW; writing a story's testable acceptance criteria is user story refinement (Table 13.13).
n.1: Effort estimation builds a shared view of the complexity and effort of each story, not its acceptance criteria (Table 13.13).
n.3: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate to form a realistic team plan for the sprint (Table 13.13).

6.q: At the digital team's retrospective after sprint 6, the team discusses why two practitioners missed the testing sessions again. It traces the problem to calendar invitations being sent late and to clashes with the practitioners' duty rotas. Under which topic of the team retrospective workshop is this discussed?
o: The learning
The bad
Team building
The good
6.w: The bad topic of the team retrospective workshop looks at the issues, risks and challenges of the last iteration and their causes (book 13.6.4.2, Table 13.14).

n.0: The learning turns the discussion into lessons, improvement suggestions and actions; identifying what went wrong and why is the bad (Table 13.14).
n.2: Team building strengthens bonds within the team, for example with a game or food (Table 13.14).
n.3: The good recognizes and celebrates what went well in the iteration (Table 13.14).

6.q: At the end of stage 2, the teams meet for the release planning workshop for stage 3. The digital team sets the objective 'People who may need care can start an assessment without phoning us', with measurable results such as 40% of new requests arriving online by month eight. Under which topic of the workshop is this agreed?
o: OKR definition
Release planning
Benefits analysis
Iteration planning
6.w: The release planning workshop at a stage boundary includes an OKR definition topic, in which teams define or update their objectives and key results; objectives are clear, aspirational goals and key results are specific, measurable outcomes (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16, 12.3.2.3).

n.1: The release planning topic breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map, rather than setting objectives and key results (Table 13.16).
n.2: Benefits analysis is a topic of the project canvas workshop in starting up, not of the release planning workshop (Table 13.2, Table 13.16).
n.3: Iteration planning is a topic of the team planning workshop, which selects the stories for the next sprint (Table 13.13).

6.q: Care Online is closing at month twelve. Text message updates for case tracking, a Could have, were not built, and two minor issues about the directory search remain open. The digital team and the social care operations team will keep improving the service as part of normal business. In the 'confirm project acceptance' activity, how should the unfinished work be handled?
o: Extend the project by one more sprint so that the text message updates and the open issues can be finished before closure.
Close the open issues as resolved and remove the text message updates from the project backlog, so that the records show completion.
Start a new PRINCE2 Agile project for the text message updates, with its own project canvas, before Care Online is closed.
Record follow-on action recommendations for the unfinished feature and open issues, and pass them to the teams who will run the service.
6.w: In confirming project acceptance, the project manager prepares follow-on action recommendations for unfinished work, open issues and risks, and confirms handover to operations (Table 13.18). The teams that will keep improving the service can then take these forward.

n.0: Time has zero tolerance and the grant must be spent by the end of the financial year; unfinished Could haves become follow-on actions instead (Table 3.1, Table 13.18).
n.1: Unresolved issues and unfinished work are not closed off as complete; they are passed on as follow-on action recommendations (Table 13.18).
n.2: Further work on the product after the project is handled through follow-on actions and ongoing product work, not by opening a new project for one feature (Table 13.18, book 14.2.2.1).

6.q: Care Online is the council's first project to use PRINCE2 Agile, and no other agile projects are planned yet; the council will decide whether to adopt agile more widely once it has seen the results. In the project initiation workshop, the group discusses how to manage the move to agile ways of working within the project. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Write a council-wide agile transformation plan in the agile enablement workshop, so that the project board owns it from the start.
Update the change management approach to cover the move to agile ways of working, as a transformation plan may not be needed yet.
Write a council-wide agile transformation plan now, as PRINCE2 Agile requires one before any project can be authorized.
Leave agile adoption out of the management approaches, as Gita Bhatt will manage it outside the project during her contract.
6.w: An agile transformation plan usually spans several projects or initiatives for wider adoption. For a single pilot project it may not be needed yet, and the change management approach can be updated instead (book 2.7.1, Table 13.7).

n.0: The agile enablement workshop reassesses the Agilometer and agile risks; a transformation plan, where needed, comes from initiation, and a single pilot may not need one (Table 13.5, book 2.7.1).
n.2: There is no such requirement; the plan is for adopting agility across several initiatives, and a pilot can update its change management approach instead (book 2.7.1).
n.3: The move to agile working affects the project and has to be managed within it; the change management approach is where this is defined (book 4.2.1, 2.7.1).

6.q: At the start of stage 3, the project board, Gita Bhatt and two senior managers from social care operations hold an agile enablement workshop. They review the latest Agilometer assessment against the initiation results, identify further threats to agile adoption, such as the return of six-week quotes for every Abacus change, and agree practical steps to reduce them. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'directing a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the workshop lets the board, agile coaches and business representatives reassess the Agilometer and agile risks after initiation.
Yes, because the agile enablement workshop is where the project board approves the updated release map for the next stage.
No, because the Agilometer is assessed once, in the project initiation workshop, and later reviews belong to team retrospectives.
No, because risks to agile adoption are managed by the agile coach, so the project board does not need to take part in the workshop.
6.w: The agile enablement workshop in directing a project brings the board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives together to reassess the Agilometer regularly in initiation and later stages, identify further agile-adoption risks, assess them and plan mitigation (Table 13.5).

n.1: The board approves the updated release map in 'authorize a stage or exception plan'; the enablement workshop deals with the Agilometer and agile-adoption risks (Table 13.4, Table 13.5).
n.2: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop, but it is reassessed regularly through the agile enablement workshop (Table 13.5, Table 13.7).
n.3: The workshop is designed for the project board together with agile coaches and business representatives (Table 13.5).

6.q: To save senior managers' time, Simon Archer drafts the whole Care Online project canvas on his own from the mandate during starting up. He then emails it to Sarah Pennington, who signs it off without a project canvas workshop being held. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager prepares the outline business case, so the project canvas can be completed by one person.
Yes, because the project canvas is a one-page artifact, so a workshop adds little value where senior managers have limited time.
No, because the executive should lead the canvas, built in a workshop that gives a shared understanding of the project's core elements.
No, because the project canvas should be written in initiation, once the project initiation workshop has agreed the management approaches.
6.w: In starting up, the project executive leads development of the project canvas from the mandate, and the project canvas workshop builds shared understanding and a clear foundation by defining the project's core elements with the people involved (Table 13.1, book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

n.0: The executive leads development of the project canvas in starting up; having the project manager write it alone loses the shared understanding the workshop is for (Table 13.1, Table 13.2).
n.1: The canvas is concise, but its workshop exists to create shared understanding among those involved, which emailing a draft does not achieve (Table 13.2).
n.3: The canvas is developed in starting up and then refined in initiation; it is not first written in initiation (Table 13.1, Table 13.7).

6.q: At the end of stage 2, Simon Archer holds the release planning workshop for stage 3. To satisfy Joan Whitaker, he asks each team to break all of its stage 3 work into tasks with hour estimates for every sprint up to month eight, and he puts this task list in the stage plan for the board. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the stage plan should give the board enough detail to approve the next stage, including the tasks for each sprint.
Yes, because the release planning workshop is where the teams agree their team plans for every sprint in the coming stage.
No, because the next stage plan is prepared by the project board in directing a project rather than by the project manager.
No, because the stage boundary updates the release map with user stories, and task-level plans are made by each team before each sprint.
6.w: At a stage boundary the release planning workshop breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map; task-level planning is done just in time for the next iteration in managing product delivery, through the team planning workshop (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16, 8.3.2).

n.0: The board approves the next stage plan as an updated release map; detailed tasks for every sprint are planned just in time, not months ahead (Table 13.4, book 8.3.2).
n.1: Team plans are produced by delivery teams for the next iteration when they accept a work package, not for every sprint at the stage boundary (Table 13.12, Table 13.13).
n.2: The project manager prepares the next stage plan in managing a stage boundary; the board approves it in directing a project (book 13.7.1, Table 13.4).

6.q: Release 3 goes live in month twelve, and Care Online then passes to the social care operations team, who will work with the digital team to run and improve it. The operations team has not taken part in the project's sprints. Simon Archer is planning the transition to operations. Which approach BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Hand over a final printed specification of the service and close the backlog and dashboards, so that operations start from a stable baseline.
Give the operations team one training session at closure and ask them to contact Abacus directly if anything goes wrong with the service.
Hand over the backlog and dashboards, tailored training and guides, clear operating and escalation procedures, and regular feedback loops.
Keep the project team running the service for six months after closure, so that the operations team can learn by watching them.
6.w: Transition to operations hands over agile artifacts and tools so that agile practice continues, provides tailored end-user training and guides, sets out explicit operating procedures and escalation pathways, and builds regular feedback loops such as surveys, retrospectives and check-ins (book 14.2.1).

n.0: Closing down the agile artifacts and tools works against keeping agile practices aligned after the transition (book 14.2.1).
n.1: A single session with no defined procedures or escalation pathways falls short of the tailored training and clear escalation routes the book describes (book 14.2.1).
n.3: The project closes at month twelve with the grant spent; transition hands over artifacts, training and procedures rather than extending the project team's role (book 14.2.1, Table 3.1).

6.q: After closure, the digital team and the social care operations team will keep improving Care Online as part of normal business. Dr Rajesh Iyer already has ideas, such as a self-assessment in other languages, and expects practitioners and carers to suggest more once the service is in use. How should these improvements be managed, following PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Through agile product management, with a high-level product vision, a flexible roadmap adjusted from feedback, and short prioritized cycles.
By starting a separate PRINCE2 Agile project for each improvement, each with its own project canvas, project board, business case and release map.
By freezing the service for a year after closure, then gathering all the requests into one large upgrade project for the following year.
By adding them to the Care Online release map and asking the cabinet to extend the project beyond the grant's spending deadline.
6.w: Agile product management keeps a high-level product vision with a flexible roadmap that is continually adjusted from stakeholder, customer and market feedback, and delivers in short cycles prioritized by value; enhancements after a project are handled this way rather than as new projects (book 14.2.2.1).

n.1: Starting a project for each enhancement adds heavy overhead; after the project, improvements are handled through product management iterations (book 14.2.2.1).
n.2: Agile product management keeps adjusting the product from feedback in short cycles; a year's freeze followed by one large upgrade works against that (book 14.2.2.1).
n.3: Time has zero tolerance and the grant must be spent within the year; later improvements belong to product management (Table 3.1, book 14.2.2.1).

6.q: Simon Archer has access to an AI tool approved by the council. He wants to use it to support the 'ensure continued business justification' principle on Care Online. Which use of the tool would do this?
o: Search the lessons logs of past council digital projects and give each role a prioritized list of the lessons relevant to its work.
Analyse spend and velocity to forecast whether the expected benefits are still achievable within the grant and timescale.
Analyse team members' skills and workload and suggest who should take the product owner and team coach roles.
Answer the board's routine questions through a project chatbot, so that board members no longer need to attend progress reviews.
6.w: For continued business justification, AI can use predictive analytics to forecast viability and benefits against timelines and budgets and give early warning of overruns (book 15.4.1).

n.0: Turning lessons into searchable, role-specific insights supports the 'learn from experience' principle (book 15.4.1).
n.2: Suggesting role assignments from skills and workload supports 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' (book 15.4.1).
n.3: A chatbot can answer frequent questions, but AI does not remove the need for human decisions and communication with stakeholders, and this does not address justification (book 15.4.2).

7.q: During starting up, Graham Doyle asks Andrea Lucas why Smart Maintenance should use PRINCE2 Agile rather than one detailed plan fixed at the start. Hannah Reece expects the prediction model to need several months of real sensor data, and the maintenance engineers are not yet sure what the dashboard should show them. Which explanation BEST supports Andrea's choice?
o: Agile frameworks deliver faster and to a higher quality once they are adopted, so the twelve-month deadline before the aerospace contract will be easier to meet.
Agile removes the need for a fixed budget and end date, so the board can extend the project if the model takes longer to train.
The work is complex and uncertain, so staying adaptable and learning from feedback on each release beats seeking a perfect design up front.
Agile matches the way the software team already works, so the engineers and Senticore can keep their current ways of working unchanged.
7.w: Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one perfect solution; it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly than to hunt for perfection. Here the model's usefulness and the engineers' needs will only become clear from real data and feedback, so frequent releases with feedback loops reduce waste (book 2.4).

n.0: This is the classic misconception: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from a change of mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile keeps time and cost fixed with zero tolerance by default, and the board has fixed both here; agility flexes what is delivered, not the budget or date (Table 3.1).
n.3: The need for agile here comes from complexity and uncertainty, not from one team's habits; the engineers are central users whose feedback drives each release (book 2.4).

7.q: At the first sprint review for Release 1, Stuart Bell and two other senior engineers give almost all of the feedback. Afterwards, two machine operators tell Tomasz Zielinski that they had ideas about the alert screen but felt their views would not count. Tomasz wants the reviews to show respect, a key characteristic of the agile mindset. Which change is MOST LIKELY to achieve this?
o: Run the feedback in small mixed groups so that every engineer and operator is heard, and record each group's ideas for the backlog.
Ask Stuart Bell to collect the operators' views before each review and present one combined set of comments on their behalf.
Invite the senior engineers to future reviews and send the operators a written summary of the decisions taken afterwards.
Ask the operators to email their ideas to Leanne Park after each review, so that she can decide which ones to add to the backlog.
7.w: Respect, as a characteristic of the agile mindset, is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness: every voice is valued and diverse perspectives are embraced (book 2.6.2). Small mixed groups let the operators, who use the machines every shift, be heard directly alongside the senior engineers.

n.1: Filtering the operators' ideas through the most senior engineer still leaves them unheard in the review, which is the problem Tomasz has noticed (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Leaving the operators out of the reviews removes their perspective altogether; respect means valuing all voices, not just the most experienced (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Sending ideas by email after the event keeps the operators out of the conversation and loses the rich, face-to-face exchange that the review provides (book 2.6.2).

7.q: In initiation, Andrea Lucas records in the PID that the software team will keep its two-week Scrum sprints, Senticore will fit sensors to an agreed fitting schedule rather than in sprints, and the board will review a project dashboard instead of monthly written reports. Which principle is Andrea applying, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because she is setting out how each stage of the project will be planned, monitored and controlled by the board.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because she is agreeing how the three teams will work with the board and each other.
Focus on products, because she is making sure that each team, including Senticore, delivers well-defined outputs rather than simply carrying out activities.
Tailor to suit the project, because she is choosing the frameworks and artifacts each part of the project uses and recording them in the PID.
7.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity, risk and context; in PRINCE2 Agile that includes deciding which agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use, and the tailoring is recorded in the PID (book 5.2.1.7, Table 5.1).

n.0: Manage by stages is about the board authorizing one stage at a time and delegating control within it; Andrea is choosing ways of working, not stage controls (book 5.2.1.4).
n.1: That principle is about the right people in clear roles with stakeholders engaged; choosing sprints, fitting schedules and dashboards is a tailoring decision (book 5.2.1.3, 5.2.1.7).
n.2: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering well-specified outputs; Andrea's decisions are about how each team works and reports (book 5.2.1.6, 5.2.1.7).

7.q: Midway through Stage 3, the burn-up chart shows that the software team will deliver failure prediction and alerts for the ten trial machines by month 8; the project canvas lists these as Must haves. However, Senticore cannot fit sensors to every remaining Factory A machine by then, which is a Should have. The budget and end date are fixed. What should Andrea Lucas recommend?
o: Ask the board to move the Release 2 date back by four weeks, so that every Factory A machine is fitted before the alerts go live.
Fit as many remaining Factory A machines as the schedule allows, keep the Must haves, and re-plan the rest in the release map.
Agree a budget increase so that Senticore can add a second fitting crew and fit every Factory A machine by month 8.
Fit sensors to all of Factory A first, and move prediction and alerts for the ten trial machines into Release 3.
7.w: PRINCE2 Agile sets zero tolerance for extra time and cost, fixes scope for Must haves and flexes it for Should and Could haves (Table 3.1). The board has also said the number of machines per release can change, so the remaining fittings are the part to flex.

n.0: Delaying the release flexes time, which has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, and the end date is fixed by the new aerospace contract (Table 3.1).
n.2: Raising the budget flexes cost, which has zero tolerance by default and which the board has fixed for this project (Table 3.1).
n.3: This protects a Should have by dropping Must haves from Release 2; scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves (Table 3.1).

7.q: Apart from the software team, nobody at Draycott has used agile before.
