For the start of Stage 2, Ruth Kenyon proposes sending the maintenance engineers and operators on a one-day course on agile theory, then leaving them to join sprint reviews and use the dashboard as they see fit. What should Andrea Lucas recommend instead?
o: Give each engineer a written guide to Scrum and the dashboard, so that they can refer to it whenever they need help.
Train the senior engineers in agile first, and let them pass what they have learned on to the operators later in the project.
Follow the course with on-the-job coaching in the engineers' own work, set out in a training and coaching plan for each stage.
Introduce a new task-tracking tool for the engineers first, so that they learn agile ways of working by using it every day.
7.w: People need theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching to apply a change; informing them and leaving them to fend for themselves breeds frustration, a leading cause of resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the agile change (book 2.7.3).

n.0: A written guide only informs people; without coaching in their own work they are still left to fend for themselves (book 2.7.3).
n.1: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why; delaying the operators' learning leaves key users behind (book 2.7.3).
n.3: Early in a transformation the priority is building knowledge and skills through training and coaching, not introducing tools (book 2.7.3).

7.q: At the project canvas workshop, Graham Doyle says Smart Maintenance is a technology installation, so organizational change management (OCM) is not needed. The maintenance engineers are proud of their skills and doubt the predictions, and after closure the maintenance team will run the dashboard as part of normal work. Which explanation BEST shows why OCM matters here?
o: OCM is the practice that controls changes to the project's baseline, so it is needed whenever the engineers ask for new dashboard features.
OCM moves the organization from its current to its target state, and evolving the culture helps stop engineers reverting to old ways after closure.
OCM replaces the communication management approach, so it gives the project one place to brief the engineers and the union about the project.
OCM sets the tolerances for adoption, so the board can decide how far the engineers' use of the new dashboard may slip before an exception is raised.
7.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to its target state. Making the change last means evolving the culture so that changes are not rolled back after the transformation (book 4.2.1). Moving from reactive and calendar maintenance to prediction-led work, with sceptical engineers, is exactly this kind of change.

n.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice, not OCM (book 11.1, 4.2.1).
n.2: OCM does not replace the communication management approach; communication is one of the things considered when planning the change (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.3: Tolerances are set through manage by exception for the performance aspects; OCM is about the transition to new ways of working (book 5.2.1.5, 4.2.1).

7.q: Andrea Lucas wants a key influencer to help the maintenance engineers at Factory A accept the dashboard's predictions. Engineers there tend to follow colleagues whose practical judgement they trust, and several doubt that a computer can tell them when a machine will fail. Using the people list, who is the BEST choice of key influencer for this group?
o: Graham Doyle, because as operations director he is the most senior person on the project and holds the budget for both factories.
Hannah Reece, because as data science lead she can explain in detail how the prediction model reaches each of its results.
Dev Patel, because as Senticore's account director he knows the sensors well and commits the teams that fit them.
Stuart Bell, because his long experience and standing with colleagues let him shape how the other engineers see the change.
7.w: Key influencers are people who can shape the perception of the majority and, through their network, most influence adoption of the change (book 4.2.2). Stuart Bell has 30 years' experience and is respected by colleagues; winning over a respected sceptic carries far more weight with the engineers than a formal instruction.

n.0: Seniority and budget give formal authority, but a key influencer is chosen for network and credibility among the affected group (book 4.2.2).
n.1: Hannah is a technical specialist and the model's builder; engineers who doubt the computer are more likely to follow a trusted peer (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Dev Patel works for the supplier and sits outside the engineers' network, so he has little influence over how they see the change (book 4.2.2).

7.q: During Stage 2, Senticore's fitting crews and Draycott's production staff argue on the shop floor about who can decide when a machine may be stopped and where on each machine a sensor may be mounted. Two fittings are delayed while people wait for answers. What should Andrea Lucas do to lead these teams across the two organizations?
o: Agree clear boundaries, such as a delegation matrix showing which decisions the fitters may take and which they advise on.
Ask Dev Patel to make all decisions about machine stops and sensor positions, as Senticore holds the fixed-price contract.
Require every decision about machine stops and sensor positions to be referred to her, so one person is accountable.
Ask Jim Halligan to settle each dispute as it arises, as he represents the engineering staff on the shop floor.
7.w: When people work across organizations and cultures, PRINCE2 Agile advises setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that shows what external parties decide and what they only advise on (book 4.3.1).

n.1: Machine stops affect Draycott's production and sensor positions affect safety certification; handing all such decisions to the supplier ignores those boundaries (book 4.3.1).
n.2: Routing every decision through the project manager creates a bottleneck and undermines self-management within agreed boundaries (book 4.3.1).
n.3: The union representative speaks for staff interests but has no authority over production schedules or fitting decisions; the gap is unclear decision rights (book 4.3.1).

7.q: The software team works at head office two days a week and from home on the others. Factory B engineers join sprint reviews by video while Factory A engineers attend in person, and the Factory B engineers say they miss much of what is decided. Which approach to communication BEST fits this hybrid arrangement?
o: Require everyone to attend every review in person at Factory A, so that all decisions are made face to face.
Send all the engineers the same written summary after each review, so both factories get identical information.
Agree how information flows and in what formats, with structured and informal time together and some in-person days.
Ask Ruth Kenyon to brief the Factory B engineers once a month, so that they hear decisions from their own manager.
7.w: Remote and hybrid teams need a deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together. Synchronized co-location days for key people help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3, 4.4).

n.0: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer for distributed teams; the book advises planned in-person days alongside structured remote working (book 4.3.3).
n.1: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be two-way and tailored to each group (book 4.4).
n.3: Periodic one-way briefings are not enough on their own; the engineers need to take part in the flow of information and feedback (book 4.4).

7.q: The maintenance engineers and operators trialling the dashboard are expert machinists, but few have read sensor trend charts or judged how confident a prediction is. Tomasz Zielinski and Ruth Kenyon want to build these skills over the three releases. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on building agile teams?
o: Rank the engineers each month by how many predicted failures they act on, and pay the top three a bonus.
Use a team skill matrix of current and planned skills, agree a training plan from it, and show it on the team dashboard.
Ask Hannah Reece to read all the trend charts for the engineers, so that gaps in skills do not slow the trial down.
Recruit a data analyst to join the trial team, so that the engineers can concentrate on their machining work.
7.w: PRINCE2 Agile suggests empowering teams with training plans, using a team skill matrix that shows current and planned skills, and using visual management such as team dashboards (book 4.5, 7.4.1).

n.0: Value-based incentives reward behaviour that models agile values, often peer-assessed and balanced with purpose and recognition; an individual ranking on one metric works against teamwork (book 4.5).
n.2: Relying on one specialist leaves the skill gap in place and makes the team dependent on Hannah; the aim is to build the team's own capability (book 4.5).
n.3: Adding a specialist does not develop the engineers, who will run the dashboard after closure; a skill matrix and training plan build their skills (book 4.5).

7.q: At the project canvas workshop, Stuart Bell asks how the engineers will know what the dashboard must do before they accept it, and how that will be measured on the shop floor. Andrea Lucas says this concern is handled by one of the PRINCE2 Agile practices. Which practice, and why?
o: Quality, because it documents the users' requirements of the project's products and sets out how they will be met and checked.
Plans, because it defines the products to be delivered, who will build them and how, and estimates when and at what cost.
Progress, because it compares what has been achieved with what was planned and forecasts whether objectives will be met.
Business case, because it judges whether the dashboard is and remains desirable, viable and achievable for the business.
7.w: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes how they will be met; it answers what is acceptable to users and how that is measured (book 9.1). Stuart's question is about acceptance criteria and how they are checked.

n.1: Plans set out what is delivered, by whom, how, when and at what cost; they do not define what users will accept (book 8.1, 9.1).
n.2: Progress monitors actual achievement against plan and forecasts; it does not define acceptance criteria (book 12.1).
n.3: The business case practice judges whether the investment stays worthwhile; users' acceptance criteria belong to quality (book 6.1, 9.1).

7.q: In initiation, Graham Doyle is refining the project canvas with Andrea Lucas. He wants the benefits section to show what Draycott will gain, with a tolerance, so that the board can later judge whether the investment paid off. Which entry belongs in the benefits section of the project canvas?
o: Sensors fitted to all 60 machining centres across both factories by the end of month 12.
A predictive maintenance dashboard in daily use by all 22 maintenance engineers across both factories after Release 3.
Weekly improvements to the dashboard released by the software team once Release 1 is live.
A measured fall in unplanned breakdown costs from last year's £1.8 million, within an agreed tolerance.
7.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that the investing organization sees as an advantage. The project canvas records expected, measurable benefits with a tolerance (Glossary, book 6.3.2). Lower breakdown costs are such an improvement.

n.0: Fitted sensors are an output (a specialist product), not a benefit; outputs belong in the scope section (Glossary, book 6.3.2).
n.1: A dashboard in use is an outcome built on outputs; the benefit is the measurable improvement it brings, such as lower breakdown costs (Glossary).
n.2: Weekly releases are a way of delivering, not a measurable improvement for the business (Glossary, book 6.3.2).

7.q: Andrea Lucas is drafting the benefits management approach in initiation. Release 1 goes live at month 4 on ten Factory A machines, and Ruth Kenyon expects fewer breakdowns on those machines soon afterwards. Graham Doyle suggests that benefits should not be measured until after the project closes at month 12. What should the benefits management approach do?
o: Leave all benefit measurement until after closure, as benefits are confirmed once the project has ended.
Plan measurement of breakdown costs from Release 1 onwards, with tolerances and responsibilities, so early benefits are tracked.
Record the expected benefits in the release map, as the release map serves as both the project plan and the stage plan.
Measure benefits by counting the user stories delivered in each sprint, as these show the value the software and trial teams have added.
7.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases to enable early delivery of benefits, and sets out measurement and tolerance guidance and responsibilities (book 6.3.2). Confirming benefits happens mostly after closure, but iterative releases can realize some during the project.

n.0: Some benefits can be realized during the project through iterative releases; the approach should plan to measure them from Release 1 (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2).
n.2: The release map shows releases, timing and features; how benefits will be measured and reviewed belongs in the benefits management approach (book 8.3.2, 6.3.2).
n.3: User stories delivered are outputs, not benefits; benefits are measurable improvements such as reduced breakdown costs (Glossary).

7.q: After the PID is approved, Graham Doyle tells Andrea Lucas that because the budget and end date are fixed, the project canvas will not be revisited until closure, when benefits will be checked. Release 1 is due at month 4, and Graham has said it is the minimum needed to show whether continuing is justified. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because time and cost have zero tolerance, so the cost side of the canvas cannot change during the project.
Yes, because benefits are mostly confirmed after closure, once the dashboard has been in use for some time.
No, because justification must stay valid throughout, so the canvas should be checked as Release 1 shows its value.
No, because once the PID is approved the project canvas should be replaced by a full written business case.
7.w: Ensure continued business justification requires the justification to remain valid throughout the life cycle (book 5.2.1.1). Release 1 is the stated minimum for continuing, so the canvas must be checked against the evidence it produces, not left until closure.

n.0: Zero tolerance on time and cost does not keep the justification valid; benefits, risks and value can all change and must be reviewed (book 5.2.1.1).
n.1: Benefits are largely confirmed after closure, but the justification still has to be checked throughout, especially at the Release 1 decision point (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).
n.3: The project canvas is a suitable replacement for the business case and is refined, not swapped for a written document, as the project goes on (book 6.3.2).

7.q: In initiation, Andrea Lucas and Dev Patel agree how Senticore's fixed-price contract will support agile delivery: sensors will be fitted release by release, the minimum viable product is the ten Release 1 machines, and a fitting is not complete until it meets an agreed Definition of Done. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the commercial management approach, as it covers how procurement and the contract support agile delivery.
In the project management team structure, as it shows how Senticore's fitters work with the other teams.
In the role descriptions, as they set out the responsibilities Dev Patel holds in the project management team.
In the quality register, as it records the planned and completed quality activities for each sensor fitting.
7.w: The commercial management approach makes sure procurement and the form of contract support agile product development, for example by defining the MVP and tolerances, an agreed Definition of Done and how the supplier tracks and reports (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.1: The project management team structure shows who is involved, their relationships and working arrangements such as co-location, not contract terms (Table 7.3).
n.2: Role descriptions set out each role's responsibilities; the terms of Senticore's contract belong in the commercial management approach (Table 7.3).
n.3: The quality register records individual quality activities and their results; it does not hold contractual arrangements (Table 9.1).

7.q: During Stage 2, the software team and the engineers' trial team disagree about which dashboard features matter most. Leanne Park wants a data export that would help the software team's testing, while the engineers want a simpler alert screen first. Andrea Lucas is asked how priorities across the teams should be set. Which arrangement follows the organization practice?
o: Andrea decides the priorities herself, because the project manager has direct authority over every member of each team.
Leanne decides, because as the software team's product owner she owns the backlog that the dashboard features come from.
The chief product owner sets priorities across the teams, and each team's product owner orders its own backlog to match.
Each team keeps its own priorities, and the team coach resolves conflicting features at the next team retrospective.
7.w: With several teams, PRINCE2 Agile has one chief product owner who represents the users and sets priorities across teams, while each team's product owner owns that team's product backlog and keeps it aligned with the project backlog (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

n.0: The project manager has direct authority over the product owners, not over delivery team members, and setting user priorities is the CPO's job (book 7.3.1).
n.1: A product owner owns one team's backlog but does not prioritize across teams; that is the chief product owner (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.3: The team coach helps a team self-manage and facilitates its workshops; cross-team priorities are set by the chief product owner (Table 7.2).

7.q: Two weeks before Release 1, Andrea Lucas is worried about the dashboard. She starts holding her own morning meeting with the software developers, telling each one which tasks to work on that day, and informs Leanne Park afterwards. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager runs the project day to day on behalf of the board within the agreed tolerances.
Yes, because close to a release date the project manager should take direct control of the delivery team's work.
No, because daily task allocation for the software team should be carried out by Tomasz Zielinski as team coach.
No, because the product owner directs the delivery team, and the project manager agrees the work with the product owner.
7.w: The project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, and the product owner is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members. The PM and PO agree work as sets of user stories within tolerances (book 7.3.1).

n.0: The PM does run the project day to day, but through work packages agreed with the product owner, not by directing developers (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.1: Nothing in PRINCE2 Agile gives the PM direct control of team members near a release; authority runs through the product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.2: The team coach helps the team self-manage and facilitates workshops; it is not a task-allocating role (Table 7.2).

7.q: Graham Doyle needs to appoint a chief product owner for Smart Maintenance. The role must represent the engineers and operators who will use the dashboard in both factories, own the project backlog and set priorities across all three teams. Using the people list, who is BEST suited to this role?
o: Leanne Park, the software team lead, who manages the software team's backlog and works with engineers on requirements.
Ruth Kenyon, the head of maintenance, who leads the engineers in both factories and will own the dashboard afterwards.
Stuart Bell, the senior maintenance engineer at Factory A, who has 30 years' experience and is respected by colleagues.
Graham Doyle, the operations director, who received the mandate and holds the capital budget for both factories.
7.w: The chief product owner represents the user community, owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams (Table 7.2). Ruth leads the 22 engineers across both factories and will own the dashboard after the project, so she speaks for all its users.

n.0: Leanne manages one team's backlog, which fits the product owner role for the software team, not a role prioritizing across all teams (Table 7.2).
n.2: Stuart is respected but works at Factory A only and has no authority over the engineers at Factory B; he suits a key influencer role (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Graham received the mandate and holds the budget, which fits the project executive, who is accountable for the project rather than representing users (Table 7.2).

7.q: The board wants someone to monitor, independently of Andrea Lucas and the teams, whether Smart Maintenance follows PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, and to build governance and quality checks into each release. Using the people list, who is BEST suited to the project assurance role?
o: Mei Chen, the quality manager, who is responsible for the aerospace quality system and approves maintenance changes.
Tomasz Zielinski, the Scrum master, who knows agile practices well and already works closely with the software team.
Colin Ashby, the production manager for Factory A, who plans the machine schedules and knows the factory well.
Robert Kale, the quality director, who is independent of operations and reports directly to the board.
7.w: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, integrates quality and governance checks into iterative delivery and advises the board and PM (Table 7.2). Robert already carries out independent checks of major projects for the board and is independent of operations.

n.0: Mei runs the aerospace quality system that approves the project's maintenance changes, so she is part of the work being checked and is not described as independent of operations (Table 7.2).
n.1: Tomasz works inside the software team, which fits the team coach role; assurance needs someone independent of the teams (Table 7.2).
n.2: Colin is a stakeholder whose machines are affected and who reports within operations; he is not independent of the project (Table 7.2).

7.q: Graham Doyle asks when the software team will finish the remaining Release 2 dashboard work, estimated at 105 story points. The team's velocity over its last three two-week sprints was 18, 24 and 21 points. A contractor says a team he worked with elsewhere managed 30 points a sprint on similar work. Using an empirical approach, what forecast should Andrea Lucas give?
o: About three and a half sprints, using the contractor's figure of 30 points a sprint for similar work.
Between four and five sprints, using the team's best recent sprint of 24 points as the rate.
Close to six sprints, using the team's slowest recent sprint of 18 points as a cautious rate.
About five sprints, using the team's own average velocity of 21 points a sprint.
7.w: Empirical planning forecasts from what the team has actually done. Velocity is the average rate of story points delivered per timebox: (18 + 24 + 21) / 3 = 21, and 105 / 21 = 5 sprints, about ten weeks. Use the team's own velocity, not another team's (book 8.3, 12.4.3).

n.0: Another team's velocity on another project is not evidence of this team's rate; empiricism uses your own team's history (book 8.3).
n.1: Velocity is an average over recent timeboxes; picking the best sprint overstates the rate and gives an optimistic forecast (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.2: Picking the slowest sprint understates the rate; the empirical forecast uses the average velocity, which is 21 points (book 8.3, 12.4.3).

7.q: In initiation, the teams have built a user story map for Smart Maintenance, and Andrea Lucas is turning it into the release map. Sensor hardware has a ten-week lead time, and each fitting needs the machine stopped for four hours, which Colin Ashby must schedule. What should Andrea do as she creates the release map?
o: Write task-level plans now for every sprint in all three releases, so that each fitting date is fixed for Colin Ashby.
Identify interdependencies such as the sensor lead time and machine stops, and plan the releases around them.
Draw a product breakdown structure alongside the story map, so that sensors and gateways appear as separate products.
Fix the number of machines in each release, so that Senticore's fitting schedule cannot change later in the project.
7.w: Turning a story map into a release map also defines interdependencies and plans the releases accordingly (book 8.3.1.1). The ten-week lead time and the need to schedule machine stops are exactly such dependencies.

n.0: Planning is just in time: the release map stays high level, and task-level planning is done for the next iteration in managing product delivery (book 8.3, Table 13.12).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, so a separate PBS is not needed (book 8.3.1).
n.3: The board has said the number of machines per release can be adjusted; fixing it removes the flexibility in what is delivered (Table 3.1).

7.q: At the end of Stage 2, Andrea Lucas prepares for the board to approve Stage 3. Because the board is used to detailed plans, she writes a task-by-task plan for every sprint in Release 2, assigns tasks to named developers, and gives it to Leanne Park to follow. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the board must approve a plan for the next stage before Stage 3 can be authorized.
Yes, because a detailed plan suits a board that is used to monthly written reports against a detailed plan.
No, because the team plans tasks for the next iteration only, and the stage plan is a high-level release map.
No, because in PRINCE2 Agile the board approves the team plan for each sprint rather than a stage plan.
7.w: The release map serves as the stage plan and stays high level; the team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts a work package and covers the next iteration at task level (book 8.3.2, Table 8.1). Planning is just in time.

n.0: The board does approve the next stage plan, but in PRINCE2 Agile that is the updated release map, not a task-level plan written by the PM (book 8.3.2, 13.7.1).
n.1: The board's habits do not change who plans at task level; detailed plans for later sprints would be out of date before the team reached them (book 8.3).
n.3: Team plans belong to the delivery team in managing product delivery; the board approves the stage plan in the form of the release map (Table 8.1, Table 13.4).

7.q: The software team's Definition of Done says a feature that changes how machines are maintained is done when Mei Chen has approved it under the aerospace quality system. At the sprint review, the new alert-driven maintenance checklist has been built and tested, but Mei's approval is still pending. Leanne Park reports it as 'almost done'. How should the team treat the checklist?
o: Count it as done for this sprint's velocity, and ask Mei Chen to approve it during the next sprint.
Show it as 90% complete on the team dashboard, so that the board can see how close it is to being done.
Treat it as not done, keep it out of the release, and return it to the product backlog for reprioritization.
Ask a tester to sign it off against its acceptance criteria, so that Mei Chen's approval is not needed for it.
7.w: The Definition of Done is the shared agreement on what makes an item complete; an item is either done or not done, and there is no 'almost done'. Unfinished work goes back to the backlog to be reprioritized (book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Counting unfinished work as done inflates velocity and breaks the agreed Definition of Done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Percentages hide the fact that the item is not done; PRINCE2 Agile treats work as done or not done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: Testers check work against acceptance criteria and the team DoD, but they cannot remove an approval step that the DoD itself requires (Table 7.2, book 9.3.2.2).

7.q: In initiation, Andrea Lucas writes the quality management approach. It records the software team's automated tests run as each dashboard feature is built, and Senticore's checks agreed before each fitting so that a mounting is proven safe before the machine restarts. It also notes A/B testing of two alert screen designs with engineers. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because it decides early what is tested first or as you go, and records agile testing methods, including the supplier's.
Yes, because A/B testing confirms that the system has been built right against its technical specification.
No, because physical products such as sensor fittings should follow the same fast build-and-fix cycle as the software.
No, because a supplier's own testing methods belong in its contract rather than in the quality management approach.
7.w: PRINCE2 Agile advises deciding early how much can be tested first and how much as you go, transferring software practices carefully to other products, and recording agile testing methods, including suppliers', in the quality management approach (book 9.3.2, 9.4.3).

n.1: A/B testing compares two versions with users, which supports validation (building the right thing), not verification against a specification (book 9.4.3).
n.2: Software practices do not transfer directly to physical work: a fitting needs a four-hour stop and must not affect safety certification, so it cannot be rebuilt in minutes (book 9.4.3).
n.3: The quality management approach should record agile testing methods, including those used by suppliers (book 9.3.2).

7.q: At the project initiation workshop, participants assess the Agilometer. Senticore's contract requires a formal variation, with legal review and a fee, before any change can be made to the agreed fitting schedule. Several participants mark one slider low because of this. Which Agilometer slider are they MOST LIKELY to have marked low?
o: Advantageous environmental conditions
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally
Level of collaboration
Ease of communication
7.w: The 'advantageous environmental conditions' slider covers how far the overall working environment supports agile, including contracts that do not inhibit agile working (book 10.3.2.2). A contract that makes every schedule change a legal variation is such an inhibitor.

n.1: This slider is about how easily benefit can be delivered through regular partial deliveries; the releases are still planned in increments here (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: Level of collaboration reflects how well people work together; the problem described is a contractual constraint in the environment (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: Ease of communication concerns how easily all parties can talk to each other; the contract terms are an environmental condition (book 10.3.2.2).

7.q: Hannah Reece's cleansing of the old maintenance records, and the IT security review that must pass before sensors connect to the network, are both responses to risks in the risk register. Leanne Park wants the software team to plan and prioritize this work alongside its user stories in each sprint. Which technique supports this?
o: A cumulative risk burn-down chart, updated at each sprint planning session to show the total risk exposure for the project.
The Agilometer, reassessed at each agile enablement workshop to show the risks of agile working.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many risk responses sit in each workflow state over time.
A risk-adjusted product backlog, holding risk responses and user stories together in one prioritized list.
7.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog places risk responses in the product backlog alongside user stories, so they are prioritized and planned together (book 10.4.1).

n.0: A cumulative risk burn-down tracks total risk exposure across iterations; it does not plan the response work alongside stories (book 10.4.2).
n.1: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, such as collaboration or contracts, not project risks like data quality or security (book 10.3.2).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows work in each workflow state to reveal bottlenecks; it does not prioritize risk responses (book 12.4.2).

7.q: From Stage 2, Andrea Lucas asks Tomasz Zielinski to make risk identification a fixed agenda item in every team planning workshop and every team retrospective. New risks, such as gateways losing signal near the large presses, are recorded and assessed by the team before Andrea updates the risk register. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the Agilometer should be reassessed by the team at every planning session and retrospective.
Yes, because in agile, identifying risks is a fixed part of every planning session and retrospective.
No, because risks should be identified by the project manager and recorded before they are shared with the teams.
No, because new risks should be gathered at progress reviews, where the project dashboard shows current risks.
7.w: PRINCE2 Agile adapts the five-step risk technique so that identification is a fixed part of every planning session and team or project retrospective, where risks are gathered and documented (book 10.3.1).

n.0: The Agilometer is assessed in the project initiation workshop and reassessed in agile enablement workshops; it is not the identification step in team workshops (book 10.3.2, Table 13.5).
n.2: The team often sees risks first; the book builds identification into team planning and retrospectives rather than leaving it to the PM (book 10.3.1).
n.3: Progress reviews look at current risks, but identification is built into every planning session and retrospective, where risks can surface early (book 10.3.1).

7.q: During a Release 1 sprint, engineers trialling the dashboard ask for the vibration trend to appear above the temperature trend on each machine screen. The change sits within an existing user story, takes the team about an hour, and does not affect the project backlog. How should it be handled?
o: Raise a request for change to the board, because any change to an agreed product alters the project's baseline.
Handle it as a detail change at team level with Leanne Park, without the formal change procedure.
Record it as an off-specification, because the screen no longer matches the layout first agreed.
Ask Ruth Kenyon as chief product owner to approve it as a change to the project backlog before work starts.
7.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change: it makes the final product more accurate and is handled informally at team level. Changes that alter the project backlog are baseline changes and go through the formal route (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Only changes that alter the project backlog are baseline changes needing a formal decision; this one sits inside an existing story (book 11.3.2).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; here the users are improving a layout within the story (book 11.3.1).
n.3: The project backlog is not affected, so there is nothing for the chief product owner to approve formally; the team handles it with its product owner (book 11.3.2).

7.q: In a Release 2 sprint, one developer has been stuck for three days because data from two gateways drops out at random. The other developers carry on with their own stories. Leanne Park records the blocker as an issue and asks Andrea Lucas to raise it with the board straight away. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a problem with an immediate negative impact is a type of issue that should go to the board.
Yes, because trading lets the blocked story be swapped for another story of similar effort from the backlog.
No, because blockers belong on the team dashboard and are not raised with the project manager as issues.
No, because the team should first swarm on the blocker together, and escalate it if they cannot resolve it.
7.w: Swarming means the team focuses together on a stuck task or blocker. PRINCE2 Agile suggests trying swarming before escalating an issue to the project manager, and escalating further only if needed (book 11.4.2).

n.0: A problem is an issue type, but that does not mean it goes straight to the board; the team should first try to resolve it, and the PM handles issues within tolerance (book 11.3.1, 11.4.2).
n.1: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort to absorb change; it is not a way to remove a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Blockers the team cannot resolve should be escalated to the PM as issues; the point is to swarm first, not to keep them off the PM's desk (book 11.4.2).

7.q: Graham Doyle tells Andrea Lucas that the board expects a monthly written report against a detailed plan, as on previous Draycott projects. Andrea wants to apply the progress practice in an agile way while keeping the board in control. What should she propose?
o: Send the board each team's dashboard every month, so that it can see the detailed status of every team.
Send the board an exception report each month, setting out options and a recommendation for the next month.
A project dashboard with release status, burn charts and current risks and issues, reviewed at progress reviews.
A monthly chart of spend against budget and days used against the end date, to show how much tolerance remains.
7.w: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report: it shows release status, burn charts and current risks and issues, is updated and reviewed in progress review workshops, and the board pulls information from it (Table 12.1, book 12.3.2.1).

n.0: Team dashboards replace checkpoint reports and serve the PM; the board's view is the project dashboard (Table 12.1).
n.1: An exception report is produced when a plan is forecast to exceed tolerance, not as a routine monthly report (Table 12.1).
n.3: With zero tolerance on time and cost, tracking them against tolerance adds little; the main aspect to monitor is what is delivered, through burn charts (book 12.3.1).

7.q: In Stage 4, Dev Patel warns that a component shortage will delay the Factory B sensors by six weeks. The updated burn-up chart now forecasts that the Must have stories for Release 3 cannot all be delivered by month 12, which would exceed the project's scope tolerance. What should Andrea Lucas do NEXT?
o: Move the closure date back by six weeks, as the delay is caused by the supplier rather than by the project.
Record the delay in the daily log and report it on the project dashboard when Stage 4 comes to an end.
Send the board an exception report straight away, recommending that Release 3 be cancelled.
Hold an immediate meeting with the people involved to explore the options, before escalating to the board.
7.w: An updated burn chart can trigger an exception. PRINCE2 Agile advises holding an immediate meeting to discuss options before escalating to the board, which is then done through an exception report with options and a recommendation (Table 12.1).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance and the end date is fixed by the aerospace contract; the PM cannot move it (Table 3.1).
n.1: A forecast breach of tolerance must be acted on now; waiting until the end of the stage removes the board's chance to decide (Table 12.1).
n.2: Escalation comes after options have been explored; jumping straight to a recommendation skips that step (Table 12.1).

7.q: During the busy weeks before Release 1, Andrea Lucas asks the software team whether she may attend some of its daily stand-ups to hear about blockers first hand. The team agrees, and Andrea listens without assigning work, then reads the rest of the status from the team dashboard. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager may attend stand-ups with the team's agreement, and pulls status from the team dashboard.
Yes, because the project manager should attend stand-ups to replace the checkpoint reports the team would send her.
No, because the stand-up is a team event, and the project manager should get status from the team coach's weekly report.
No, because status should come from the project dashboard, which the project manager updates after each progress review.
7.w: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups when the delivery team agrees, and pulls progress information from the team dashboard, which replaces the checkpoint report (Table 12.1).

n.1: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report; stand-ups are the team's own event, which the PM attends by agreement, not as a reporting channel (Table 12.1).
n.2: The PM may attend with the team's agreement, and PRINCE2 Agile uses the team dashboard for team status, not a weekly report from the team coach (Table 12.1).
n.3: The project dashboard serves the board; the PM pulls team-level status from the team dashboards (Table 12.1).

7.q: During starting up, Graham Doyle runs the project canvas workshop with Andrea Lucas, Ruth Kenyon, Colin Ashby and Leanne Park. The dashboard could serve several groups, and the budget will not stretch to serving them all equally well in Release 1. The group discusses whether the maintenance engineers, the machine operators or the production planners should come first, and agrees to prioritize the engineers. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop does this discussion belong?
o: User group definition
Business option selection
Project vision definition
Benefits analysis
7.w: The user group definition topic of the project canvas workshop identifies one to three key user groups and prioritizes them (book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

n.1: Business option selection weighs alternative ways of meeting the need, not which users matter most (Table 13.2).
n.2: Project vision definition sets out the long-term outcomes and aligns the project with business value and sustainability goals (Table 13.2).
n.3: Benefits analysis identifies benefits, dis-benefits and their tolerances, not the ranking of user groups (Table 13.2).

7.q: During Stage 3, the board holds an agile enablement workshop with Graham Doyle, Robert Kale, an agile coach and business representatives from both factories. After reviewing the latest Agilometer, they note a further threat to agile adoption that the Agilometer does not cover: supervisors at Factory B plan to keep calendar maintenance whatever the dashboard shows. Nobody has yet judged how likely or serious this is. Under which topic of the workshop should this threat first be raised?
o: Agilometer assessment review
Risk planning
Risk assessment
Risk identification
7.w: The risk identification topic of the agile enablement workshop captures additional threats and opportunities to agile adoption that the Agilometer does not cover (Table 13.5).

n.0: The Agilometer assessment review links the Agilometer's risk areas to agile values and transformation goals; this threat sits outside the Agilometer (Table 13.5).
n.1: Risk planning sets practical mitigation steps once threats have been identified and assessed (Table 13.5).
n.2: Risk assessment estimates probability and impact and prioritizes threats that have already been identified (Table 13.5).

7.q: In Stage 2, Colin Ashby refuses to release two machines for sensor fitting during a rush order, and Senticore's fitting crew is standing idle at Factory A. The issue is within tolerance, but because it involves production priorities, Andrea Lucas asks the board for guidance. Graham Doyle replies the same day, asking Colin to release the machines on the night shift. Which activity of the 'directing a project' process is being carried out?
o: Authorize a stage or exception plan
Give ongoing direction
Authorize the project
Authorize initiation
7.w: Give ongoing direction is the board's informal guidance at any time, in response to requests for advice, escalated issues, exception reports or the project dashboard (Table 13.4).

n.0: Authorizing a stage or exception plan happens at a stage boundary or after an exception, when the board approves an updated release map (Table 13.4).
n.2: Authorizing the project happens at the end of initiation, when the board approves the PID and commits resources (Table 13.4).
n.3: Authorizing initiation happens after starting up, when the board approves the project brief and the release map for initiation (Table 13.4).

7.q: At the project initiation workshop, Ruth Kenyon, Mei Chen and the team leads discuss what the engineers will expect from every release. They agree the criteria that any piece of Smart Maintenance work must meet before the engineers will accept it as complete, including approval under the aerospace quality system and a successful trial on the shop floor. Under which topic of the project initiation workshop should these criteria be agreed?
o: Project Definition of Ready
Management approaches
Project Definition of Done
Project canvas refinement
7.w: The project Definition of Done topic sets the criteria that work must meet to be acceptable to the users and the chief product owner (book 13.4.4.1, Table 13.7).

n.0: The project Definition of Ready sets the product-wide criteria for starting work, not for accepting it as complete (Table 13.7).
n.1: The management approaches topic co-creates the approaches themselves; completion criteria have their own topic, the project Definition of Done (Table 13.7).
n.3: Project canvas refinement updates the business justification, not the criteria for accepting work (Table 13.7).

7.q: At the project kickoff workshop, the software team and the engineers' trial team meet together for the first time. They want to avoid waiting for answers during sprints, so they agree which decisions they can take themselves, such as the alert threshold for a single machine, and which must go to Ruth Kenyon or Mei Chen. Under which topic of the project kickoff workshop does this agreement belong?
o: Team delegation matrix
Team values and norms
Team skill matrix
Psychological safety
7.w: The team delegation matrix topic of the project kickoff workshop clarifies who decides what, simplifying decisions and empowering self-management (book 13.4.4.2, Table 13.8, 7.4.3).

n.1: Team values and norms build an agile culture and shared expectations of behaviour, not decision rights (Table 13.8).
n.2: The team skill matrix maps skills, gaps and overlaps, not who may take which decisions (Table 13.8, 7.4.1).
n.3: The psychological safety topic assesses whether people feel safe to speak up, not the split of decision authority (Table 13.8).

7.q: At a progress review workshop in Stage 3, the board and several engineers from both factories attend. Stuart Bell shows them how the new alert on machine 14 warned of a spindle bearing failure two days before it happened, walks through the screens he used, and gathers their feedback on whether the alert is ready for wider use. Under which topic of the progress review workshop does this take place?
o: Project highlights
Product demo
Current risks and issues
Welcome
7.w: The product demo topic of the progress review workshop shows completed features and gathers user acceptance and feedback (book 13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

n.0: Project highlights reviews the metrics on the project dashboard rather than demonstrating a working feature (Table 13.10).
n.2: Current risks and issues reviews open risks and issues; Stuart is showing a working feature and seeking acceptance (Table 13.10).
n.3: The welcome opens the workshop and sets its purpose; demonstrations come under the product demo (Table 13.10).

7.q: Release 2 is behind its forecast and the board has asked for a closer watch on the software team. In the middle of a sprint, Andrea Lucas checks the team's updated team dashboard, has an informal conversation with Leanne Park about a new gateway risk, and then updates the release map with actuals and forecasts for the work package. Which activity of the 'controlling a stage' process is she carrying out?
o: Report highlights
Receive completed work package
Authorize a work package
Evaluate work package status
7.w: In evaluate work package status, the PM talks informally with the product owner about issues and risks, pulls progress from the updated team dashboard and updates the release map with actuals, forecasts and adjustments (Table 13.9).

n.0: Report highlights assembles team dashboards and release map changes to update the project dashboard for the board (Table 13.9).
n.1: Receiving a completed work package confirms that the set of user stories was delivered; this work package is still in progress (Table 13.9).
n.2: Authorizing a work package is when the PM co-creates the work package description with the PO and team and authorizes the work (Table 13.9).

7.q: At a team planning workshop, the software team and two engineers look at the story 'As an engineer, I want an alert when bearing vibration rises, so that I can plan a repair'. The story is already near the top of the backlog. They agree testable acceptance criteria, such as the alert threshold and how quickly the alert must appear, and what will count as done. Under which topic of the team planning workshop does this happen?
o: User story refinement
Product backlog refinement
Effort estimation
Iteration planning
7.w: User story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable and agrees what counts as done for each story (book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.1: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes the backlog as a whole, for example with MoSCoW (Table 13.13).
n.2: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's complexity and effort, not its acceptance criteria (Table 13.13).
n.3: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate into a realistic team plan (Table 13.13).

7.q: At a team retrospective after a Release 2 sprint, Tomasz Zielinski asks the software team to look back honestly. The team lists what went wrong: two stories were missed because gateways dropped data, and the security review of a new data connection took longer than planned. The team then discusses what caused each problem, before moving on. Under which topic of the team retrospective does this discussion belong?
o: The learning
The good
The bad
Team building
7.w: The bad covers the issues, risks and challenges of the last iteration and their causes (book 13.6.4.2, Table 13.14).

n.0: The learning turns experience into lessons, improvement suggestions and actions; listing problems and their causes comes under the bad (Table 13.14).
n.1: The good looks at what went well and celebrates it (Table 13.14).
n.3: Team building uses a game or food to strengthen bonds within the team (Table 13.14).

7.q: Release 2 has been accepted and the board has asked for Factory B to be brought up to the same standard. At the release planning workshop before Stage 4, the team leads set an objective to make Factory B as reliable as Factory A, with measurable key results such as every Factory B machine sending data by month 10 and every alert acknowledged within one shift. Under which topic of the release planning workshop does this belong?
o: Release planning
OKR definition
Introduction
Wrap-up
7.w: The OKR definition topic of the release planning workshop defines or updates team objectives and key results; objectives are clear, aspirational goals and key results are specific, measurable outcomes (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16, 12.3.2.3).

n.0: Release planning breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map, rather than setting objectives and key results (Table 13.16).
n.2: The introduction sets out the workshop's purpose and context before the planning work starts (Table 13.16).
n.3: The wrap-up closes the workshop by confirming outcomes and next steps (Table 13.16).

7.q: The final release has been demonstrated and accepted by the engineers. At the project closure workshop, Ruth Kenyon, Leanne Park and Andrea Lucas agree who will support the dashboard after closure, what the maintenance team needs in order to run it day to day, and which actions will track the fall in breakdown costs over the coming year. Under which topic of the project closure workshop does this belong?
o: Final product demo
Project canvas refinement
Progress review
Final handover planning
7.w: Final handover planning in the project closure workshop agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and the actions for benefits realization (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19).

n.0: The final product demo confirms user acceptance and readiness for handover; it does not assign support or benefits actions (Table 13.19).
n.1: Project canvas refinement is a topic of the project initiation workshop, where the business justification is refined; support and benefits actions at closure come under final handover planning (Table 13.7, Table 13.19).
n.2: The progress review topic updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer (Table 13.19).

7.q: Release 1 is due at month 4 and Senticore's sensors have a ten-week lead time. To keep to the date on this large, complex project, Andrea Lucas uses the 'controlling a stage' process during initiation to authorize a work package for ordering and preparing sensors for the ten Release 1 machines, as the board-approved initiation plan allows. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the processes, and why?
o: Yes, because once the project brief is approved the project manager may commit the project's resources.
Yes, because controlling a stage can be used during initiation for large or complex projects like this one.
No, because no work package can be authorized until the board has approved the PID and the project.
No, because initiation must be complete before any spending, so that no expenditure is committed early.
7.w: Controlling a stage is normally first used after the project is authorized, but it can be used during initiation for large or complex projects (book 13.5.1). Here it lets long-lead sensors be ordered in time for Release 1 within the approved initiation plan.

n.0: Committing the project's resources is a board decision in 'authorize the project', not something the PM does after the brief is approved (Table 13.4).
n.2: The book allows controlling a stage, and so work packages, during initiation for large or complex projects (book 13.5.1).
n.3: Initiating avoids committing significant expenditure before the work is understood; it does not forbid a planned, board-approved early order on a complex project (book 13.4.1, 13.5.1).

7.q: In starting up, Graham Doyle passes the mandate to Andrea Lucas and asks her to write the project canvas on her own, saying he will review it once it is finished. Andrea has not yet met Ruth Kenyon or Dev Patel. Is this an appropriate application of the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager prepares the outline business case and the executive approves it later.
Yes, because the project canvas is a one-page artifact that one person can draft quickly from the mandate.
No, because the executive should lead the development of the project canvas from the mandate.
No, because the project canvas is created in initiation, after the board has approved the project brief.
7.w: In 'prepare the outline business case', the executive leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate, while the PM works with the CPO, senior supplier and executive on the project backlog (Table 13.1).

n.0: In PRINCE2 Agile the executive leads the development of the project canvas in starting up; it is not handed to the PM to write alone (Table 13.1).
n.1: Being one page does not change who leads it; the canvas is developed under the executive's lead, normally in a collaborative project canvas workshop (Table 13.1, Table 13.2).
n.3: The project canvas is first developed in starting up and refined into a more detailed canvas in initiation (Table 13.1, Table 13.6).

7.q: At the end of Stage 2, Andrea Lucas holds a release planning workshop with Leanne Park, Ruth Kenyon, Dev Patel and the trial team lead. They review the project canvas, project backlog and release map, break the Release 2 work into user stories and update the release map. Senticore's fitters do not work in sprints but are represented. Which statement BEST assesses Andrea's use of this workshop?
o: It is well tailored: it plans the next stage and aligns all teams, including the supplier, on the release map.
It is well tailored: holding the workshop means the board no longer needs to approve the next stage plan.
It is poorly tailored: release map updates belong in the team planning workshop at the start of each sprint.
It is poorly tailored: Senticore should be left out because its fitters do not plan their work in sprints.
7.w: The release planning workshop at a stage boundary builds shared understanding, aligns the teams with the vision and plans the next stage by reviewing the project canvas, project backlog and release map (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16). Including the supplier helps align the fitting schedule with the release map.

n.1: The workshop prepares the plan, but the board still reviews the stage and approves the next stage plan in directing a project (book 13.7.1, Table 13.4).
n.2: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration in managing product delivery; release map updates for the next stage belong at the stage boundary (Table 13.13, Table 13.16).
n.3: Aligning all teams with the vision is the workshop's purpose; Senticore's fittings drive the release dates even though the fitters do not work in sprints (Table 13.16).

7.q: For Stage 3, Andrea Lucas plans that the agile enablement workshops will be attended by the software team and Tomasz Zielinski, as they have the most agile experience; the board will read the results on the project dashboard. Apart from the software team, nobody at Draycott, including the board, has used agile before. Is this an appropriate application of the 'directing a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the people with the most agile experience give the most accurate Agilometer assessment.
Yes, because the board pulls information from the project dashboard rather than attending workshops.
No, because the Agilometer is assessed once, in the project initiation workshop, and not in later stages.
No, because the workshop is for the board, agile coaches and business representatives to assess agile risks.
7.w: The agile enablement workshop in directing a project is for the project board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives, who regularly reassess the Agilometer and the risks to agile adoption (Table 13.5). With a board new to agile, its own involvement matters most.

n.0: Experience does not make the software team the right audience; the workshop exists so the board and business representatives understand the risks of agile adoption (Table 13.5).
n.1: The board does pull dashboard information, but the agile enablement workshop is a directing workshop that the board itself attends (Table 13.5).
n.2: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop and then reassessed regularly in agile enablement workshops in later stages (Table 13.5, Table 13.7).

7.q: Near the end of Stage 4, Ruth Kenyon's maintenance team is preparing to take over the dashboard as part of normal work, with the software team continuing to improve it. Andrea Lucas is planning the transition to operations. Which plan BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Hand over a full user manual at closure, and ask the engineers to email the software team if they need help.
Keep the project board in place for six months after closure, so that it can approve every change the engineers and the software team ask for.
Hand over the backlog, dashboards and tools, give tailored training and clear procedures, and set up regular feedback loops.
Ask the software team to stop changing the dashboard for a year, so that the engineers can settle into using it.
7.w: Transition to operations should hand over agile artifacts and tools so agile practices continue, provide tailored training and materials, set out explicit operational procedures and escalation paths, and create regular feedback loops such as surveys, retrospectives and check-ins (book 14.2.1).

n.0: A manual alone, with ad hoc email support, lacks tailored training, clear procedures, escalation paths and structured feedback loops (book 14.2.1).
n.1: The project board ends at closure; after the project the dashboard moves into normal business with its own feedback and improvement loops (book 14.2.1, 14.2.2.1).
n.3: Regular feedback loops after transition are meant to drive continued improvement; freezing the product ignores them (book 14.2.1).

7.q: After Release 1, the software team plans to release small dashboard improvements every week and, after closure, to keep improving it as part of normal business. At present each release needs two days of manual testing and a manual installation by IT on the factory servers. Which approach BEST supports continuous agile development and operations?
o: Group the weekly improvements into one large release each quarter, so that manual testing and installation happen less often.
Bring development, testing and IT operations together to automate testing and deployment, so the dashboard is always deployable.
Ask the engineers to test each weekly release on the shop floor during their shifts, so that the two days of manual testing can be dropped.
Hand the dashboard over to IT operations after closure, so that the software team can move on to other work.
7.w: Continuous agile development and operations aims for rapid, automated delivery with minimal manual effort so the product is always deployable. In DevOps, development, testing and operations work closely together, and continuous delivery releases small increments to production with fast feedback (book 14.2.2.2).

n.0: Batching changes into large, infrequent releases is the opposite of continuous delivery's small, frequent increments (book 14.2.2.2).
n.2: User feedback is valuable, but replacing tests with shop-floor trials does not automate delivery or keep the product always deployable (book 14.2.2.2).
n.3: Handing over to a separate operations silo works against DevOps, where development and operations collaborate closely (book 14.2.2.2).

7.q: Draycott has approved an AI assistant for project use. As Senticore's fitters and the engineers' trial team join the project, Andrea Lucas wants to use the assistant to support the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle. Which use of the assistant would do this?
o: Analyse skills and workload data to suggest who could take which role, and flag gaps or overlaps for Andrea to review.
Forecast from velocity and spend data whether the project canvas still shows a viable investment for the board.
Search the lessons logs and retrospective notes of earlier Draycott projects and give each role a prioritized list of relevant lessons.
Decide on Andrea's behalf who should fill each role, so that appointments can be made without any delay.
7.w: AI can support defined roles by analysing data, skills and workload to suggest role assignments and flag gaps or overlaps. It supports, but does not remove, human decision-making (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).

n.1: Forecasting viability supports the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, not defined roles (book 15.4.1).
n.2: Turning lessons into prioritized, role-specific insights supports 'learn from experience', not defined roles (book 15.4.1).
n.3: AI supports human decision-making but does not replace it; appointing people stays with the project's managers (book 15.4.2).

8.q: Three months into Repairs Reimagined, the service design team holds daily stand-ups, keeps a Kanban board and uses agile terms in every meeting. When tenant testing shows that a new phone script confuses callers, the team keeps using the script until Ian Thursby, the repairs director, has reviewed and signed off a change, which takes several weeks. Which statement BEST explains this situation?
o: The team is being agile but is not yet doing agile: it has the right mindset, but it has not adopted enough agile techniques and tools.
The team is both being and doing agile, because its stand-ups and Kanban board show that it inspects and adapts its work.
The team is doing agile but is not yet being agile, because it uses agile practices but is not allowed to adapt its work to feedback.
The team is neither being nor doing agile, because a Kanban board is a flow tool and is not part of agile ways of working.
8.w: Doing agile is the practical use of frameworks, processes, techniques and terms; being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset within appropriate self-management (book 2.3.1). The stand-ups and board show the doing; waiting weeks for a director's sign-off before acting on tenant feedback shows the team is not free to adapt, so it is not yet being agile.

n.0: The team has adopted the techniques (stand-ups, Kanban, agile terms); what it lacks is the freedom to act on feedback, which is the being side (book 2.3.1).
n.1: Inspecting is not enough: the team cannot adapt the script for weeks, so the mindset is not being applied. Ceremonies alone do not show being agile (book 2.3, 2.3.1).
n.3: Kanban is one of the popular agile approaches, using visualisation and limits on work in progress (Glossary), so the team is doing agile.

8.q: In a team retrospective, Raj Malhotra notices that the staff who came from the repairs team talk over the newer contact centre advisers, whose ideas are often dismissed as 'not technical'. Raj introduces a round in which each person speaks in turn, and the team agrees to weigh every suggestion on its merits, whoever makes it. Which key characteristic of the agile mindset is Raj MOST LIKELY strengthening?
o: Respect, which is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness, so that every voice is valued and different perspectives are welcomed.
Empowerment, which gives the team autonomy to manage its own work and to make decisions about the call scripts without seeking approval.
Adaptability, which helps the team to inspect its results and change its ways of working in response to feedback.
Transparency and rich communication, which makes the status of the team's work visible to stakeholders outside the team.
8.w: Respect, as a key characteristic of the agile mindset, rests on empathy and open-mindedness: all voices are valued and diverse perspectives are embraced (book 2.6.2). Raj is making sure the advisers' views count as much as the repairs staff's.

n.1: Empowerment is about autonomy and self-management of the team as a whole; the problem here is that some members' views are dismissed by others (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Adaptability is inspection and adaptation in response to change; Raj is not changing the work in response to results but making sure all members are heard (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Making work status visible to stakeholders is transparency; the issue in the retrospective is how members treat one another's ideas (book 2.6.2).

8.q: During initiation, Deborah Kiely points out that many tenants do not use the internet and some do not read English well. The teams therefore add a phone route into the new reporting service and plan translated text updates, so that what the project delivers meets the needs of all tenants. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Tailor to suit the project, because the teams are adapting the method's processes and artifacts to the project's context.
Ensure continued business justification, because the teams are checking that the investment is still desirable and viable.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the teams are engaging tenants as stakeholders in the project.
Focus on products, because the teams are defining what the outputs must do so that they meet users' needs and expectations.
8.w: Focus on products means delivering well-defined outputs that meet users' expectations, which sets clear expectations and avoids unnecessary work (book 5.2.1.6, Table 5.1). Adding a phone route and translated updates so the service works for all tenants is shaping the products around user needs.

n.0: Tailoring adapts the way the method is applied (frameworks, artifacts, workshops); here the teams are changing what the products must do (book 5.2.1.7).
n.1: Nothing in the situation re-tests whether the project is still worth the investment; the change is to the products' features (book 5.2.1.1).
n.2: This principle is about having the right people in clear roles; the action described changes the outputs so they meet users' needs (book 5.2.1.3).

8.q: Midway through Stage 4, the burn-up chart shows that the teams cannot finish everything planned for Release 3 by month 12. Tenant-chosen appointment slots for all homes are Must haves; video reporting and a live engineer tracker are Could haves. Ian Thursby suggests a two-month extension so that no features are lost. What should Sally Greaves, the project manager, recommend?
o: Agree the two-month extension, because the Must and Could haves together give tenants the full benefit of Release 3.
Keep the month 12 end date and the budget, deliver the Must haves and drop or defer the Could haves that will not fit.
Ask the board for extra budget to add agency contractors to both teams, so that every feature can be finished by month 12.
Re-label some Must haves as Should haves, so that the end date can be met without referring the change to the board.
8.w: By default PRINCE2 Agile allows no tolerance on time or cost at any plan level, fixes scope for Must haves and flexes Should and Could haves (book Table 3.1). The board has also said budget and timescale will not change, so the Could haves give way.

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, and the board has fixed the twelve months; extending to protect Could haves breaks the fixed aspect (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Cost also has zero tolerance, and the £1.3 million is fixed; the aspect to flex is lower-priority scope (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Scope is fixed for Must haves; downgrading them to hit the date would drop essential features and avoid the governance that a change to them needs (book Table 3.1, 11.3.2).

8.q: Joy Ansah's contact centre has high staff turnover, and advisers fear that online reporting will lead to job losses. To prepare them for the new diagnosis guide in Release 2, Joy plans to email every adviser a copy of the guide with a short explanation and then leave them to use it on live calls. Which approach would BEST build the agile maturity needed for this change?
o: Combine training on the guide with on-the-job coaching, set out in a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change.
Send the guide by email as planned, then monitor call handling times so that the advisers who struggle can be identified and replaced.
Train the team leaders in depth and ask them to pass the guide on to their own advisers once the release has gone live.
Delay all training until Release 3, so that advisers learn the whole new service at once when it reaches all homes.
8.w: Under agile maturity, people need both theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching; informing people and leaving them to fend for themselves breeds frustration, demotivation and resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change (book 2.7.3).

n.1: Informing people and leaving them to cope is exactly what undermines the change; it would deepen the advisers' fears (book 2.7.3).
n.2: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why, through training and coaching, not second-hand after go-live (book 2.7.3).
n.3: The guide arrives in Release 2; coaching should be mapped to the stages of the change rather than held back to the end (book 2.7.3).

8.q: At the starting up workshop, Ian Thursby says that organizational change management is unnecessary for Repairs Reimagined: once the portal, scripts and parts list are delivered, advisers and engineers will simply start using them. Sally Greaves disagrees. Which statement BEST explains why OCM matters for this project?
o: OCM takes the place of the project's management approaches, so that the board can direct the change without needing a project canvas.
OCM is needed because the project uses agile delivery, whereas a project delivered in a linear way would not change how people work.
OCM makes sure the Coastline contract is renegotiated first, so that engineers are paid for each new way of working they adopt.
OCM moves the organization from its current to its target state, and evolving the culture stops the new ways of working being rolled back.
8.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current to its target state (book 4.2.1). Delivering products does not change how people work; the change management approach should consider the evolving culture and how to make sure changes are not rolled back after the transformation (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: OCM works alongside the project; the change management approach is one of the management approaches, and business justification is still needed (book 4.2.1, 6.3.1).
n.1: Any project that changes how people work needs its change managed; the delivery method does not remove that need (book 4.2.1).
n.2: Contract terms belong to the commercial management approach; OCM is about moving people from the current to the target state and making the change stick (book 4.2.1, 7.3.2).

8.q: Joy Ansah's advisers fear that online reporting will cost them their jobs, and a staff survey shows that they trust what colleagues tell them far more than messages from managers. Sally Greaves wants a key influencer to help shape how advisers see the change. Which person in the scenario is BEST suited to this, and why?
o: Joy Ansah, because as contact centre manager she has formal authority over the 28 advisers and can instruct them to support it.
Kyle Morgan, because as an experienced adviser and informal leader who trains new starters, his network can shape most advisers' views.
Winston Clarke, because as chair of the tenants' panel he can explain to advisers how much tenants want to report repairs online.
Amara Okeke, because as data and insight analyst she can show advisers the evidence on call waiting times and repair satisfaction.
8.w: Key influencers are people who can shape the perception of the majority and, through their network, most influence adoption of the change (book 4.2.2). Kyle is an informal leader trusted by advisers and trains new starters, so his credibility reaches the affected group.

n.0: The survey shows advisers trust peers more than managers; a key influencer works through network and credibility, not formal authority (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Winston influences tenants, not the advisers whose perception needs shaping; he lacks a network inside the contact centre (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Evidence helps, but a key influencer is someone whose network shapes the majority's view; Amara is a specialist, not a trusted voice among advisers (book 4.2.2).

8.q: Coastline Property Services engineers are trialling the new parts list on the pilot estate. They keep phoning the service design team to ask whether they may add parts to the list, use a different supplier or change appointment lengths, and work stalls while they wait for answers. Frank Tolley says his engineers want to help but are unsure what they are allowed to decide. What should Sally Greaves do?
o: Agree a delegation matrix with Frank Tolley and the team, showing which decisions engineers can make and which need agreement under the contract.
Ask Ian Thursby to instruct Coastline's engineers directly under the repairs contract, so that the association's managers decide each of the questions they raise.
Bring the engineers into the service design team's daily stand-ups, so that the whole team can make each of the decisions they need.
Record each question as an issue in the issue register, so that the project board can decide on each one at its next meeting.
8.w: When teams span organizations, leaders should set clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that makes clear what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3). This lets Coastline's engineers act without waiting while respecting the contract.

n.1: Routing every decision through a director slows the work further and ignores that Coastline's engineers are managed through Coastline; clear boundaries are needed instead (book 4.3.1).
n.2: Daily stand-ups with 90 field engineers are impractical and still leave unclear who decides what; the gap is the lack of agreed decision boundaries (book 4.3.1).
n.3: These are routine operating decisions, not issues for the board; escalating them would stall the trial further (book 4.3.1, 11.3.1).

8.q: The digital team of three works from home most of the week, while the service design team works together in the association's office. The two teams must agree how the portal's online reporting form matches the new phone scripts, and misunderstandings have already caused rework. Which approach to communication is MOST appropriate for this hybrid arrangement?
o: Require the digital team to work in the office every day, so that the two teams can communicate face to face as one co-located team and stop the rework.
Rely on the board's quarterly written reports, which give both teams a single, formal record of decisions about the form and scripts.
Plan it deliberately: agree how information flows and in which formats, hold co-location days for key people and keep some unstructured time.
Let each team communicate in its own way, as remote and co-located teams need the same approach and little extra planning.
8.w: Remote and hybrid working needs a more deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows and in which formats, identifying key relationships, and agreeing structured and unstructured time together; sync co-location days for key people help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3, 4.4).

n.0: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer; the book suggests planned co-location days and deliberate online arrangements (book 4.3.3).
n.1: Periodic reporting is insufficient and far too slow for two teams aligning their work every iteration (book 4.4).
n.3: Remote and hybrid teams need a more deliberate and structured approach than co-located ones, not the same approach (book 4.4).

8.q: The service design team brings together staff from the contact centre, the repairs team and tenant engagement. In the first iterations, members disagree about who can approve changes to call scripts and when a decision must go to the project manager, and some changes are made twice. What should the team do FIRST to address this?
