o: Ask Joy Ansah to approve each script change before it is used, because most of the scripts are used by the advisers in her contact centre.
Complete a team skill matrix, so that the team can see the current and planned skills of each of its members.
Introduce peer-assessed bonus points, so that members are rewarded for behaviour that models the agile values.
Co-decide the team's values and accountabilities, including the limits of its self-management and when a decision must be escalated.
8.w: Building agile teams starts with co-deciding team values and accountabilities, so that members know the boundaries of self-management and when decisions must be escalated (book 4.5). That is exactly the gap causing duplicated changes.

n.0: Adding a manager's approval removes self-management and slows the team; the team needs agreed accountabilities and escalation limits (book 4.5).
n.1: A skill matrix shows capabilities and training needs; it does not settle who decides what or when to escalate (book 4.5, 7.4.1).
n.2: Value-based incentives support motivation, but they do not resolve unclear decision rights and escalation (book 4.5).

8.q: Deborah Kiely asks how the project will decide whether the new online reporting form is acceptable to older tenants and to tenants whose first language is not English, and how that will be measured before the form goes live across all homes. Which practice is designed to answer this question, and why?
o: Business case, because it judges whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable for the association.
Quality, because it documents what users require of the project's products and establishes how those requirements will be met.
Progress, because it compares what has actually been achieved with what was planned and forecasts the project's objectives.
Plans, because it defines which products are needed and who will produce them, how, where, when and at what cost.
8.w: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes the means by which they will be met; it answers what is acceptable to users and how that is measured (book 9.1, 9.3.1).

n.0: The business case practice supports investment decisions; it does not set or check what users will accept from a product (book 6.1).
n.2: Progress tracks achievement against plans and controls exceptions; defining and measuring acceptability to users is quality (book 12.1, 9.1).
n.3: Plans set out what is to be delivered and by what means; the acceptance criteria users require and how they are checked belong to quality (book 8.1, 9.1).

8.q: In the project initiation workshop, the teams plan to write personas for the new repairs service. Deborah Kiely suggests basing them on the association's tenant profile data, with one persona for each age band, ethnic group and household type, which would give 14 personas. How should the personas be developed?
o: Write up to five fictional personas based on tenants' needs, such as reporting by phone, in a cross-functional workshop with the team.
Use the 14 profiles, because personas built on age, ethnic group and household type make sure every group of tenants is represented.
Base each persona on a real member of the tenants' panel, using their name and history, so that the personas are accurate.
Ask Amara Okeke to write the personas from the tenant satisfaction and repairs data on her own, so that they are evidence-based and quick to produce.
8.w: Personas help articulate specific benefits for users. They should be written in a cross-functional workshop with team members, kept fictional, based on user needs rather than demographics, and limited to no more than five for pilots or new products unless agile maturity is high (book 6.4.1).

n.1: Demographics no longer predict shared needs, and 14 personas exceeds the suggested maximum of five for a new service at low agile maturity (book 6.4.1).
n.2: Personas should be fictional; abstraction widens innovation and avoids designing for a few individuals (book 6.4.1).
n.3: Personas are written collaboratively in a cross-functional workshop with team members, not by one analyst (book 6.4.1).

8.q: Margaret Oyelaran is leading the development of the project canvas for Repairs Reimagined. She wants it to show the board's minimum expectation of a measurable fall in second visits, which currently affect 30% of repairs. Where and how should this be shown in the project canvas?
o: In the scope section, as an epic for Release 2 that the diagnosis guide and parts list will deliver.
In the major risks section, as a threat that second visits may not fall if engineers do not use the parts list.
In the costs section, as the saving the board expects to use to fund Release 3 and the AI assistant pilot.
In the benefits section, as an expected, measurable benefit with its current baseline of 30% and a tolerance.
8.w: The project canvas includes a benefits element: expected, measurable benefits with tolerance (book 6.3.2, Table 6.1). A fall in second visits is a measurable improvement the association expects, so it is a benefit, with the minimum the board expects reflected in its tolerance.

n.0: Scope lists the project product and its epics, which are outputs; the fall in second visits is the measurable improvement those outputs should bring (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.1: That threat could be a major risk, but the board's expected improvement itself is a benefit to be measured (book 6.3.2).
n.2: The costs element records the estimated costs of the project; the expected fall in second visits is a benefit (book 6.3.2).

8.q: Amara Okeke and Sally Greaves draft the benefits management approach. To keep the effort small, they plan to measure repair satisfaction and second visits once, at a benefits review six months after the project closes, even though Release 1 goes live on the pilot estate in month 4 and Release 2 in month 8. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because benefits are confirmed mainly after closure, when the products are in operational use and their effects can be measured.
Yes, because the benefits management approach is agreed in initiation and does not need to change while the releases are delivered.
No, because frequent releases are planned so that some benefits arrive early, and reviews should measure them as each release goes live.
No, because benefits should be measured by the project executive in person, rather than by an analyst or the project manager.
8.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases to enable early delivery of benefits, and iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2). With releases in months 4 and 8, reviews should measure satisfaction and second visits as each release goes live, so the board can see whether the minimum improvement is on track.

n.0: Confirming benefits is mostly after closure, but iterative releases realize some benefits during the project; a single post-project review misses the early evidence (book 6.3.1).
n.1: The approach is agreed in initiation, but that does not justify ignoring benefits that the releases deliver during the project (book 6.3.2).
n.3: The benefits management approach sets out responsibilities for measurement; nothing requires the executive to measure benefits in person, so this is not why the plan is weak (book 6.3.2).

8.q: Ian Thursby and Frank Tolley are agreeing how Coastline will take part in the project. They want to record how the pay-per-job contract will support trialling new ways of working in short iterations, the Definition of Done for new engineer procedures, and how Coastline will track and report its part of the work. In which management product should this be recorded?
o: The project management team structure.
The role descriptions.
The commercial management approach.
The benefits management approach.
8.w: The commercial management approach sets out how procurement and contracts will support agile product development, for example costs per iteration, the MVP and tolerances, an agreed Definition of Done and how the supplier tracks and reports (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: The team structure shows who is involved, their relationships and working arrangements such as co-location; contract terms with Coastline go in the commercial management approach (book 7.3.2).
n.1: Role descriptions set out each project role's responsibilities; they do not hold the contractual arrangements with a supplier (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits are measured and reviewed, not how the supplier contract supports iterative work (book 6.3.2).

8.q: At the project kickoff workshop, the service design team needs to see who can facilitate tenant testing, who can write call scripts and who understands repair diagnosis, and where training is needed before Release 2. Which technique should the team use, and where should the result be shown?
o: A team skill matrix, completed by the project manager and shown on the project dashboard.
A team skill matrix, completed together by the team and shown on the team dashboard.
A delegation matrix, completed by the team and shown in the role descriptions.
Delegation poker, played by the team and recorded in its team plan.
8.w: The team skill matrix gives an overview of capabilities, strengths, gaps and development areas, helping assign people and identify training needs. It is completed collaboratively in the project kickoff workshop and, for delivery teams, shown on the team dashboard (book 7.4.1, Table 13.8).

n.0: The matrix is completed collaboratively by the team, and a delivery team's matrix belongs on its team dashboard, not the board-level project dashboard (book 7.4.1).
n.2: A delegation matrix shows who decides what; it does not map skills, gaps and training needs (book 7.4.3).
n.3: Delegation poker defines decision-making levels within a team; mapping skills and training needs is the team skill matrix (book 7.4.2, 7.4.1).

8.q: Halfway through Stage 2, Ian Thursby is unhappy with the service design team's pace. Each Monday he emails individual team members the tasks he wants them to complete that week, bypassing Raj Malhotra, the team's product owner, who agrees the team's work with the project manager. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the repairs director manages the in-house repairs team and can direct the staff who joined from that team.
Yes, because a senior manager may step in to direct the work when a team's pace threatens the stage's tolerances.
No, because the chief product owner should assign each member's tasks, as it is the role that sets the priorities across all the teams.
No, because the product owner holds direct authority over the team, and work reaches it as user stories agreed with the project manager.
8.w: In the PRINCE2 Agile structure the project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, and the product owner is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members; the PM and PO agree work as sets of user stories (book 7.3.1). A director emailing tasks to individuals bypasses this structure and undermines self-management.

n.0: Line management outside the project does not give Ian authority over the delivery team; within the project, work reaches the team through its product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.1: If tolerances are threatened, the project manager deals with it and escalates to the board if needed; a director does not take over the team's work (book 7.3.1, Table 12.1).
n.2: The CPO prioritizes the project backlog across teams; it does not assign individual tasks, and authority over team members sits with the product owner (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).

8.q: Repairs Reimagined needs a chief product owner who will represent tenants as the main user community, own the project backlog and set priorities across the service design and digital teams. Which person in the scenario is BEST suited to the chief product owner role?
o: Deborah Kiely, because she works closely with the tenants' panel and knows tenants' needs well.
Raj Malhotra, because he facilitates the service design team's iterations and prioritizes its work with tenants.
Ellen Price, because she leads the digital team that configures the tenant portal.
Margaret Oyelaran, because she received the mandate and is accountable for performance.
8.w: The CPO represents the user community, owns and refines the project backlog with user input and sets priorities across teams (book Table 7.2). As head of tenant engagement, Deborah works closely with the tenants' panel and understands tenants' needs, and her remit spans both teams.

n.1: Prioritizing one team's work with users is the product owner's role; the CPO sets priorities across all teams (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Ellen leads the digital team's technical work; she does not represent tenants across the whole project (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Accountability for the project and receiving the mandate fit the project executive; the CPO represents users and owns the project backlog (book Table 7.2).

8.q: The board wants someone independent of the project manager to check that the project follows PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, to build governance checks into the iterative delivery, and to advise the board on exception reports and risks. Which person in the scenario is BEST suited to the project assurance role?
o: Amara Okeke, because as data and insight analyst she measures the service's performance and tenant satisfaction.
Sally Greaves, because as project manager she makes sure risks are identified, assessed and controlled.
Dr Laura Benn, because her governance and assurance role lets her monitor independently and advise the board.
Ian Thursby, because as repairs director he manages the Coastline contract and the in-house repairs team.
8.w: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, integrates quality and governance checks into iterative delivery, and advises the board and PM on issues, risks and exception reports (book Table 7.2). Laura's governance and assurance role, reporting to the audit and risk committee, makes her independent of the PM.

n.0: Measuring service performance suits testing or benefits measurement; it is not independent oversight of governance and adherence to the method (book Table 7.2).
n.1: The board wants someone independent of the project manager; Sally cannot assure her own management of the project (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Ian is a senior business manager with a strong interest in the contract outcome, not an independent governance specialist (book Table 7.2).

8.q: The service design team completed 14, 18 and 16 story points in its first three iterations of Stage 3, and about 96 points of its Release 2 work remain. Ellen Price suggests using the digital team's velocity of 24 points per iteration, which would show Release 2 finishing sooner. How many more iterations should Sally Greaves forecast for the service design team's remaining work?
o: Four, based on the digital team's velocity of 24 points per iteration.
Six, based on the team's own average of 16 points per iteration.
About five, based on the team's best iteration so far of 18 points.
Seven, based on the team's first iteration of 14 points.
8.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans empirically: start work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that rate, using the team's own velocity rather than another team's (book 8.3). The team's average is (14 + 18 + 16) / 3 = 16 points, and 96 / 16 = 6 iterations.

n.0: Velocity should come from the team doing the work; another team's rate says nothing about this team's capacity (book 8.3).
n.2: Velocity is the average rate over timeboxes; using the best iteration gives an optimistic forecast (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: A single early iteration is not the team's measured average; the forecast should use 16 points per iteration (book 8.3).

8.q: In initiation, the service design and digital teams have built a story map. Starting from their personas, they listed tenant activities from reporting a repair to confirming it is fixed, ordered them in time and broke them into user stories. Sally Greaves now needs a plan for the project. What should she do NEXT?
o: Create a product breakdown structure from the story map, to act as the formal basis for the project plan and for its releases.
Ask each team to write task-level plans for all of its iterations in Stages 2 to 4 before the project is authorized.
Estimate each user story in hours with Coastline, so that a fixed completion date can be set for every story in Release 3.
Cluster the user stories into releases on a release map, showing dependencies such as the diagnosis guide before appointment slots.
8.w: Turning a story map into a release map clusters stories into releases and defines interdependencies, so releases can be planned accordingly; the release map serves as the project plan (book 8.3.1.1, 8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).

n.0: In PRINCE2 Agile the product breakdown structure is recommended to be replaced by the user story map, so a separate PBS is not needed (book 8.3.1).
n.1: Planning is just in time: task-level plans are made for the next iteration in managing product delivery, not for the whole project in initiation (book 8.3.2).
n.2: Agile estimation is relative (for example story points), and plans fix the timebox rather than a date for each story (book 8.4.3).

8.q: At the end of Stage 2, Sally Greaves prepares for the board's decision on Stage 3. She spends two weeks producing a detailed plan of every task for every iteration of Releases 2 and 3, with each task assigned to a named team member, so that the board can see exactly who will do what until month 12. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the board must see a detailed plan for the whole of the next stage before it can authorize that stage to begin.
Yes, because detailed plans for Releases 2 and 3 help to keep time and cost within their zero tolerances.
No, because task-level planning is for the next iteration, done by the teams; a stage boundary needs a high-level release map.
No, because the chief product owner plans each team member's tasks when it sets the priorities across all of the teams.
8.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans just in time: the stage boundary produces a high-level update of the release map, and task-level planning happens for the next iteration only, by the team in managing product delivery (book 8.3.2, 8.4.4). Planning every task to month 12 wastes effort and removes the teams' self-management.

n.0: The board approves the next stage plan, which in PRINCE2 Agile is the updated release map, not a task-level plan of every iteration (book 8.3.2, 13.7.1).
n.1: Time and cost are protected by flexing what is delivered, not by detailed upfront task plans that will change as the teams learn (book Table 3.1, 8.3).
n.3: The CPO prioritizes the project backlog across teams; the delivery team produces its own team plan when it accepts a work package (book Table 7.2, 8.3.2).

8.q: At the end of an iteration in Stage 2, the digital team reviews the story 'As a tenant, I want to upload a photo of my repair so that the engineer brings the right parts'. Photo upload from smartphones meets the team's Definition of Done, but upload from tablets has not yet been tested with tenants. Ellen Price says the story is 'almost done'. How should the team treat the story?
o: Report it as 90% done on the team dashboard and finish testing the tablet upload early in the next iteration.
Count the whole story as done, because the way most tenants upload photos already meets the Definition of Done.
Split it: count the smartphone part as done and return the tablet part to the product backlog to be reprioritized.
Leave the whole story as not done and carry it into the next iteration without changing its priority.
8.w: The Definition of Done allows only 'done' or 'not done'; there is no 'almost done'. A partly done story is split, with the done part counted and the rest returned to the backlog for reprioritization (book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Percentage-complete reporting is the 'almost done' the Definition of Done rules out; the story should be split (book 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Untested work does not meet the Definition of Done, so the whole story cannot count as done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: The done part should be recognized and the remainder returned to the backlog for reprioritization, rather than carried over as one block (book 9.3.2.2).

8.q: Some appointments are wasted because nobody is at home when the engineer arrives. Ellen Price has two versions of the text message sent the day before an appointment: one gives the engineer's name and arrival window, the other adds a reply option to rearrange. She wants evidence from tenants on the pilot estate about which version reduces missed appointments. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
o: Refactoring, improving the structure of the message while keeping what it does the same.
A/B testing, sending each version to similar groups of tenants and comparing the results.
Technical debt, recording the cost of the weaker version so that it can be removed later.
Test first, writing the message's acceptance criteria before either version is sent.
8.w: A/B testing compares two versions with users to see which performs better (book 9.4.3). Sending each message to comparable groups on the pilot estate and comparing missed appointments gives the evidence Ellen needs.

n.0: Refactoring changes internal structure without changing behaviour; it does not compare two versions with users (book 9.4.1).
n.2: Technical debt describes the consequences of poor design owed as future work; it is not a way of comparing versions with users (book 9.4.2).
n.3: Deciding tests first is useful, but it does not give comparative evidence from tenants on which version works better (book 9.4.3).

8.q: Every new phone script must pass the association's existing compliance review before advisers use it with tenants. In initiation, the service design team decides to keep this review as part of its quality control for scripts instead of designing a new method, and Sally Greaves records the decision in the project initiation documentation. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because an organization's own procedures may be used, and recording this as a tailoring decision in the PID is correct.
Yes, because the compliance review removes the need for a Definition of Done for the service design team's scripts.
No, because the quality management approach must describe agile testing methods rather than existing procedures.
No, because tailoring decisions about quality should be recorded in the quality register rather than in the PID.
8.w: In PRINCE2 Agile, an organization's own design, development and testing procedures may be used instead of the standard quality cycle, and this should be recorded as a tailoring decision in the PID (book 9.3.1). Keeping the compliance review is sensible for scripts used with tenants.

n.1: The review is one quality control activity; the team still needs a Definition of Done to agree when a script is complete (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: The quality management approach records agile ways of working and testing methods, but it may include an organization's own procedures as a tailoring choice (book 9.3.1, 9.3.2).
n.3: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities and their results; tailoring decisions are recorded in the PID (book 9.3.1, 9.3.2).

8.q: The risk management approach for Repairs Reimagined is being updated. In Stage 1, risks were identified only at the monthly board meeting, and several risks that advisers raised in team meetings were never recorded. How should risk identification be built into the service design team's iterations?
o: Hold a separate risk workshop at each stage boundary, where the board identifies the risks for the next release.
Ask project support to identify the risks each month from the team dashboards and add them to the risk register.
Reassess the Agilometer with the board at the end of each iteration, so that the risks to the repairs service are identified there.
Make risk identification a fixed part of each team planning session and retrospective, where risks are gathered and recorded.
8.w: PRINCE2 Agile adapts the five-step risk technique to iterations: identification is a fixed part of every planning session and team or project retrospective, where risks are gathered and documented, while implementing and communicating responses run through the iteration cycles (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.0: Risks can surface at any time; leaving identification to stage boundaries repeats the Stage 1 problem of missed risks (book 10.3.1).
n.1: Project support can help with risk administration, but identification should happen with the team in its planning sessions and retrospectives (book 10.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.2: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, reviewed in initiation and the agile enablement workshop; it is not the tool for identifying all project risks each iteration (book 10.3.2).

8.q: In the project initiation workshop, participants assess the Agilometer. They note that Coastline is paid per job, that any change to how engineers work must be agreed with Coastline, and that the current contract gives engineers no reason to trial new ways of working. Which Agilometer slider is MOST affected by these points?
o: Level of collaboration, covering how closely the customer and the supplier work together on the project.
Ease of communication, covering how easily information passes between all the parties involved.
Advantageous environmental conditions, covering whether the environment, including contracts, supports agile.
Flexibility on what is delivered, covering how comfortable the stakeholders are with flexing the scope.
8.w: The advantageous environmental conditions slider covers whether the overall working environment supports agile, including contracts that do not inhibit agile working (book 10.3.2.2). A pay-per-job contract that discourages trialling new ways of working sits here.

n.0: The points describe how the pay-per-job contract and its terms shape the working environment, not how closely the parties work together; contracts that inhibit agile sit under environmental conditions (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: Nothing in the points concerns how information flows; they concern contract terms (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: This slider is about stakeholders' comfort with prioritizing and flexing scope, not about contracts (book 10.3.2.2).

8.q: In the project initiation workshop, Sally Greaves asks everyone present, including Frank Tolley from Coastline, Winston Clarke from the tenants' panel and members of both teams, to rate the Agilometer sliders anonymously in small groups. She then combines their ratings into one Agilometer for the project. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the Agilometer helps identify agile working risks, and all participants assess it before the views are combined.
Yes, because the Agilometer is a progress tool that shows the board how quickly each of the delivery teams is completing work.
No, because the project manager should rate the Agilometer, as the person who runs the project day to day.
No, because the Agilometer belongs to the agile enablement workshop, so it should not be assessed during the initiation stage.
8.w: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working. In the project initiation workshop all participants assess it, anonymously or in groups, and the results are combined into one project Agilometer (book 10.3.1, 10.3.2, Table 13.7). Including Coastline and tenants gives a fuller view.

n.1: The Agilometer is a risk tool in the risk practice; it does not measure delivery speed (book 10.3.2).
n.2: The book has all participants assess it so that different views are captured; one person's rating would miss them (Table 13.7).
n.3: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop and reassessed in agile enablement workshops in later stages (Table 13.5, Table 13.7).

8.q: During Stage 2, Winston Clarke asks for online reporting in Release 1 to be available in five community languages. The request would add a new Must have epic to the project backlog and would need extra work from the digital team. How should this request be handled?
o: As a request for change: record it in the issue register, assess it and refer it to the board or the delegated change authority.
As a detail change: ask the digital team's product owner to add it to the product backlog and trade out a story of similar effort.
As a problem: ask the digital team to swarm on the translation work until it is finished within the current iteration.
As an exception: prepare an exception report at once, because a new requirement takes the project beyond its scope tolerance.
8.w: A new requirement that changes the project backlog is a change to the project baseline, handled formally and decided by the project board or the person(s) with delegated change authority; it is captured as an issue (request for change) and assessed before the decision (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2, Table 11.1).

n.1: Detail changes do not affect the project backlog; a new Must have epic does, so it needs formal handling (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Swarming helps with a stuck task or blocker; a new requirement is a request for change, not a problem (book 11.3.1, 11.4.2).
n.3: An exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; the request has not yet been assessed or approved (book Table 12.1).

8.q: In Stage 3, tenants testing the diagnosis guide ask for a short question about boiler error codes to be added to the heating section. The request fits within an existing epic and does not change the project backlog. Raj Malhotra, the team's product owner, agrees with the team to swap out a lower-priority story of similar effort so that the iteration's scope does not grow. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because swarming lets the whole team focus together on the new question so that it is finished quickly.
Yes, because trading swaps in work of similar effort, absorbing a detail change at team level with the product owner.
No, because a request from tenant testers is a request for change that the project board has to decide.
No, because trading is a technique for removing blockers, so it is not the way to absorb a new request.
8.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, handled informally at team level (book 11.3.2). Trading or swapping replaces requirements with others of similar effort so that change is absorbed without growing scope, with priorities agreed with the product owner (book 11.4.1).

n.0: Swarming is the team focusing together on a stuck task or blocker; what Raj and the team did is trading (book 11.4.2, 11.4.1).
n.2: Who raises a request does not make it a baseline change; this one does not change the project backlog, so it is a detail change for the team (book 11.3.2).
n.3: Trading absorbs change by swapping work of similar effort; removing blockers is swarming (book 11.4.1, 11.4.2).

8.q: The board, which includes tenant members, is used to receiving quarterly written reports. For Repairs Reimagined, Sally Greaves wants the board to be able to see release status, burn charts and current risks and issues between its meetings, without waiting for a written report. What should she set up?
o: Team dashboards for each team, sent to the board after each iteration so that members can see the detailed tasks.
A project dashboard, updated and reviewed in progress review workshops, from which the board pulls the information it needs.
Fortnightly checkpoint reports from each product owner, combined by project support into a written report sent to the board between meetings.
An end stage report at the end of each iteration, so that the board can decide whether each iteration should continue.
8.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project dashboard replaces the highlight report: it shows release status, burn charts, current risks and issues and other trends, is updated and reviewed in progress review workshops, and the board pulls information from it (book 12.3.2.1, Table 12.1).

n.0: Team dashboards replace checkpoint reports; the project manager pulls from them, and they are too detailed for board-level control (book Table 12.1).
n.2: Checkpoint reports are team-to-PM reports, replaced in PRINCE2 Agile by team dashboards; the board needs the project dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.3: End stage reports belong to stage ends, not iterations, and the board does not authorize individual iterations (book Table 12.1, 13.7.1).

8.q: Because the £1.3 million budget and the twelve-month timescale are both fixed, Sally Greaves proposes that the main progress measure reported to the board each fortnight should be spend against budget and days used against the timescale. She does not plan to report which features or user stories have been delivered until the end of each stage. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because time and cost are the aspects the board has said will not change, so they need the closest fortnightly tracking.
Yes, because reporting delivered features each fortnight would add detail that belongs on the team dashboards.
No, because the reports should be written in the quarterly format that the tenant board members are used to.
No, because with zero tolerance on time and cost, what is delivered is the key aspect, and burn charts suit every level.
8.w: With zero tolerance on time and cost, flexibility in what is delivered is the primary performance aspect of interest, so burn charts suit every level; tracking spend and time against tolerances that are zero adds little (book 12.3.1). The board should see progress in delivered features each period.

n.0: Fixing time and cost is exactly why they are not the useful measure: the aspect that moves is what is delivered (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.1: Team dashboards hold team detail, but the board still needs to see what is being delivered at project level, for example burn-up charts on the project dashboard (book 12.3.1, 12.4.3).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile favours informal, visual reporting such as dashboards and burn charts; the problem is what is measured, not the board's preferred format (book 12.2, 12.3.1).

8.q: In starting up a project, Margaret Oyelaran runs the project canvas workshop. The group agrees that the key users are tenants who report repairs by phone, tenants who will report online and the contact centre advisers who take the reports, and it ranks these three groups in order of priority. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop is this being discussed?
o: User group definition
Persona definition
Benefits analysis
Business value definition
8.w: The user group definition topic of the project canvas workshop identifies one to three key user groups and prioritizes them (book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

n.1: Personas are written in the project initiation workshop and describe fictional users' needs; this group is naming and ranking the key user groups (Table 13.7, 6.4.1).
n.2: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits with tolerances; it does not define who the users are (Table 13.2).
n.3: Business value definition sets out the value the project brings to the organization; identifying and ranking user groups is user group definition (Table 13.2).

8.q: Still in starting up a project, Sally Greaves confirms the project's objectives, scope and exclusions, the fixed budget and end date, the requirement that phone reporting must remain, and the fact that the project depends on the renewal of the Coastline contract at month 12. Which starting up activity is she carrying out?
o: Prepare the outline business case
Select the project approach
Assemble the project brief
Plan the initiation stage
8.w: Assembling the project brief confirms the objectives, outcomes, scope, exclusions, tolerances, constraints, assumptions and dependencies, such as dependencies on other initiatives (book Table 13.1).

n.0: This activity develops the project canvas from the mandate, led by the executive, and creates the project backlog; Sally is confirming objectives, constraints and dependencies (Table 13.1).
n.1: Selecting the project approach evaluates delivery solutions and determines how the work will be done; it does not confirm scope, constraints and dependencies (Table 13.1).
n.3: Planning the initiation stage sets out the time, cost, release map and controls for initiation itself (Table 13.1).

8.q: During Stage 2, the board, an external agile coach and business representatives meet for the agile enablement workshop. After reviewing the latest Agilometer, Joy Ansah raises a threat that it does not cover: high turnover in the contact centre means advisers trained in the new ways of working may leave before Release 3. Under which topic of the workshop should this threat FIRST be discussed?
o: Agilometer assessment review
Risk assessment
Risk planning
Risk identification
8.w: In the agile enablement workshop, the risk identification topic captures additional threats and opportunities to agile adoption that the Agilometer does not cover; assessment and planning of responses follow (book Table 13.5).

n.0: That topic reviews the Agilometer itself and links its risk areas to agile values; Joy's threat is outside the Agilometer (Table 13.5).
n.1: Risk assessment estimates the probability and impact of risks that have already been identified; the threat must first be identified (Table 13.5).
n.2: Risk planning agrees practical mitigation steps after risks are identified and assessed (Table 13.5).

8.q: Midway through Stage 3, Frank Tolley says Coastline will not trial the new parts list on more estates unless trial jobs are paid at a higher rate. The stage is still forecast to finish within tolerance, but Sally Greaves escalates the issue to the board for advice. Margaret Oyelaran replies the same day with guidance. Which directing a project activity is this?
o: Authorize a stage or exception plan
Give ongoing direction
Authorize the project
Authorize initiation
8.w: Give ongoing direction covers the board's informal guidance at any time, in response to business advice, informal requests and escalated issues (book Table 13.4). No exception has arisen and no stage decision is being made.

n.0: That activity reviews the project dashboard and approves an updated release map at a stage end or after an exception; neither applies here (Table 13.4).
n.2: Authorizing the project approves the PID and commits resources at the end of initiation, not mid-stage advice (Table 13.4).
n.3: Authorizing initiation approves the project brief and the release map for initiation before the project starts (Table 13.4).

8.q: In the project initiation workshop, both teams and Deborah Kiely agree criteria that any piece of work must meet before either team starts it: the tenant need is clear, any effect on Coastline's engineers has been checked, and the acceptance criteria can be tested. Under which topic of the workshop does this belong?
o: Project Definition of Ready
Project Definition of Done
Management approaches
High-level release planning
8.w: The project Definition of Ready topic of the project initiation workshop sets product-overarching criteria that work must meet before it starts (book Table 13.7, 9.3.2.1).

n.1: The project Definition of Done sets criteria for work to be acceptable to users and the CPO when complete, not before it starts (Table 13.7, 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Management approaches are co-created there too, but criteria for starting work belong under the project Definition of Ready topic (Table 13.7).
n.3: Release planning develops or updates the release map; it does not set entry criteria for work (Table 13.7).

8.q: At the project kickoff workshop, several advisers on the service design team seem uneasy, and one says privately that she is afraid to admit mistakes in case her job is cut. Before the team agrees its values, Raj Malhotra runs a short anonymous check of how safe people feel to speak up and take risks. Which topic of the kickoff workshop is Raj covering?
o: Team values and norms
Icebreaker, project intro and team intro
Team delegation matrix
Psychological safety
8.w: The project kickoff workshop includes a psychological safety topic, assessing whether people feel safe to speak up, take risks and challenge ideas (book Table 13.8, 2.7.4).

n.0: Values and norms come next in Raj's plan; the anonymous check of how safe people feel is the psychological safety topic (Table 13.8).
n.1: These build familiarity and connections; they do not assess whether people feel safe to speak up (Table 13.8).
n.2: The delegation matrix clarifies who decides what to support self-management; it does not measure how safe people feel (Table 13.8, 7.4.3).

8.q: In Stage 2, Sally Greaves has an informal conversation with the digital team's product owner about risks to the photo upload feature, pulls the team's latest progress from its team dashboard and updates the release map with actuals and a revised forecast. Which controlling a stage activity is she carrying out?
o: Evaluate stage status
Report highlights
Evaluate work package status
Receive completed work package
8.w: Evaluating work package status involves informal conversations with the product owner on issues and risks, pulling progress from the updated team dashboard and updating the release map with actuals and forecasts (book Table 13.9).

n.0: Evaluating stage status reviews the progress of the whole stage in a progress review and decides on actions; Sally is checking one team's work package (Table 13.9).
n.1: Reporting highlights assembles team dashboards and log and release map changes to update the project dashboard for the board (Table 13.9).
n.3: This confirms that the set of user stories has been delivered; the photo upload work is still in progress (Table 13.9).

8.q: At the progress review workshop near the end of Stage 2, tenants from the pilot estate try the new online reporting form and the text updates, say what works for them and what does not, and confirm which features they accept. Under which topic of the progress review workshop does this take place?
o: Project highlights
Product demo
Current risks and issues
Final product demo
8.w: The product demo topic of the progress review workshop shows completed features and gathers user acceptance and feedback (book 13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

n.0: Project highlights reviews the project dashboard metrics; tenants trying the features and giving feedback is the product demo (Table 13.10).
n.2: This topic covers open risks and issues, not users trying and accepting completed features (Table 13.10).
n.3: The final product demo is a topic of the project closure workshop at the end of the project, not of a progress review (Table 13.19).

8.q: At the team planning workshop, the service design team works through the stories it may take on next. For the story about a new damp and mould question in the diagnosis guide, members agree that its acceptance criteria are vague and rewrite them so that tenant testing can show clearly whether it is done. Under which topic is the team working?
o: User story refinement
Product backlog refinement
Effort estimation
Iteration planning
8.w: User story refinement in the team planning workshop makes acceptance criteria clear and testable and agrees what counts as done (book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.1: Backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes the backlog, for example with MoSCoW; sharpening one story's acceptance criteria is user story refinement (Table 13.13).
n.2: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's size; the team is rewriting acceptance criteria, not estimating (Table 13.13).
n.3: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate into a realistic team plan; it comes after stories are refined (Table 13.13).

8.q: In managing a stage boundary, the teams meet for the release planning workshop before Stage 3. They agree an objective of getting repairs right first time, with key results such as cutting second visits on the pilot estate from 30% to 20% by month 8. Under which topic of the workshop is this agreed?
o: Release planning
Introduction
Project canvas refinement
OKR definition
8.w: The release planning workshop includes an OKR definition topic, where team objectives and key results are defined or updated; objectives are aspirational goals and key results are measurable outcomes (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16, 12.3.2.3).

n.0: Release planning breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map; setting objectives and key results is OKR definition (Table 13.16).
n.1: The introduction sets the scene for the workshop; it does not define objectives and key results (Table 13.16).
n.2: Project canvas refinement is a topic of the project initiation workshop, not the release planning workshop (Table 13.7).

8.q: In the project closure workshop at month 12, Sally Greaves, Joy Ansah, Ian Thursby and Ellen Price agree who will support the new repairs service after the project, what the contact centre and repairs team need in order to run it as normal business, and which actions will track the benefits. Under which topic of the workshop is this being agreed?
o: Final product demo
Current risks and issues
Final handover planning
Progress review
8.w: Final handover planning in the project closure workshop agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and benefits actions for handover (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19).

n.0: The final product demo confirms user acceptance and readiness for handover by showing the product; it does not assign support responsibilities (Table 13.19).
n.1: Current risks and issues is a topic of the progress review workshop in controlling a stage; it reviews open risks and issues rather than planning support after the project (Table 13.10).
n.3: The progress review topic updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer (Table 13.19).

8.q: Before the project kickoff workshop, Sally Greaves designs a team dashboard template with fixed charts and columns. At the workshop she tells the service design and digital teams to use it unchanged, so that all reporting looks the same, and moves on to the next topic. Is this an appropriate application of the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because one template makes it easier for the project manager to pull progress from the teams' dashboards.
Yes, because the project dashboard is created in the kickoff workshop, so the team dashboards should match it.
No, because team dashboards are created at a stage boundary, in the release planning workshop for Stage 2.
No, because team dashboards should be co-created by each team in the workshop to support self-management.
8.w: The project kickoff workshop aims to build an agile culture of openness and self-management; team dashboards are co-created by each team there, not dictated (book Table 13.8). Imposing a fixed template works against that purpose.

n.0: The project manager does pull from team dashboards, but convenience for the PM does not outweigh the teams co-creating them (Table 13.8, Table 12.1).
n.1: The project dashboard is created in the kickoff workshop, but that does not mean team dashboards should be dictated to match it (Table 13.8).
n.2: Team dashboards are a topic of the project kickoff workshop in initiation, not of the release planning workshop (Table 13.8, Table 13.16).

8.q: At the end of Stage 2, Sally Greaves updates the release map for Stage 3 using what was learned in the pilot, updates the project canvas with early results on repair satisfaction, and presents both with the project dashboard. The board reviews them and approves Stage 3. Is this an appropriate application of the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
o: Yes, because a stage boundary is where the teams write task-level plans for every iteration of the next stage.
Yes, because the board needs the updated release map and canvas to review the stage and confirm continued justification.
No, because the release map is updated in the team planning workshop, rather than at the end of a stage.
No, because the project canvas is fixed once the project is authorized and should not change at a stage boundary.
8.w: Managing a stage boundary gives the board enough information to review the current stage, approve the next stage plan (the updated release map) and confirm continued business justification, which in PRINCE2 Agile means the updated project canvas (book 13.7.1).

n.0: Task-level plans are made by teams for the next iteration in managing product delivery; the stage boundary updates the high-level release map (book 8.3.2).
n.2: Team planning workshops produce team plans for the next iteration; the release map for the next stage is updated at the stage boundary (book 13.7.1, Table 13.16).
n.3: The project canvas is kept up to date so that continued business justification can be confirmed at each stage boundary (book 13.7.1).

8.q: Sally Greaves runs the agile enablement workshop for Stage 3 with members of the service design and digital teams. The board members do not attend, as they prefer to read a summary later. The teams review the Agilometer and agree actions on the agile risks they identify. What is the MOST significant weakness in how this workshop is being run?
o: The board is absent, yet the workshop is for the board, agile coaches and business representatives to assess agile risks and maturity.
The Agilometer should not be reviewed after initiation, as the risks of agile working are set at the start of the project.
The workshop should produce the agile transformation plan, which the teams have not been asked to write.
The teams should estimate the effort of their Stage 3 stories in the workshop, so that the board's summary includes a forecast for Release 2.
8.w: The agile enablement workshop sits in directing a project. It brings together the project board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives so that agile maturity and agile risks are assessed regularly through the Agilometer (book Table 13.5). Running it without the board defeats its purpose.

n.1: The agile enablement workshop exists to reassess the Agilometer regularly in initiation and later stages (Table 13.5).
n.2: The agile transformation plan is considered in the project initiation workshop, not the agile enablement workshop (Table 13.7, 2.7.1).
n.3: Effort estimation is a team planning workshop topic in managing product delivery, not part of agile enablement (Table 13.13).

8.q: Near month 12, Sally Greaves proposes to save time by leaving the final product demo out of the project closure workshop. Instead she plans to send the end project report to the repairs team and the contact centre, noting that they have seen the project dashboard throughout. What is the MOST significant weakness in this tailoring?
o: The project dashboard would be out of date, because it is updated when a product demo takes place.
The lessons report could not be written, because lessons are gathered during the final product demo.
Users would lose the chance to confirm that the final service meets their requirements and is ready for handover.
Benefits could not be measured, because the final product demo is where the benefits review of the fall in second visits takes place.
8.w: The final product demo in the project closure workshop lets users accept the final product and confirms it meets requirements and is ready for handover, which is central to the workshop's purpose of formally concluding the project (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19). A report and dashboards do not replace users confirming acceptance.

n.0: The project dashboard is updated in progress reviews, including the closure workshop's progress review topic; that is not the main loss here (Table 13.19).
n.1: Lessons are gathered under the project lessons and lessons report topics, not the product demo (Table 13.19).
n.3: Benefits reviews are planned in the benefits management approach and largely happen after closure; the demo is about user acceptance (book 6.3.1, Table 13.19).

8.q: As Repairs Reimagined nears closure, the repairs team and the contact centre prepare to run the new repairs service as normal business. Ian Thursby suggests handing over the final scripts and portal settings and switching off the project's boards and dashboards. Which approach BEST supports the transition to operations?
o: Hand over the final scripts and portal settings as Ian suggests, as operational teams set their own ways of working.
Hand over the agile artifacts and tools, with tailored training, clear procedures and escalation routes, and regular feedback loops.
Keep the project open until advisers and engineers have used the new service for a year, so the project team can support them.
Ask the digital team to run the whole repairs service, as it will continue to improve the portal after the project ends.
8.w: Transition to operations should hand over agile artifacts and tools so agile practices continue, provide tailored training and guides, set out explicit operational procedures and escalation pathways, and keep regular feedback loops such as surveys and retrospectives (book 14.2.1).

n.0: Handing over products without the artifacts, training, procedures and feedback loops risks the new ways of working being lost (book 14.2.1).
n.2: The project is temporary and has a fixed end at month 12; support continues through operational arrangements agreed at handover (book 14.2.1, 1.3.1).
n.3: The scenario says the repairs team and contact centre will run the service; the digital team's continuing role is improving the portal (book 14.2.1).

8.q: After the project closes, Ellen Price's digital team will keep improving the tenant portal. Tenants are already asking for new features, such as tracking the engineer's arrival on a map. Ian Thursby suggests starting a new PRINCE2 Agile project for each enhancement. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Start a separate project for each enhancement, so that each one has its own business case, project board, release map and closure.
Freeze the portal after closure and collect the requests for a single large upgrade project in two years' time.
Pass the requests to Coastline, as its engineers will be the main users of any arrival-tracking feature.
Manage the portal as a product, with a flexible roadmap and short cycles prioritized by value and tenant feedback.
8.w: Agile product management uses a high-level product vision with a flexible roadmap continually adjusted from feedback, and short cycles prioritized by business value and feedback; enhancements after a project are handled through product management iterations rather than a new project each time (book 14.2.2.1).

n.0: A project for every small enhancement adds needless overhead; ongoing improvements fit agile product management (book 14.2.2.1).
n.1: Agile product management keeps adjusting the product in short cycles from feedback rather than batching changes for years (book 14.2.2.1).
n.2: The feature serves tenants, and the scenario gives the digital team the role of improving the portal after the project (book 14.2.2.1).

8.q: The digital team wants to pilot an AI assistant on the tenant portal that suggests the likely repair type from a tenant's description and photo. The tenants' panel asks for it to be tested with older tenants and with tenants whose first language is not English. Which statement BEST describes how AI should support PRINCE2 Agile on this project?
o: AI can draft suggestions and speed diagnosis, but people keep the decisions and still need to engage tenants and stakeholders.
AI can take over the contact centre's diagnosis once its suggestions are accurate, so phone reporting can be withdrawn.
AI can set the project's priorities from tenant data, so the chief product owner no longer needs to consult tenants.

8.w: AI can support principles, people and practices, for example by automating information collection or helping define products, but it does not remove human decision-making or the need to communicate with stakeholders (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).

n.1: AI supports rather than replaces human judgement, and phone reporting must remain for tenants who do not use the internet (book 15.4.2).
n.2: AI can help prioritize backlogs, but people decide and the CPO still engages users; AI does not remove the need to communicate (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile describes how AI can support its principles, people and practices, so the pilot is managed within the project (book 15.4).
